lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • 10 cm equals 100 mm, because 1 cm = 10 mm.
  • A micrometer (screw gauge) measures length, and a vernier caliper best measures the internal diameter of a pipe.
  • Prefix order for large multiples: mega < giga < peta < exa, with exa the largest of those listed; atto is the smallest prefix among atto, pico, nano and femto.
  • 6 x 10^2 shows one significant digit, while 900.8 shows four significant digits.
  • 9.460 x 10^15 m has four significant figures, the digits 9, 4, 6 and 0.
  • 0.2 mm = 0.0002 m = 2 x 10^-4 m.
  • KITAB UL MANAZIR was written by Ibnal Haitham.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Multiple Choice Questions

Q: 1. How many millimeters are there in 10 cm?

Options: (a) 100 mm (b) 200 mm (c) 50 mm (d) 10 mm

Correct answer: 100 mm

Q: 2. Which of the following quantity can be measured using a micrometer?

Options: (a) current (b) force (c) length (d) mass

Correct answer: length

Q: 3. The instrument best measures the internal diameter of a pipe is

Options: (a) screw gauge (b) vernier caliper (c) meter rule (d) measuring tape

Correct answer: vernier caliper

Q: 4. Which prefix represents a largest value?

Options: (a) mega (b) giga (c) peta (d) exa

Correct answer: exa

Q: 5. Which of the following is the smallest prefix?

Options: (a) atto (b) pico (c) nano (d) femto

Correct answer: atto

Q: 6. Which of the following numbers shows one significant digit?

Options: (a) 1.1 (b) 6.0 (c) 7.1 (d) 6 x 10^2

Correct answer: 6 x 10^2

Q: 7. Which of the following numbers shows 4 significant digits?

Options: (a) 900.8 (b) 4 (c) 5174.00 (d) 0.0002

Correct answer: 900.8

Q: 8. A light year is distance traveled by light in one year. It travels about 9.460 x 10^15 m. How many significant figures are in this number

Options: (a) 6 (b) 2 (c) 3 (d) 4

Correct answer: 4

Q: 9. 0.2 mm in units of meters is

Options: (a) 0.0002 m (b) 2 x 10^-4 m (c) none (d) both A and B

Correct answer: both A and B

Q: 10. KITAB UL MANAZIR is the name of book written by

Options: (a) Yaqub Kindi (b) Ibnal Haitham (c) Al Beruni (d) none

Correct answer: Ibnal Haitham

mcqs.q: How many millimeters are there in 10 cm?
mcqs.why: Working: 1 cm = 10 mm, so 10 cm = 10 x 10 mm = 100 mm. The book marks 100 mm as correct.

mcqs.q: Which of the following quantity can be measured using a micrometer?
mcqs.why: A micrometer (screw gauge) is a length-measuring instrument for very small thicknesses and diameters, so it measures length, not current, force or mass.

mcqs.q: The instrument best measures the internal diameter of a pipe is
mcqs.why: A vernier caliper has inside jaws made for internal measures such as the internal diameter of a pipe or hollow cylinder, so it is the best instrument here.

mcqs.q: Which prefix represents a largest value?
mcqs.why: The multiples increase as mega = 10^6, giga = 10^9, peta = 10^15 and exa = 10^18, so exa represents the largest value of the four.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the smallest prefix?
mcqs.why: Atto = 10^-18 is smaller than femto = 10^-15, pico = 10^-12 and nano = 10^-9, so atto is the smallest prefix listed.

mcqs.q: Which of the following numbers shows one significant digit?
mcqs.why: In scientific notation all figures other than the power of ten are significant; 6 x 10^2 has only the single digit 6, while the others each have two significant digits.

mcqs.q: Which of the following numbers shows 4 significant digits?
mcqs.why: 900.8 contains the digits 9, 0, 0 and 8, and zeros between significant digits are significant, giving four significant digits in total.

mcqs.q: A light year is distance traveled by light in one year. It travels about 9.460 x 10^15 m. How many significant figures are in this number
mcqs.why: In scientific notation only the mantissa counts: 9.460 has the four digits 9, 4, 6 and 0, and the trailing zero after the decimal point is significant, so there are 4 significant figures.

mcqs.q: 0.2 mm in units of meters is
mcqs.why: Working: 0.2 mm = 0.2 x 10^-3 m = 0.0002 m, and 0.0002 written in standard form is 2 x 10^-4 m, so both forms are the same value.

mcqs.q: KITAB UL MANAZIR is the name of book written by
mcqs.why: The source marks Ibnal Haitham as the author of KITAB UL MANAZIR, the book on optics, rather than Yaqub Kindi or Al Beruni.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Physics principles shape technology: optics and electromagnetism give CT scan, MRI, PET imaging and laser surgery; electronics gives mobile phones and hologram technology.
  • Physics links with biology: the eye works as an optical instrument, bones and muscles work as levers, and blood circulation follows the physics of fluids.
  • Measurement is a comparison between an unknown quantity and a chosen standard (unit).
  • Area is a derived quantity because area = length x length, and its unit m^2 is derived from the base unit metre.
  • Derived units in base units: force newton N = kg m/s^2, pressure pascal Pa = kg m^-1 s^-2, energy joule J = kg m^2/s^2, density = kg/m^3.
  • Scientific notation writes a number as a mantissa (greater than 1 and less than 10) times a power of 10, e.g. Moon mass about 7 x 10^22 kg and nucleus diameter about 1 x 10^-14 m.
  • Least count is the minimum value an instrument can measure: vernier callipers 1 mm / 10 = 0.1 mm (0.01 cm); screw gauge example 0.5 mm / 50 = 0.01 mm.
  • Volume of a small pebble with a measuring cylinder = second water reading minus first water reading, the volume of water displaced.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Conceptual Questions

Q: 1. How technology is shaped by physics?

Ans: Physics is concerned with gathering and organizing knowledge, while technology lets humans use that knowledge for practical purposes. Every technology stands on a physics principle first discovered by physicists: the principles of optics and electromagnetism give us CT scan, MRI, PET imaging and laser surgery in medicine, and electronics gives us mobile phones and hologram technology in communication. Aeroplane pilots likewise depend on a large number of measuring and information instruments built on physics. So as physics discovers new principles, new technology is shaped from them, and physics therefore plays a key role in the progress of humankind and in improving the quality of living.

Q: 2. Physics and biology are considered different branches of science, how physics links with biology?

Ans: Physics is at the root of every field of science, including biology. Living bodies obey physical laws: the eye works as an optical instrument, bones and muscles work as levers, and blood circulation follows the physics of fluids. The book's own table lists Biophysics and Medical Physics as a branch of physics, dealing with the physical interactions of biological processes and the application of physics to prevention, diagnosis and treatment, for example MRI, CT scan, radiotracers and conduction in living cells. Microscopes, X-rays and other instruments of physics are also the basic tools with which biologists study living things, so physics and biology are closely linked.

Q: 3. Why are measurements important?

Ans: Science is based on physical quantities, and a physical quantity is known only when it is measured. Measurement is a comparison between an unknown quantity and a chosen standard (unit), which tells us how many times as big the quantity is. Without measurement we cannot describe nature exactly, results obtained by one person cannot be checked or reproduced by another, and no accurate work is possible in the laboratory, in engineering, in medicine or in daily life, for example the tailor must take the required measurements before sewing our clothes. Measurements with standard SI units also make results understandable all over the world.

Q: 4. Why area is a derived quantity?

Ans: A derived quantity is one that is defined in terms of base quantities. Area is not chosen as an independent base quantity; it is obtained from the base quantity length multiplied by itself, area = length x length. Its unit, the square metre (m^2), is likewise derived from the base unit metre. Hence area is a derived quantity.

Q: 5. Name any four derived units and write them as their base units?

Ans: Four derived units expressed in base units are: (1) Force, newton (N) = kg m/s^2. (2) Pressure, pascal (Pa) = kg/(m s^2), i.e. kg m^-1 s^-2. (3) Energy, joule (J) = kg m^2/s^2. (4) Density, kilogram per cubic metre = kg/m^3. In the same way velocity has the derived unit m/s and acceleration m/s^2, all built only from the base units kilogram, metre and second.

Q: 6. Why in physics we need to write in scientific notation?

Ans: In physics we deal with numbers that are either very small or very large, such as the mass of the Moon, about 7 x 10^22 kg, and the diameter of an atomic nucleus, about 1 x 10^-14 m. Writing such numbers in full is lengthy, hard to read and invites mistakes in counting zeros. Scientific notation writes a number compactly as a mantissa (greater than 1 and less than 10) times a power of 10. It makes very large and very small measurements easy to write, read, compare and use in calculations, and it shows the significant figures clearly.

Q: 7. What is least count? How least count for vernier calliper and screw gauge are defined?

Ans: Least count is the minimum value that can be measured on the scale of a measuring instrument. For vernier callipers, the least count (vernier constant) is the difference between one main scale division and one vernier scale division; it is also found as: Least count = smallest division on main scale / total number of divisions on vernier scale = 1 mm / 10 = 0.1 mm (0.01 cm). For a screw gauge, the least count is found by dividing its pitch by the total number of divisions on the circular scale: Least count = pitch of screw gauge / total divisions on circular scale, for example 0.5 mm / 50 = 0.01 mm.

Q: 8. How can we find the volume of a small pebble with the help of measuring cylinder?

Ans: Pour water into a measuring cylinder until it is about half full and note the volume; this is the first reading. Then lower the small pebble (an irregular solid) gently into the water until it is completely immersed, and note the new level; this is the second reading. The volume of the pebble is the difference of the two readings, second reading minus first reading, because the rise in water level is exactly the volume of water displaced by the pebble, as shown for the key in Figure 1.5 of the unit.

mcqs.q: According to the solved answer, the principles behind CT scan, MRI, PET imaging and laser surgery in medicine come mainly from which areas of physics?
mcqs.why: The solved answer states that the principles of optics and electromagnetism give us CT scan, MRI, PET imaging and laser surgery in medicine.

mcqs.q: How does physics link with biology in the working of the human eye?
options: The eye works as a lever
The eye works as an optical instrument
The eye follows the physics of fluids
The eye works as a measuring cylinder
mcqs.why: The solved answer says living bodies obey physical laws: the eye works as an optical instrument, bones and muscles work as levers, and blood circulation follows the physics of fluids.

mcqs.q: Measurement is best defined as a comparison between what?
options: An unknown quantity and a chosen standard (unit)
A quantity and its significant figures
A base quantity and a derived quantity
mcqs.why: The solved answer defines measurement as a comparison between an unknown quantity and a chosen standard (unit), which tells us how many times as big the quantity is.

mcqs.q: Why is area a derived quantity?
options: Because area is chosen as a base quantity
Because area = length x length, built from the base quantity length
Because area is measured with a vernier caliper
mcqs.why: Area is not an independent base quantity; it is obtained from the base quantity length multiplied by itself, area = length x length, and its unit m^2 is derived from the metre.

mcqs.q: The derived unit of force, the newton (N), expressed in base units is
mcqs.why: The solved answer lists force, newton (N) = kg m/s^2, built only from the base units kilogram, metre and second.

mcqs.q: The derived unit of pressure, the pascal (Pa), expressed in base units is
mcqs.why: The solved answer lists pressure, pascal (Pa) = kg/(m s^2), which is written with indices as kg m^-1 s^-2, using only kilogram, metre and second.

mcqs.q: In scientific notation, the mantissa (M) in N = M x 10^exponent must be
mcqs.why: Scientific notation writes a number compactly as a mantissa greater than 1 and less than 10 times a power of 10, as used for the Moon mass about 7 x 10^22 kg.

mcqs.q: Least count of a measuring instrument is
options: The largest value it can measure
The minimum value that can be measured on its scale
The zero error of the instrument
mcqs.why: By definition the least count is the minimum value that can be measured on the scale of a measuring instrument; a smaller least count means finer measurement.

mcqs.q: What is the least count of vernier callipers whose smallest main scale division is 1 mm with 10 vernier divisions?
mcqs.why: Formula: least count = smallest division on main scale / total divisions on vernier scale. Substitution: 1 mm / 10 = 0.1 mm, which is 0.01 cm, so the least count is 0.1 mm.

mcqs.q: The volume of a small pebble found with a measuring cylinder equals
mcqs.why: The pebble is lowered until completely immersed; the rise in water level is the volume of water displaced, so pebble volume = second reading - first reading.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Physics is the branch of science that studies the physical universe: energy, matter, and how they are related.
  • SI has seven base quantities: length metre (m), mass kilogram (kg), time second (s), electric current ampere (A), temperature kelvin (K), amount of substance mole (mol), luminous intensity candela (cd).
  • Base quantities are the minimum selected quantities in terms of which all others are expressed; derived quantities such as area, volume, velocity, acceleration, density and force are defined in terms of base quantities.
  • Standard form: number N = mantissa M x 10^exponent; Earth-Moon distance 384,400,000 m = 3.844 x 10^8 m and hydrogen bond length 0.000000000074 m = 7.4 x 10^-11 m.
  • Prefixes: kilo (k) = 10^3, mega (M) = 10^6, giga (G) = 10^9, milli (m) = 10^-3, centi (c) = 10^-2, micro = 10^-6, nano (n) = 10^-9, pico (p) = 10^-12, femto (f) = 10^-15, peta (P) = 10^15, exa (E) = 10^18.
  • Vernier calipers measure up to 0.1 mm or 0.01 cm; example diameter = 1.9 cm + 6 x 0.01 cm = 1.96 cm.
  • Screw gauge least count = pitch / divisions on circular scale, e.g. 0.5 mm / 50 = 0.01 mm; example sphere diameter = 5.5 mm + 28 x 0.01 mm = 5.78 mm.
  • Significant figures are the accurately known figures plus the first doubtful figure; zeros to the left of significant figures are not significant, so 0.00467 has 3, and 9.11 x 10^-31 kg has three.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Comprehensive Questions

Q: 1. Define physics. How physics play a crucial role in science technology and society?

Ans: Physics is the branch of science that involves the study of the physical universe: energy, matter, and how they are related. It tries to answer the fundamental questions of how and why things happen, from the smallest sub-atomic particles to the largest galaxies. Its role is crucial: in science, physics is at the root of every field, and most major developments in chemistry, biology, geology, agriculture, environmental science, astronomy, engineering and medicine have been made by physicists. In technology, physics provides the basic understanding for developing new instrumentation and devices, such as CT scan, MRI and laser surgery. In society, physics-based technology, for example information technology and mobile phones, has improved the standard of communication and the quality of living of humankind.

Q: 2. What is SI? Name SI base quantities and their units.

Ans: SI is the International System of Units (from the French Systeme International d'Unites), a complete and internationally accepted system built on seven base units from which all other units are derived. The seven base quantities, their SI base units and symbols are: length — metre (m); mass — kilogram (kg); time, duration — second (s); electric current — ampere (A); thermodynamic temperature — kelvin (K); amount of substance — mole (mol); luminous intensity — candela (cd). Each SI base unit is defined carefully so that it is unique and accurate, reproducible measurements can be made with it anywhere in the world.

Q: 3. What are physical quantities? Distinguish between base and derived physical quantities.

Ans: All the quantities that can be measured are called physical quantities, for example length, mass, time, density and temperature; quantities that cannot be measured are not physical quantities. Physical quantities are of two kinds. Base quantities are the minimum number of physical quantities selected and their units defined and standardized, in terms of which all other physical quantities can be expressed; there are seven of them, such as length, mass and time, with base units metre, kilogram and second. Derived quantities are the physical quantities defined in terms of base quantities, such as area, volume, velocity, acceleration, density and force, and their units, built from base units, are called derived units.

Q: 4. What is standard form or scientific notation?

Ans: Standard form or scientific notation is a way of writing numbers that are too big or too small to be easily written in decimal form. A number is written as the product of a number greater than 1 and less than 10, called the mantissa, and a power of 10, called the exponent: number (N) = mantissa (M) x 10^exponent. To convert, the decimal point is moved to just after the first non-zero digit; if it is moved to the left the power of 10 is positive, and if moved to the right the power is negative, the number of places moved giving the exponent. For example, the average Earth-Moon distance 384,400,000 m = 3.844 x 10^8 m, and the bond length of hydrogen 0.000000000074 m = 7.4 x 10^-11 m.

Q: 5. What are prefixes? Explain with examples.

Ans: A prefix is a mechanism through which a very small or very large number is expressed in terms of a power of ten by giving a proper name and symbol to that power of ten, used with SI units to replace powers of 10. Prefixes make standard form even easier and let us choose a convenient unit for a measurement. Examples: kilo (k) = 10^3, as in 1 kilometre = 10^3 m for the distance between two cities; mega (M) = 10^6; giga (G) = 10^9; milli (m) = 10^-3, as in expressing the thickness of a paper in millimetres; centi (c) = 10^-2; micro = 10^-6; nano (n) = 10^-9; pico (p) = 10^-12; femto (f) = 10^-15; and for large multiples, peta (P) = 10^15 and exa (E) = 10^18.

Q: 6. Describe the construction and use for measurement of the following instruments: a. Vernier Calipers b. Screw gauge

Ans: a. Vernier calipers: It is a device used to measure a fraction of the smallest scale division by sliding another scale over it, and it measures small lengths accurately up to 0.1 mm or 0.01 cm, such as the thickness, diameter or width of an object and the internal and external diameter of a hollow cylinder. It has two scales: a main (fixed) scale with markings usually of 1 mm, carrying jaw A at its left end, and a vernier (sliding) scale, usually 9 mm long and divided into 10 equal divisions, carrying the second jaw. Its labelled parts (Figure 1.1) are: 1. Outside jaws for external measures, 2. Inside jaws for internal measures, 3. Depth probe for depth, 4. Main scale in centimetre/millimetre, 5. Main scale in inches, 6. Vernier scale in centimetre/millimetre, 7. Vernier scale in inches, 8. Retainer to block the movable parts. Use: note the least count (0.01 cm); close the jaws to check zero error; fix the object between the jaws; read the main scale reading just before the vernier zero; find which vernier division coincides with a main scale division, multiply it by the least count and add. In the unit's example the diameter of a solid cylinder is found as 1.9 cm + 6 x 0.01 cm = 1.96 cm. b. Screw gauge: It is a device used to measure a fraction of the smallest scale division by the rotatory motion of a circular scale over the main scale, used for very small thicknesses such as a metal strip or wire. Its labelled parts (Figure 1.3) are the anvil, spindle, main scale, datum (central) line, thimble and ratchet, with the object (sphere) held between anvil and spindle. The pitch is the distance travelled by the circular scale on the linear scale in one rotation, and the least count = pitch / total divisions on circular scale, e.g. 0.5 mm / 50 = 0.01 mm. Use: note pitch and least count; place the object between anvil and spindle and turn the ratchet until it clicks, so the grip is gentle; read the main scale reading and the circular scale division in front of the datum line, multiply the latter by the least count and add. In the unit's example (Figure 1.4) the diameter of a sphere is 5.5 mm + 28 x 0.01 mm = 5.78 mm.

Q: 7. What is meant by the significant figures of measurement? What are the main points to be kept in mind while determining the significant figures of a measurement?

Ans: In a measurement, the number of accurately known figures and the first doubtful figure are known as significant figures; the last figure is doubtful because a fraction smaller than the least count can only be guessed. The main points (general rules) for determining them are: (1) Non-zero digits are always significant, e.g. 47.73 has 4. (2) Zero between two significant digits is always significant, e.g. 32.50063 has 7. (3) Zeros to the left of significant figures are not significant, e.g. 0.00467 has 3. (4) Zeros to the right of significant figures may or may not be significant: in a decimal fraction they are significant, e.g. 7.400 has 4, while in an integer such as 80,000 the count depends on the accuracy of the measuring instrument. (5) In scientific notation, all figures other than the power of ten are significant, e.g. the mass of an electron 9.11 x 10^-31 kg has three significant figures. Calculator results must also be rounded off to the proper number of significant figures using the rounding-off rules.

mcqs.q: Physics is the branch of science that involves the study of
options: The physical universe: energy, matter, and how they are related
mcqs.why: The comprehensive answer defines physics as the branch of science that involves the study of the physical universe: energy, matter, and how they are related.

mcqs.q: How many base quantities are there in the SI system?
mcqs.why: SI is built on seven base units: length, mass, time, electric current, thermodynamic temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity, so there are seven base quantities.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following is an SI base quantity with its correct unit?
mcqs.why: Mass is one of the seven base quantities and its SI base unit is the kilogram (kg); area, velocity and force are derived quantities with derived units.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a derived physical quantity?
mcqs.why: Derived quantities are defined in terms of base quantities; area is defined as length x length, while length, mass and time are base quantities.

mcqs.q: The average Earth-Moon distance 384,400,000 m written in standard form is
mcqs.why: Working: move the decimal point 8 places to the left to sit after the first non-zero digit 3, giving mantissa 3.844 and exponent +8, so 384,400,000 m = 3.844 x 10^8 m.

mcqs.q: The prefix mega (M) represents which power of ten?
mcqs.why: From the prefixes answer: kilo (k) = 10^3, mega (M) = 10^6 and giga (G) = 10^9, so mega represents 10^6.

mcqs.q: In the vernier calipers example, a cylinder has main scale reading 1.9 cm and the 6th vernier division coincides, with least count 0.01 cm. Its diameter is
mcqs.why: Working: diameter = main scale reading + coinciding division x least count = 1.9 cm + 6 x 0.01 cm = 1.9 cm + 0.06 cm = 1.96 cm.

mcqs.q: In the screw gauge example, the sphere gives main scale reading 5.5 mm and circular division 28 with least count 0.01 mm. Its diameter is
mcqs.why: Working: diameter = main scale reading + circular division x least count = 5.5 mm + 28 x 0.01 mm = 5.5 mm + 0.28 mm = 5.78 mm.

mcqs.q: How many significant figures are there in 0.00467?
mcqs.why: Rule: zeros to the left of significant figures are not significant, so in 0.00467 only the digits 4, 6 and 7 count, giving 3 significant figures.

mcqs.q: The mass of an electron is given as 9.11 x 10^-31 kg. How many significant figures does it have?
mcqs.why: In scientific notation all figures other than the power of ten are significant; the mantissa 9.11 has the three digits 9, 1 and 1, so it has three significant figures.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems and Assignments
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Mass of Earth in standard form is 5.98 x 10^24 kg; mass of a house fly 0.0000214 kg is 2.14 x 10^-5 kg.
  • Seconds in a week: 7 x 24 x 60 x 60 = 604,800 s = 6.048 x 10^5 s.
  • Bee hummingbird length 0.057 m = 5.7 x 10^-2 m = 57 mm.
  • Peshawar to Lahore 489 km = 489 x 10^6 mm = 4.89 x 10^8 mm by motorway; the air route is about 376 km because the aeroplane follows the nearly straight shortest path.
  • Accuracy test: vernier least count 1 mm / 50 = 0.02 mm is smaller than screw gauge 1 mm / 25 = 0.04 mm, so the vernier callipers is more accurate.
  • 200 mL of water = 200 cm^3 = 200 x 10^-6 m^3 = 2.0 x 10^-4 m^3.
  • Leap-year correction: average year = (3 x 365 + 366) / 4 = 365.25 days, giving 365.25 x 86400 = 3.15576 x 10^7 s in a year.
  • Prefix results: 10^-21 kg = 1.0 ag, 3.00 x 10^18 m = 3.00 Em, Earth-Sun 149.6 million km = 149.6 Gm; 1 angstrom = 0.1 nm = 10^5 fm and 1.0 m = 10^10 angstroms; bacterial cell mass = 5 x 10^-12 kg and Sun diameter = 1.39 x 10^9 m.

Solved Exercises

Assignment 1.1 — Mass of Earth

Q: The mass of Earth is 5,980,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 kg, write this number in Standard form / scientific notation.

Ans: Given: Mass of Earth = 5,980,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 kg
Formula: Standard form = mantissa (M) x 10^exponent, where the mantissa has only one non-zero digit before the decimal point
Substitution: Place the decimal point after the first non-zero digit, 5, which gives the mantissa 5.98
Step: Count the digits the decimal point has been moved to the left = 24, so the exponent is +24
Answer: 5.98 x 10^24 kg

Assignment 1.2 — Seconds in a Week

Q: Calculate the number of seconds in a week. Express the number in power of 10 notation.

Ans: Given: 1 week = 7 days, 1 day = 24 hours, 1 hour = 60 minutes, 1 minute = 60 seconds
Formula: Seconds in a week = 7 x 24 x 60 x 60
Substitution: 7 x 24 = 168 hours
Step: 168 x 60 = 10,080 minutes
Step: 10,080 x 60 = 604,800 s
Step: In power of 10 notation, move the decimal point 5 places to the left: 604,800 = 6.048 x 10^5
Answer: 6.048 x 10^5 s

Assignment 1.3 — Average Mass of House Fly

Q: Adult housefly (Musca domestica) is having a mass of only about 0.000,021,4 kg. Express this number in standard form / scientific notation.

Ans: Given: Mass of housefly = 0.0000214 kg
Formula: Standard form = mantissa (M) x 10^exponent
Substitution: Move the decimal point to the right until it is after the first non-zero digit, 2, which gives the mantissa 2.14
Step: The decimal point has been moved 5 places to the right, so the exponent is -5
Answer: 2.14 x 10^-5 kg

Assignment 1.4 — Smallest Bird

Q: The smallest bird is the bee hummingbird. Males measure only 0.057 m. Convert this number to standard form and write this number in millimetre.

Ans: Given: Length = 0.057 m
Formula: Standard form = mantissa (M) x 10^exponent; and 1 m = 1000 mm
Substitution (standard form): Move the decimal point 2 places to the right to get the mantissa 5.7, so the exponent is -2
Step: 0.057 m = 5.7 x 10^-2 m
Substitution (millimetres): 0.057 m x 1000 mm / 1 m = 57 mm
Answer: 5.7 x 10^-2 m, and 57 mm

Assignment 1.5 — mm to Lahore

Q: Calculate the distance from Peshawar to Lahore in millimetres. (The distance from Peshawar to Lahore through motorway is 489 km, as in Example 1.5.)

Ans: Given: Distance from Peshawar to Lahore = 489 km
Formula: 1 km = 10^3 m and 1 m = 10^3 mm, so 1 km = 10^6 mm
Substitution: Distance = 489 x 10^6 mm
Step: 489 x 10^6 = 4.89 x 10^2 x 10^6 = 4.89 x 10^8
Answer: 4.89 x 10^8 mm

Assignment 1.6 — Which Instrument Is More Accurate?

Q: Which of the following is the accurate device for measuring length: A) a vernier callipers with main scale of 1 mm marking and 50 divisions on the sliding scale B) a screw gauge of pitch 1 mm and 25 divisions on the circular scale

Ans: Given: Vernier callipers: smallest main scale division = 1 mm, divisions on sliding (vernier) scale = 50. Screw gauge: pitch = 1 mm, divisions on circular scale = 25
Formula: Least count of vernier callipers = smallest division on main scale / total divisions on vernier scale. Least count of screw gauge = pitch / total divisions on circular scale. The smaller the least count, the more accurate the instrument
Substitution (vernier callipers): Least count = 1 mm / 50 = 0.02 mm
Substitution (screw gauge): Least count = 1 mm / 25 = 0.04 mm
Step: 0.02 mm is smaller than 0.04 mm, so the vernier callipers can measure a smaller length accurately
Answer: A) the vernier callipers is the more accurate device

Assignment 1.7 — mL Conversion

Q: A beaker contains 200 mL of water, what is volume of water in cm^3 and m^3.

Ans: Given: Volume of water = 200 mL
Formula: 1 mL = 1 cm^3, and 1 cm^3 = 10^-6 m^3 (because 1 cm = 10^-2 m, so 1 cm^3 = (10^-2 m)^3 = 10^-6 m^3)
Substitution (cm^3): 200 mL = 200 x 1 cm^3 = 200 cm^3
Substitution (m^3): 200 cm^3 x 10^-6 m^3 / 1 cm^3 = 200 x 10^-6 m^3 = 2.0 x 10^-4 m^3
Answer: 200 cm^3, and 2.0 x 10^-4 m^3 (0.0002 m^3)

Extension Exercise 1.1

Q: Why we used the word average in problem statement. (Example 1.1 gives the average distance between Earth and Moon as 384,400,000 m.)

Ans: The Moon does not move around the Earth in a perfect circle; its orbit is elliptical (oval-shaped), so the distance between the Earth and the Moon keeps changing as the Moon moves — it is smaller at some times and larger at other times.
Because there is no single fixed distance, the value 384,400,000 m used in Example 1.1 is the mean of the varying distances.
That is why the word 'average' is used in the problem statement.
Answer: The Earth-Moon distance varies because the Moon's orbit is elliptical, so 384,400,000 m is only its average (mean) value.

Extension Exercise 1.2

Q: Is this value exact? After each 4 years we have a leap year in which we have 366 days, how would we account for that? (Example 1.2 finds 3.1536000 x 10^7 s in a year of 365 days.)

Ans: No, the value is not exact, because Example 1.2 counts every year as exactly 365 days, while every fourth year (leap year) has 366 days.
Given: In 4 years there are 3 ordinary years of 365 days and 1 leap year of 366 days, so the extra day must be shared over the 4 years.
Formula: Average days in one year = (3 x 365 + 1 x 366) / 4 = 365.25 days; seconds in a year = days x 24 x 60 x 60
Substitution: 1 year = 365.25 x 24 x 60 x 60 s
Working: 365.25 x 86400 s = 31,557,600 s = 3.15576 x 10^7 s
Answer: We account for the leap year by taking the average year as 365.25 days, which gives 3.15576 x 10^7 s in a year instead of 3.1536 x 10^7 s.

Extension Exercise 1.3

Q: If we go to Lahore by aeroplane, the distance shortens to 376 km, why? (Example 1.5 gives the Peshawar to Lahore distance through motorway as 489 km.)

Ans: The 489 km of Example 1.5 is the length of the motorway route, and a road does not run in a straight line — it bends and turns to pass through towns, cross rivers and avoid hills, so the road path between the two cities is longer than the direct distance.
An aeroplane does not have to follow the road; it flies almost along the straight line joining Peshawar and Lahore, which is the shortest possible path between the two cities.
That straight air route measures only about 376 km.
Answer: The road distance (489 km) is longer because the motorway is not straight, while the aeroplane follows the nearly straight, shortest route (376 km).

Exercise — Numerical Problems

Q: 1. Write the number in prefix to power of ten a. Mechanical nano-oscillators can detect a mass change as small as 10^-21 kg. b. The nearest neutron star (a collapsed star made primarily of neutrons) is about 3.00 x 10^18 m away from Earth. c. Earth to sun distance is 149.6 million km

Ans: Given: (a) 10^-21 kg (b) 3.00 x 10^18 m (c) Earth to Sun distance = 149.6 million km
Formula: A power of ten is replaced by its SI prefix: 10^-18 = atto (a), 10^18 = exa (E), 10^9 = giga (G); also 1 kg = 10^3 g
Substitution (a): 10^-21 kg = 10^-21 x 10^3 g = 10^-18 g = 1.0 ag (one attogram)
Substitution (b): 3.00 x 10^18 m = 3.00 Em (three exametres)
Substitution (c): 149.6 million km = 149.6 x 10^6 km = 149.6 x 10^6 x 10^3 m = 149.6 x 10^9 m = 149.6 Gm
Answer: (a) 1.0 ag (b) 3.00 Em (c) 149.6 Gm
Note: The book's printed key gives 194.6 Gm for part (c), which is wrong because 149.6 million km = 149.6 x 10^9 m, and the prefix for 10^9 is giga, so the value must keep the same digits, 149.6 Gm; the key has transposed the digits.

Q: 2. An angstrom (symbol A) is a unit of length (commonly used in atomic physics), defined as 10^-10 m which is of the order of the diameter of an atom. a. How many nanometers are in 1.0 angstrom? b. How many femtometers or fermis (the common unit of length in nuclear physics) are in 1.0 angstrom? c. How many angstroms are in 1.0 m?

Ans: Given: 1 angstrom = 10^-10 m; 1 nanometre = 10^-9 m; 1 femtometre = 10^-15 m
Formula: To convert, divide the value in metres by the size of the required unit in metres
Substitution (a): 10^-10 m / 10^-9 m = 10^-1 = 0.1, so 1.0 angstrom = 0.1 nm
Substitution (b): 10^-10 m / 10^-15 m = 10^5, so 1.0 angstrom = 10^5 fm
Substitution (c): 1.0 m / 10^-10 m = 10^10, so 1.0 m = 10^10 angstroms
Answer: (a) 0.1 nm (b) 10^5 fm (c) 10^10 angstroms

Q: 3. The speed of light is c = 299,792,458 m/s. a. Write this value in scientific notation. b. Express the speed of light to i. five significant figures, ii. three significant figures.

Ans: Given: Speed of light c = 299,792,458 m/s
Formula: Standard form = mantissa (M) x 10^exponent, with the decimal point placed after the first non-zero digit
Substitution (a): Move the decimal point 8 places to the left: c = 2.99792458 x 10^8 m/s
Step (b)(i): For five significant figures keep five digits, 2.9979, the next digit 2 being less than 5: c = 2.9979 x 10^8 m/s
Step (b)(ii): For three significant figures keep three digits, 3.00, rounding 2.997... up: c = 3.00 x 10^8 m/s
Answer: (a) 2.99792458 x 10^8 m/s (b)(i) 2.9979 x 10^8 m/s (ii) 3.00 x 10^8 m/s

Q: 4. Express the following in terms of powers of 10. a. 7 nanometre b. 96 megawatt c. 2 gigabite d. 43 picofarad e. 2 millimetre.

Ans: Given: (a) 7 nanometre (b) 96 megawatt (c) 2 gigabite (d) 43 picofarad (e) 2 millimetre
Formula: Replace each prefix by its power of ten: nano = 10^-9, mega = 10^6, giga = 10^9, pico = 10^-12, milli = 10^-3
Substitution (a): 7 nanometre = 7 x 10^-9 m
Substitution (b): 96 megawatt = 96 x 10^6 W = 9.6 x 10^7 W
Substitution (c): 2 gigabite = 2 x 10^9 (bits)
Substitution (d): 43 picofarad = 43 x 10^-12 F = 4.3 x 10^-11 F
Substitution (e): 2 millimetre = 2 x 10^-3 m
Answer: (a) 7 x 10^-9 m (b) 9.6 x 10^7 W (c) 2 x 10^9 (d) 4.3 x 10^-11 F (e) 2 x 10^-3 m
Note: The book's printed key lists only four values for this question and omits part (c); the value for 2 gigabite, 2 x 10^9, is given here.

Q: 5. Write the following numbers in standard form: a. Mass of Bacterial cell: 0.000,000,000,005 kg b. Diameter of Sun: 1,390,000,000 m

Ans: Given: (a) Mass of bacterial cell = 0.000000000005 kg (b) Diameter of Sun = 1,390,000,000 m
Formula: Standard form = mantissa (M) x 10^exponent
Substitution (a): Move the decimal point 12 places to the right to get the mantissa 5, so the exponent is -12: 5 x 10^-12 kg
Substitution (b): Move the decimal point 9 places to the left to get the mantissa 1.39, so the exponent is +9: 1.39 x 10^9 m
Answer: (a) 5 x 10^-12 kg (b) 1.39 x 10^9 m

mcqs.q: The mass of Earth, 5,980,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 kg, in standard form is
mcqs.why: Working: standard form = mantissa x 10^exponent. Place the decimal after the first non-zero digit 5 to get mantissa 5.98; the point moved 24 places to the left, so exponent is +24, giving 5.98 x 10^24 kg.

mcqs.q: The number of seconds in a week, in power of 10 notation, is
mcqs.why: Working: seconds = 7 x 24 x 60 x 60. Step 1: 7 x 24 = 168 hours. Step 2: 168 x 60 = 10,080 minutes. Step 3: 10,080 x 60 = 604,800 s. Step 4: move decimal 5 places left, 604,800 = 6.048 x 10^5 s.

mcqs.q: The mass of an adult house fly, 0.0000214 kg, in standard form is
mcqs.why: Working: move the decimal point to the right until it is after the first non-zero digit 2, giving mantissa 2.14; the point moved 5 places to the right, so exponent is -5, giving 2.14 x 10^-5 kg.

mcqs.q: The bee hummingbird measures 0.057 m. This length in millimetres is
mcqs.why: Working: 1 m = 1000 mm. Substitution: 0.057 m x 1000 mm / 1 m = 57 mm. In standard form the same length is 5.7 x 10^-2 m.

mcqs.q: The Peshawar to Lahore motorway distance of 489 km, in millimetres, is
mcqs.why: Working: 1 km = 10^3 m and 1 m = 10^3 mm, so 1 km = 10^6 mm. Substitution: 489 x 10^6 mm = 4.89 x 10^2 x 10^6 mm = 4.89 x 10^8 mm.

mcqs.q: Vernier callipers (1 mm main scale, 50 vernier divisions) vs screw gauge (pitch 1 mm, 25 circular divisions): which is more accurate?
options: The screw gauge, least count 0.02 mm
The vernier callipers, least count 0.02 mm
The screw gauge, least count 0.04 mm
mcqs.why: Working: vernier least count = 1 mm / 50 = 0.02 mm. Screw gauge least count = pitch / divisions = 1 mm / 25 = 0.04 mm. The smaller least count, 0.02 mm, is more accurate, so the vernier callipers wins.

mcqs.q: A beaker contains 200 mL of water. Its volume in m^3 is
Why is the word average used for the Earth-Moon distance of 384,400,000 m?
options: Because the Moon is sometimes hidden
Because the Moon orbit is elliptical, so the distance keeps changing
mcqs.why: The Moon does not move in a perfect circle; its orbit is elliptical, so the Earth-Moon distance is smaller at some times and larger at others, and 384,400,000 m is only the mean (average) value.

mcqs.q: Accounting for a leap year every 4 years, the number of seconds in an average year is
Why is the Peshawar to Lahore distance by aeroplane (376 km) shorter than by motorway (489 km)?
options: The motorway is not straight, while the aeroplane follows the nearly straight shortest route
The road distance was measured wrongly
mcqs.why: The road bends and turns to pass through towns, cross rivers and avoid hills, so it is longer; the aeroplane flies almost along the straight line joining the cities, the shortest path, about 376 km.

mcqs.q: A mass change of 10^-21 kg, expressed with a prefix, is
mcqs.why: Working: 1 kg = 10^3 g, so 10^-21 kg = 10^-21 x 10^3 g = 10^-18 g. The prefix for 10^-18 is atto (a), so the value is 1.0 ag (one attogram).

mcqs.q: The Earth to Sun distance, 149.6 million km, expressed with a prefix is
mcqs.why: Working: 149.6 million km = 149.6 x 10^6 km = 149.6 x 10^6 x 10^3 m = 149.6 x 10^9 m. Prefix for 10^9 is giga (G), keeping the same digits, so 149.6 Gm. The book printed key gives 194.6 Gm, which is wrong because it transposes the digits.

mcqs.q: How many nanometres are in 1.0 angstrom (1 angstrom = 10^-10 m)?
mcqs.why: Working: 1 nanometre = 10^-9 m. Substitution: 10^-10 m / 10^-9 m = 10^-1 = 0.1, so 1.0 angstrom = 0.1 nm.

mcqs.q: How many angstroms are in 1.0 m?
mcqs.why: Working: 1 angstrom = 10^-10 m. Substitution: 1.0 m / 10^-10 m = 10^10, so 1.0 m contains 10^10 angstroms.

mcqs.q: The speed of light c = 299,792,458 m/s expressed to three significant figures is
mcqs.why: Working: in standard form c = 2.99792458 x 10^8 m/s. For three significant figures keep three digits and round 2.997... up: 2.99 becomes 3.00, giving 3.00 x 10^8 m/s. To five significant figures it is 2.9979 x 10^8 m/s.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A bus at average speed 20 ms^-1 travels 20 x 10 = 200 m in 10 s.
  • A truck accelerating from 15 ms^-1 to 20 ms^-1 in 5 s has acceleration (20 - 15) / 5 = 1 ms^-2.
  • A car at 20 m s^-1 with acceleration 4 ms^-2 reaches 20 + 4 x 2 = 28 ms^-1 after 2 s.
  • A bird accelerating at 0.3 m/s^2 for 3 s changes velocity by 0.3 x 3 = 0.9 m/s.
  • A car going backwards at 5 m/s then forwards at 10 m/s in 10 s has acceleration (10 - (-5)) / 10 = 1.5 m/s^2.
  • The slope of a distance-time graph represents speed, and the area under a speed-time graph represents distance.
  • Covering one 100 m block every 7 seconds on a straight flat road means both constant speed and constant velocity.
  • Two rocks dropped 4 m apart in free fall increase their separation as they fall.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Multiple Choice Questions

Q: 1. The average speed of a bus is 20 ms^-1, how far can it travel in 10 s?

Options: (a) 100 m (b) 200 m (c) 150 m (d) 250 m

Correct answer: 200 m

Q: 2. A truck accelerates uniformly from 15 ms^-1 to 20 ms^-1 in 5 s. What is the acceleration of the truck?

Options: (a) 2 ms^-2 (b) 1.5 ms^-2 (c) 1 ms^-2 (d) 2.5 ms^-2

Correct answer: 1 ms^-2

Q: 3. A car moving along a straight line at 20 m s^-1 undergoes an acceleration of 4 ms^-2. After 2 s, its speed will be

Options: (a) 28 ms^-1 (b) 16 ms^-1 (c) 12 ms^-1 (d) 8 ms^-1

Correct answer: 28 ms^-1

Q: 4. A bird begins to accelerate at a constant 0.3 m/s^2 for 3 s. Its change in velocity is

Options: (a) 0.9 m/s (b) 1.5 m/s (c) 1.95 m/s (d) 2.4 m/s

Correct answer: 0.9 m/s

Q: 5. A car is going backwards at 5 m/s. After 10 s of uniform acceleration, the car is going forward at 10 m/s. The acceleration is

Options: (a) 0.5 m/s^2 (b) 0.75 m/s^2 (c) 1.5 m/s^2 (d) 5 m/s^2

Correct answer: 1.5 m/s^2

Q: 6. The slope of distance-time graph represents:

Options: (a) acceleration (b) change in acceleration (c) speed (d) distance

Correct answer: speed

Q: 7. The area under a speed-time graph represents:

Options: (a) acceleration (b) change in acceleration (c) distance (d) velocity

Correct answer: distance

Q: 8. A student riding his bicycle on a straight flat road covers one block every 7 seconds. If each block is 100 m long, he is traveling at:

Options: (a) Constant speed (b) Constant velocity (c) 10 m/s (d) Both A and B

Correct answer: Both A and B

Q: 9. You drop a rock from a bridge to the river below. When the rock has fallen 4 m, you drop a second rock. As the rocks continue their free fall, their separation

Options: (a) increase (b) decrease (c) stay the same (d) none

Correct answer: increase

mcqs.q: The average speed of a bus is 20 ms^-1, how far can it travel in 10 s?
mcqs.why: Working: distance = average speed x time = 20 ms^-1 x 10 s = 200 m, so the bus travels 200 m in 10 s.

mcqs.q: A truck accelerates uniformly from 15 ms^-1 to 20 ms^-1 in 5 s. What is the acceleration of the truck?
mcqs.why: Working: acceleration a = (vf - vi) / t = (20 ms^-1 - 15 ms^-1) / 5 s = 5 / 5 = 1 ms^-2, so the truck acceleration is 1 ms^-2.

mcqs.q: A car moving along a straight line at 20 m s^-1 undergoes an acceleration of 4 ms^-2. After 2 s, its speed will be
mcqs.why: Working: first equation vf = vi + at = 20 m s^-1 + 4 ms^-2 x 2 s = 20 + 8 = 28 ms^-1, so its speed after 2 s is 28 ms^-1.

mcqs.q: A bird begins to accelerate at a constant 0.3 m/s^2 for 3 s. Its change in velocity is
mcqs.why: Working: change in velocity = acceleration x time = 0.3 m/s^2 x 3 s = 0.9 m/s, so the bird changes velocity by 0.9 m/s.

mcqs.q: A car is going backwards at 5 m/s. After 10 s of uniform acceleration, the car is going forward at 10 m/s. The acceleration is
mcqs.why: Working: take forward as positive, vi = -5 m/s and vf = +10 m/s. a = (vf - vi) / t = (10 - (-5)) / 10 = 15 / 10 = 1.5 m/s^2.

mcqs.q: The slope of distance-time graph represents:
mcqs.why: On a distance-time graph the slope is distance change divided by time change, which is speed; the steeper the line, the greater the speed.

mcqs.q: The area under a speed-time graph represents:
mcqs.why: The area under a speed-time graph is speed x time, which gives the distance covered, as used in the cyclist graph calculation in the assignments.

mcqs.q: A student riding his bicycle on a straight flat road covers one block every 7 seconds. If each block is 100 m long, he is traveling at:
options: Both constant speed and constant velocity
mcqs.why: Equal blocks in equal times on a straight flat road mean the speed does not change and the direction does not change, so both speed and velocity are constant.

mcqs.q: You drop a rock from a bridge to the river below. When the rock has fallen 4 m, you drop a second rock. As the rocks continue their free fall, their separation
mcqs.why: The first rock is already moving faster when the second is dropped and both gain speed at g, so the faster first rock pulls further ahead and their separation increases.

mcqs.q: The slope of a velocity-time graph represents:
mcqs.why: Authored top-up from Unit 2: in the velocity-time graph proof, the slope of the line is (vf - vi) / t, which is the acceleration a, while the area under the graph gives displacement.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Displacement can be zero while distance is not, e.g. a runner completing one lap returns to the start; displacement magnitude equals distance only for straight-line motion in one direction without turning back.
  • A speedometer measures a car instantaneous speed, not velocity, because it shows magnitude only and no direction.
  • An object can be at rest and accelerating at the same time: a ball at the highest point of a vertical throw has zero velocity but acceleration due to gravity downward.
  • An object can have zero acceleration and nonzero velocity, e.g. a car travelling straight at a steady 60 km/h.
  • A ball thrown down at 8.0 m/s has acceleration due to gravity, magnitude about 9.8 m/s^2 (taken as 10 m/s^2 in this book), directed vertically downward, whatever the throw speed.
  • Speed can be constant while velocity changes in uniform circular motion, because direction changes continuously.
  • Velocity and acceleration can be in opposite directions: a northward-moving car braking has southward acceleration (deceleration).
  • In free fall the acceleration stays the same (g) while velocity increases; a ball thrown up at 5 m/s returns to the start point at 5 m/s downward.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Conceptual Questions

Q: 1. Is it possible that displacement is zero but not the distance. Under what condition displacement will be equal to distance.

Ans: Yes, it is possible. Displacement is the shortest directed distance between the initial and final positions, while distance is the total length of the path travelled. If a body moves and returns to its starting point, for example a runner completing one lap of a circular track, its displacement is zero but the distance covered is the full length of the lap, which is not zero. The magnitude of displacement is equal to the distance only when the body moves in a straight line in one direction without turning back, so that the path length and the straight-line separation are the same.

Q: 2. Does a speedometer measure a car's speed or velocity?

Ans: A speedometer measures a car's (instantaneous) speed, not its velocity. It shows only the magnitude, how fast the car is moving at that instant, and gives no information about the direction of motion. Velocity needs both magnitude and direction, so the same speedometer reading can belong to many different velocities as the car turns.

Q: 3. Is it possible for an object to be accelerating and at rest at the same time? Explain with example.

Ans: Yes. Consider a ball thrown vertically upward. At the highest point of its flight the ball is momentarily at rest, its velocity is zero for that instant, yet gravity is still acting on it, so it has the acceleration due to gravity directed downward throughout, including at that instant. Rest describes velocity at an instant, while acceleration describes how velocity is changing; the ball's velocity is changing from upward to downward through zero, so it is accelerating while instantaneously at rest.

Q: 4. Can an object have zero acceleration and nonzero velocity at the same time? Give example.

Ans: Yes. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, so if velocity is constant, neither changing in size nor in direction, the acceleration is zero while the velocity itself is not. For example, a car travelling along a straight road at a steady 60 km/h has a nonzero velocity but zero acceleration; by Newton's first law this is also the state of any body moving with uniform velocity when the net force on it is zero.

Q: 5. A person standing on the roof of a building throws a rubber ball down with a velocity of 8.0 m/s. What is the acceleration (magnitude and direction) of the ball?

Ans: Once the ball leaves the hand, the only force acting on it (neglecting air resistance) is gravity, so its acceleration is the acceleration due to gravity, g, whatever the speed with which it was thrown. Its magnitude is g, about 9.8 m/s^2 (taken as 10 m/s^2 for freely falling bodies in this book), and its direction is vertically downward, toward the centre of the Earth, the same direction as the throw. The initial 8.0 m/s affects the ball's velocity, not its acceleration.

Q: 6. Describe a situation in which the speed of an object is constant while the velocity is not.

Ans: Uniform circular motion is such a situation. A ball tied to a string and whirled at a steady rate, or a car going round a circular track at a constant speedometer reading, keeps the same speed, but its direction of motion changes continuously from point to point. Since velocity is speed together with direction, the velocity changes at every instant even though the speed is constant, and this change of velocity is the centripetal acceleration directed toward the centre.

Q: 7. Can an object have a northward velocity and a southward acceleration? Explain.

Ans: Yes. Velocity tells the direction in which the object is moving now, while acceleration tells the direction in which its velocity is changing; the two need not be in the same direction. For example, a car moving northward whose driver applies the brakes is still moving north, but its velocity is decreasing, so its acceleration (deceleration) points southward, opposite to the velocity. In general, whenever a body slows down, its acceleration is opposite to its velocity.

Q: 8. As a freely falling object speeds up, what is happening to its acceleration — does it increase, decrease, or stay the same?

Ans: It stays the same. In free fall (air resistance neglected) every body near the Earth's surface falls with the constant acceleration due to gravity, g. It is the velocity that increases steadily, by g in every second; the acceleration itself does not increase or decrease during the fall, which is why the equations of motion for constant acceleration can be used with a replaced by g.

Q: 9. A ball is thrown upward with an initial speed of 5 m/s. What will be its speed when it returns to starting point?

Ans: Neglecting air resistance, the ball rises, stops momentarily at the top and falls back, gaining speed at the same rate at which it lost it on the way up. It therefore returns to the starting point with the same speed with which it was thrown, 5 m/s. Only the direction is reversed: its velocity on return is 5 m/s downward, whereas it was 5 m/s upward at the throw.

mcqs.q: A runner completes one full lap of a circular track and returns to the start. Which statement is correct?
options: Distance is zero and displacement is zero
Distance is the lap length and displacement is zero
Distance is zero and displacement is the lap length
Both distance and displacement equal the lap length
mcqs.why: Distance is the total path length, the full lap, while displacement is the shortest directed distance between start and finish, which is zero because the runner returns to the starting point.

mcqs.q: A car speedometer measures which quantity?
options: Instantaneous speed, because it shows magnitude only
mcqs.why: A speedometer shows only how fast the car is moving at that instant, the magnitude, and gives no direction, so it measures instantaneous speed, not velocity.

mcqs.q: A ball thrown vertically upward is momentarily at rest at its highest point. At that instant it is
mcqs.why: Rest describes velocity at an instant (zero at the top), while gravity still acts throughout the flight, so the ball has acceleration due to gravity directed downward even at the highest point.

mcqs.q: Which example shows zero acceleration with nonzero velocity?
options: A car speeding up from rest
A ball at the top of its throw
A car travelling straight at a steady 60 km/h
mcqs.why: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity; a car at a steady 60 km/h in a straight line has velocity that is not changing in size or direction, so acceleration is zero while velocity is nonzero.

mcqs.q: A ball is thrown down from a roof with velocity 8.0 m/s. Neglecting air resistance, its acceleration is
options: About 9.8 m/s^2 (taken as 10 m/s^2 in this book) downward
mcqs.why: Once the ball leaves the hand only gravity acts, so its acceleration is g, about 9.8 m/s^2 and taken as 10 m/s^2 for freely falling bodies in this book, vertically downward; the 8.0 m/s affects velocity, not acceleration.

mcqs.q: In uniform circular motion at a steady rate, which statement is correct?
options: Speed and velocity are both constant
Speed is constant but velocity changes because direction changes
Velocity is constant but speed changes
mcqs.why: A ball whirled on a string or a car round a circular track keeps the same speed, but direction changes continuously, and velocity includes direction, so velocity changes at every instant.

mcqs.q: A car moving northward applies its brakes. Its acceleration points
mcqs.why: The car is still moving north but its velocity is decreasing, so the change in velocity and the acceleration (deceleration) point southward, opposite to the velocity.

mcqs.q: As a freely falling object speeds up, its acceleration
mcqs.why: In free fall, with air resistance neglected, every body falls with the constant acceleration due to gravity g; it is the velocity that increases by g every second, not the acceleration.

mcqs.q: A ball is thrown upward with an initial speed of 5 m/s. Neglecting air resistance, its speed when it returns to the starting point is
mcqs.why: The ball gains speed on the way down at the same rate it lost it on the way up, so it returns to the starting point with the same speed, 5 m/s, now directed downward.

mcqs.q: Displacement magnitude is equal to the distance travelled when the body
options: Moves in a straight line in one direction without turning back
mcqs.why: Only when the body moves in a straight line in one direction without turning back are the path length and the straight-line separation the same, so displacement magnitude equals distance.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A body is in motion with respect to an observer if it changes its position with respect to that observer; motion and rest are relative, so two observers in relative motion can hold conflicting but valid views.
  • Types of motion: translatory (rectilinear e.g. free-falling bodies, curvilinear e.g. a cricket ball hit for a six, random e.g. flight of a butterfly), rotatory (wheel of a cycle, hands of a clock) and vibratory (mass on a spring, swing, plucked violin string).
  • Scalars are described by magnitude only (mass, speed, distance, density, energy, temperature); vectors need magnitude and direction (velocity, displacement, weight, friction) and are drawn as arrows whose length gives magnitude and head gives direction.
  • Tank example: scale 1 cm = 10 m, so a 50 m displacement at 30 degrees North of East is drawn as a 5 cm arrow at 30 degrees.
  • Distance is the total path length, a scalar, never negative; displacement is the shortest directed distance between initial and final positions, a vector; distance is always at least the magnitude of displacement.
  • Speed v = distance / elapsed time, scalar, SI unit m/s; velocity v = displacement / elapsed time, vector, SI unit m/s; acceleration a = (vf - vi) / (tf - ti), vector, SI unit m/s^2.
  • From a velocity-time graph: slope gives acceleration, area gives displacement; proofs give vf = vi + at, s = vit + 1/2 at^2 and 2as = vf^2 - vi^2.
  • Free fall is motion under gravity alone with air resistance neglected; g near Earth surface is approximately 9.80 m/s^2 (unit checklist directs 10 ms^-2), and without air resistance a rock and a sheet of paper fall at the same rate.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Comprehensive Questions

Q: 1. What is motion? Describe that motion is relative. How two observers in relative motion can have conflicting views about same object?

Ans: A body is in motion with respect to an observer if it changes its position with respect to that observer; if it does not change its position, it is at rest. Motion and rest are not absolute but relative, because position itself needs a reference, so the observer must always be specified. The same object can therefore appear in motion to one observer and at rest to another. In the unit's Figure 2.1, Sara travelling in a train sees her cousin John, who came to see her off, moving to the right as the train leaves, with the same speed with which John, standing on the platform, sees Sara moving to the left. Similarly, a teacher moving in a classroom is in motion for the seated students, while the moving teacher observes the students to move as well. The two observers in relative motion thus hold conflicting but equally valid views of the same object.

Q: 2. Explain different types of motion and give an example of each.

Ans: Motion is of three main types (Table 2.1). (1) Translatory motion: the position of the body as a whole changes; the path may be straight or curved. Its kinds are: rectilinear motion, straight-line motion, e.g. motion of free-falling bodies; curvilinear motion, motion along a circular or curved path, e.g. a cricket ball hit for a six; and random motion, irregular motion, e.g. the flight of a butterfly or the motion of gas molecules. Other translatory examples are a moving car, falling bodies, rowing boats and flying birds. (2) Rotatory motion: the body rotates as a whole around a fixed axis and its particles move in circles, e.g. the wheel of a cycle, the hands of a clock and the wings of a turning fan. (3) Vibratory motion: repeated to-and-fro motion about a mean position, e.g. the oscillation of a mass attached to an elastic spring, the motion of a swing and the vibration of a plucked violin string. Motions can also combine, e.g. a cricket ball can have translatory motion and spin (rotatory motion) at the same time.

Q: 3. Define scalar and vector quantities. Explain with example the graphical representation of vector quantities.

Ans: Diagram (in words): Figure 2.4 shows the position of the Al-Khalid tank, 50 m from the origin at 30 degrees North of East, drawn in two panels. In the upper (geographical, NEWS) panel the axes are North up, South down, East right and West left from origin O, the scale is 1 cm = 10 m so 5 cm = 50 m, and a 5 cm arrow leaves O at an angle of 30 degrees above the East line, labelled 50 m = 5 cm. The lower (Cartesian) panel is the same drawing with Y up, Y' down, X to the right (taken as East) and X' to the left, the same 5 cm arrow at 30 degrees from the X-axis. Scalars are physical quantities completely described by magnitude (number with proper unit) only, e.g. mass of 2 kg, speed, distance, density, energy and temperature; they are added by ordinary algebra. Vectors are quantities completely described by magnitude as well as direction, e.g. velocity, displacement, weight and friction. Graphically a vector is represented by an arrow: the length of the arrow, under a certain chosen scale, gives the magnitude, and the arrowhead points in the direction of the vector; the starting point is called the tail and the ending point the head. The steps are: draw a coordinate system, select a suitable scale, draw a line in the specified direction with length equal to the magnitude under the scale, and put an arrowhead in the direction of the vector, exactly as the tank's 50 m displacement is drawn as a 5 cm arrow at 30 degrees North of East.

Q: 4. What is position. Explain the difference between distance traveled, displacement, and displacement magnitude.

Ans: Position is the location of an object relative to some reference (a fixed point or origin in a chosen coordinate system); on Earth the position of an object is usually described in relation to nearby stationary objects. Distance travelled is the total length of the actual path followed between two positions; it is a scalar quantity, has SI unit metre and is never negative. Displacement is the shortest directed distance between the initial and final positions, a straight line from the starting point to the ending point with direction; it is a vector quantity with the same unit, metre. The magnitude of displacement is simply the size (length) of that straight-line separation, without direction. Hence distance is always at least as large as the magnitude of displacement: the two are equal for straight-line motion in one direction (Figure 2.6, left), while for a closed path the displacement and its magnitude can be zero although the distance travelled is not zero (Figure 2.6, right).

Q: 5. State and explain the terms: a. speed b. velocity c. acceleration

Ans: a. Speed is the measure of the distance covered with the passage of time, v = distance / elapsed time = (sf - si) / (tf - ti). It is a scalar quantity with SI unit metre per second (m/s). Average speed is the total distance divided by the total time; instantaneous speed is the speed for a very short time interval approaching zero, as shown by a speedometer; speed is uniform if equal distances are covered in equal intervals of time, otherwise variable. b. Velocity is the measure of the displacement covered with the passage of time, v = displacement / elapsed time. It is a vector quantity, in the direction of the displacement, with SI unit m/s. Average velocity is the total displacement divided by the total time and can be positive or negative, while instantaneous velocity is the velocity for a very short interval and is directed along the tangent to a curved path. A body has uniform velocity when its average and instantaneous velocities are equal. c. Acceleration is the measure of the change in velocity with the passage of time, or the time rate of change of velocity, a = (vf - vi) / (tf - ti). It is a vector quantity in the direction of the change in velocity, with SI unit metre per second squared (m/s^2). Average acceleration is the total change in velocity divided by the total time, instantaneous acceleration is the acceleration at a particular instant, and acceleration is uniform when average and instantaneous accelerations are equal. A body that is slowing down is said to decelerate or retard.

Q: 6. Use velocity-time graph to prove the following equations of motion a. vf = vi + at b. s = vit + 1/2 at^2 c. 2as = vf^2 - vi^2

Ans: Diagram (in words): Figures 2.14 to 2.16 show one velocity-time graph: velocity v (ms^-1) is on the vertical axis and time t (s) on the horizontal axis. A straight line rises from point A on the velocity axis to point B; OA = DC represents the initial velocity vi, DB represents the final velocity vf, OD = AC represents the time t, and the vertical segment CB = vf - vi is labelled at. The slope of line AB is the acceleration a, and the area under the line is the displacement s. Proof: The slope of the velocity-time graph gives acceleration, so a = CB / AC; since AC = t, CB = at. a. Now DB = DC + CB, that is vf = vi + at, the first equation of motion. b. The displacement is the area under the graph, the area of rectangle OACD plus the area of triangle ACB: s = (OA x AC) + 1/2 x (AC x CB) = vi x t + 1/2 x (t x at), that is s = vit + 1/2 at^2, the second equation of motion. c. The same area is the area of trapezium OABD, s = 1/2 (OA + DB) x OD = 1/2 (vi + vf) x t. From the first equation, t = (vf - vi) / a; substituting, s = 1/2 (vi + vf) (vf - vi) / a = (vf^2 - vi^2) / 2a, that is 2as = vf^2 - vi^2, the third equation of motion.

Q: 7. What is free-fall, what is its value near the surface of earth. Explain with example that rock and sheet of paper will fall at the same rate without air resistance.

Ans: Diagram (in words): Figure 2.18 shows two vertical tubes. In tube (a), which is air filled, a rock is shown well below a sheet of paper (feather), because the rock falls faster through air. In tube (b), from which the air has been evacuated, the rock and the paper are shown side by side at the same level, falling together. Free fall is the motion of a body falling under gravity alone when air resistance is neglected and the acceleration is nearly constant. In the absence of air resistance all bodies at the same location above the Earth fall vertically with the same acceleration, the acceleration due to gravity g, whose value near the Earth's surface is approximately 9.80 m/s^2 (the unit checklist directs the use of 10 ms^-2 for freely falling bodies). The familiar fact that a rock falls faster than a sheet of paper is an effect of air resistance on the paper, not of gravity: when the air is removed from the tube, as in Figure 2.18(b), the rock and the paper have exactly the same acceleration and fall at the same rate, both falling freely.

mcqs.q: A body is in motion with respect to an observer when it
options: Changes its position with respect to that observer
mcqs.why: By definition a body is in motion with respect to an observer if it changes its position with respect to that observer; if it does not change position, it is at rest.

mcqs.q: Rectilinear motion, a kind of translatory motion, is shown by
mcqs.why: Table 2.1 lists rectilinear motion as straight-line translatory motion, with the motion of free-falling bodies as its example; clock hands are rotatory and a swing is vibratory.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of rotatory motion?
mcqs.why: In rotatory motion the body rotates as a whole around a fixed axis and its particles move in circles, as in the wheel of a cycle, the hands of a clock and the wings of a turning fan.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of vibratory motion?
options: A cricket ball hit for a six
The oscillation of a mass attached to an elastic spring
mcqs.why: Vibratory motion is repeated to-and-fro motion about a mean position, e.g. the oscillation of a mass attached to an elastic spring, the motion of a swing and a plucked violin string.

mcqs.q: Which of the following quantities is a scalar?
mcqs.why: Scalars are completely described by magnitude only, e.g. mass, speed, distance, density, energy and temperature; velocity, displacement and weight are vectors needing direction as well.

mcqs.q: On a scale of 1 cm = 10 m, a displacement of 50 m at 30 degrees North of East is drawn as
options: A 5 cm arrow at 30 degrees North of East
mcqs.why: Working: scale 1 cm = 10 m, so length = 50 m / 10 m per cm = 5 cm. The tank example draws the 50 m displacement as a 5 cm arrow at 30 degrees North of East, arrow length giving magnitude and head giving direction.

mcqs.q: For a closed path returning to the start, which statement is correct?
options: Displacement can be zero although distance travelled is not zero
mcqs.why: Distance is the total path length and is never negative, while displacement is the straight-line separation of start and finish, which is zero for a closed path even though the distance travelled is not zero.

mcqs.q: Velocity differs from speed because velocity
options: Is a vector in the direction of the displacement, with SI unit m/s
mcqs.why: Velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time, a vector quantity in the direction of the displacement with SI unit m/s; speed is the scalar distance divided by elapsed time.

mcqs.q: Acceleration is defined as
options: The time rate of change of velocity, a = (vf - vi) / (tf - ti)
mcqs.why: Acceleration is the measure of the change in velocity with the passage of time, a = (vf - vi) / (tf - ti), a vector with SI unit metre per second squared (m/s^2).

mcqs.q: Without air resistance, a rock and a sheet of paper dropped together fall at the same rate because
options: Air resistance in air is what makes the paper fall slower; in a vacuum both have the same acceleration g
The paper becomes heavier in a vacuum
Gravity acts only on the rock
mcqs.why: Free fall is motion under gravity alone; in the evacuated tube of Figure 2.18 both rock and paper have exactly the same acceleration g and fall together, the usual difference being an effect of air resistance on the paper.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems and Assignments
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Usain Bolt average speed for 100 m in 9.58 s is 100 / 9.58 = 10.44 m/s.
  • One 270 m lap in 30 s: average speed 270 / 30 = 9 m/s, average velocity 0 / 30 = 0 m/s because displacement is zero.
  • Car speedometer 20 km/h at 4 s to 32 km/h at 9 s: acceleration (8.89 - 5.56) / 5 = 0.67 m/s^2.
  • Cyclist speed-time graph area = 40 m + 160 m + 80 m = 280 m total distance; cyclist with a = 1.2 m/s^2 needs (12 - 6) / 1.2 = 5 s to go from 6 m/s to 12 m/s.
  • Car braking from 120 km/h (33.33 m/s) over 30 m has deceleration 18.5 m/s^2; cricket ball thrown up at 40 m/s reaches 80 m in 4 s with g = 10 m/s^2.
  • Snail average speed 0.330 m / 140 s = 0.0024 m/s = 0.00864 km/h; braking of an eastward car gives westward acceleration.
  • Motorcyclist reaching 41.8 m/s = 150.48 km/h is unsafe; distance verified by third equation as 459.8 m. Boeing 777 landing needs about 1.40 km to 1.68 km, longer than its 1.20 km takeoff minimum.
  • Numerical results: squash ball acceleration 400 m/s^2 east; golf ball displacement 10 m; bullet exit speed 896 m/s; driver needs 44.4 m to stop so cannot stop in 20.0 m; antelope covers 66 m reaching 17 m/s in 6.00 s; ball to rise 50 m must be thrown at 31.6 m/s with g = 10 m/s^2.

Solved Exercises

Assignment 2.1 — Fastest Man

Q: In 2009 a Jamaican sprinter Usain Bolt created a World Record in Berlin by running 100 m in just 9.58 s. What is his average speed?

Ans: Given: Total distance s = 100 m, total time t = 9.58 s
Formula: Average speed <v> = total distance / total time = s / t
Substitution: <v> = 100 m / 9.58 s
Step: 100 / 9.58 = 10.44
Answer: 10.44 m/s

Assignment 2.2 — Average Velocity of Complete Lap

Q: A runner makes one lap around a 270 m circular track in 30 s. What is his (a) average speed and (b) average velocity?

Ans: Given: Distance of one lap = 270 m, time t = 30 s; after one complete lap the runner returns to his starting point, so total displacement = 0 m
Formula: Average speed = total distance / total time; Average velocity = total displacement / total time
Substitution (a): Average speed = 270 m / 30 s = 9 m/s
Substitution (b): Average velocity = 0 m / 30 s = 0 m/s
Answer: (a) 9 m/s (b) 0 m/s

Assignment 2.3 — Car's Acceleration

Q: If in the same experiment you take the readings of the speedometer of the car as 20 km/h in the 4th second and 32 km/h in the 9th second. What is the acceleration of your car in this interval?

Ans: Given: Initial velocity vi = 20 km/h at t = 4 s, final velocity vf = 32 km/h at t = 9 s
Formula: Acceleration a = (vf - vi) / (tf - ti). First convert km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6
Substitution: vi = 20 / 3.6 = 5.56 m/s; vf = 32 / 3.6 = 8.89 m/s; time interval = 9 s - 4 s = 5 s
Step: a = (8.89 m/s - 5.56 m/s) / 5 s = 3.33 m/s / 5 s = 0.67 m/s^2
Answer: 0.67 m/s^2

Assignment 2.4 — Graphical Analysis of Cyclist

Q: A cyclist increases his speed from ZERO to 8 ms^-1 in 10 s. Then he moves with uniform speed for the next 20 seconds and then its speed decreases uniformly to ZERO in the next 20 seconds. The graph is plotted for the journey, use this graph to calculate the total distance covered.

Ans: Diagram (in words): The speed-time graph has speed v (ms^-1) on the vertical axis (0 to 8) and time t (s) on the horizontal axis (0 to 50). From O the line rises steadily to point A at (10 s, 8 m/s), runs horizontally to point B at (30 s, 8 m/s), then falls steadily to point C at (50 s, 0). E is the foot of A at 10 s and D is the foot of B at 30 s, so the figure under the graph is a trapezium made of triangle OAE, rectangle ABDE and triangle CDB.
Given: Maximum speed = 8 m/s; rising time = 10 s; uniform-speed time = 20 s (10 s to 30 s); falling time = 20 s (30 s to 50 s)
Formula: Total distance covered = area under the speed-time graph = area of triangle OAE + area of rectangle ABDE + area of triangle CDB
Substitution: Triangle OAE = 1/2 x 8 m/s x 10 s = 40 m
Step: Rectangle ABDE = 8 m/s x 20 s = 160 m
Step: Triangle CDB = 1/2 x 8 m/s x 20 s = 80 m
Step: Total distance = 40 m + 160 m + 80 m = 280 m
Answer: 280 m

Assignment 2.5 — Cyclist Motion

Q: A cyclist is moving with uniform acceleration of 1.2 m/s^2. How much time will it require to change his velocity from 6 m/s to 12 m/s.

Ans: Given: Initial velocity vi = 6 m/s, final velocity vf = 12 m/s, acceleration a = 1.2 m/s^2
Formula: First equation of motion vf = vi + at, so t = (vf - vi) / a
Substitution: t = (12 m/s - 6 m/s) / 1.2 m/s^2 = 6 m/s / 1.2 m/s^2
Step: t = 5 s
Answer: 5 s
Note: The book's printed key gives 5 m/s for this assignment, which is wrong because the quantity asked for is a time; (12 - 6) / 1.2 = 5 and its unit is the second, not m/s.

Assignment 2.6 — Breaking Car

Q: On Motorway M1, a car is moving at speed limit of 120 km/h. By applying breaks the car comes to rest after covering a distance of 30 m. What is the deceleration of the car?

Ans: Given: Initial velocity vi = 120 km/h, final velocity vf = 0, distance s = 30 m
Formula: Third equation of motion 2as = vf^2 - vi^2. First convert km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6
Substitution: vi = 120 / 3.6 = 33.33 m/s
Step: a = (vf^2 - vi^2) / 2s = (0 - (33.33 m/s)^2) / (2 x 30 m) = -1111 / 60
Step: a = -18.5 m/s^2; the negative sign shows the acceleration is opposite to the motion
Answer: Deceleration of 18.5 m/s^2 (a = -18.5 m/s^2)
Note: The book's printed key gives -18.5 m/s for this assignment; the value is correct but the unit is wrong, because an acceleration must be in m/s^2, not m/s.

Assignment 2.7 — Cricket Ball

Q: In a cricket match ball go straight up with a velocity of 40 m/s. Calculate a) maximum height ball will reach b) time to reach that height.

Ans: Given: Initial velocity vi = 40 m/s upward; at maximum height vf = 0; acceleration due to gravity g = 10 m/s^2, taken negative because the ball moves against gravity
Formula: (a) Third equation for free fall 2gh = vf^2 - vi^2, with a = -g. (b) First equation vf = vi - gt, so t = vi / g
Substitution (a): h = (0 - (40 m/s)^2) / (2 x -10 m/s^2) = -1600 / -20 = 80 m
Substitution (b): t = 40 m/s / 10 m/s^2 = 4 s
Answer: (a) 80 m (b) 4 s
Note: The book's printed key, which uses g = 9.8 m/s^2, gets 81.6 m and 4.08 s and itself rounds these off to 80 m and 4 s. The values above use g = 10 m/s^2, as directed for freely falling bodies in the unit checklist.

Extension Exercise 2.1

Q: Why we used average speed formula in this example? Also convert 0.0024 m/s to 0.000066 km/h. (Example 2.1: a garden snail covers 330 mm in 2 minutes and 20 seconds.)

Ans: The snail does not crawl with the same speed all the time — its speed varies during the journey (it moves faster at some moments and slower at others), and we are given only the total distance covered (0.330 m) and the total time taken (140 s), not its speed at any one instant.
Therefore only the average speed can be found, from the formula <v> = total distance / total time, which gives 0.330 m / 140 s = 0.0024 m/s.
Conversion of 0.0024 m/s into km/h:
Given: speed = 0.0024 m/s
Formula: 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h, so multiply the value in m/s by 3.6 (that is, x 3600 s/h and / 1000 m/km)
Substitution: 0.0024 m/s = 0.0024 x 3.6 km/h
Working: 0.0024 x 3.6 = 0.00864
Answer: The average speed formula is used because the speed of the snail varies; 0.0024 m/s = 0.00864 km/h (about 0.0086 km/h).

Q: Note on Extension Exercise 2.1

Ans: The value 0.000066 km/h printed in the question (and repeated in the text of Example 2.1) is wrong. To convert m/s into km/h we multiply by 3.6, so 0.0024 m/s x 3.6 = 0.00864 km/h, not 0.000066 km/h. The printed key gives no conversion value for this item (it only states 'Speed of snail varies'), so the correct converted value 0.00864 km/h is kept.

Extension Exercise 2.2

Q: In this example, when the driver apply breaks in what direction will the resulting acceleration points? (Example 2.3: a car accelerates towards the east, reaching 140 km/h from rest.)

Ans: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, and it points in the direction of the change in velocity.
The car is moving towards the east. When the driver applies the brakes, the car's speed decreases while its direction of motion stays eastward, so the change in velocity is opposite to the motion, that is, towards the west.
Therefore the resulting acceleration (deceleration) also points towards the west, opposite to the velocity.
Answer: West — opposite to the direction of motion of the car.

Extension Exercise 2.3

Q: This problem is captioned speeding motorcyclist. Is 41.8 m/s safe speed for motorcycle ride? Also verify the distance covered in this problem by third equation of motion. (Example 2.5: a motorcyclist starts from rest and moves with uniform acceleration of 1.9 m/s^2 for 22 s, reaching 41.8 m/s and covering 459.8 m by the second equation of motion.)

Ans: Part 1 — Is 41.8 m/s a safe speed?
Given: final speed v_f = 41.8 m/s
Formula: speed in km/h = speed in m/s x 3.6
Substitution: 41.8 x 3.6 = 150.48 km/h
Working: The motorcyclist is travelling at about 150 km/h, which is far above ordinary road speed limits and leaves almost no time to react or stop.
Answer: No — 41.8 m/s = 150.48 km/h, which is a high and unsafe speed for a motorcycle ride.
Part 2 — Verification of the distance by the third equation of motion:
Given: initial velocity v_i = 0 m/s, final velocity v_f = 41.8 m/s, acceleration a = 1.9 m/s^2
Formula: 2 a s = v_f^2 - v_i^2, so s = (v_f^2 - v_i^2) / (2 a)
Substitution: s = ((41.8 m/s)^2 - (0 m/s)^2) / (2 x 1.9 m/s^2)
Working: s = 1747.24 / 3.8 = 459.8 m
Answer: s = 459.8 m — exactly the distance given by the second equation of motion in Example 2.5, so the distance is verified.

Extension Exercise 2.4

Q: At landing, the 777's velocity is about the same as at takeoff, and after touchdown its acceleration is normally between -2.0 m/s^2 to -2.4 m/s^2. How does this affect consideration of a safe runway length? (Example 2.6: a Boeing 777 takes off at 295 km/h after accelerating from rest at 2.80 m/s^2, needing a minimum runway of 1.20 km.)
