Ans: Given: landing (touchdown) speed is about the same as the takeoff speed, v_i = 295 km/h = 81.9 m/s; the plane must slow to v_f = 0 m/s; the deceleration is only between -2.0 m/s^2 and -2.4 m/s^2, smaller in magnitude than the takeoff acceleration of 2.80 m/s^2.
Formula: 2 a s = v_f^2 - v_i^2, so the stopping distance is s = (v_i^2) / (2 x |a|)
Substitution (strongest braking, a = -2.4 m/s^2): s = (81.9 m/s)^2 / (2 x 2.4 m/s^2) = 6707.61 / 4.8 = 1397 m, about 1.40 km
Substitution (weakest braking, a = -2.0 m/s^2): s = (81.9 m/s)^2 / (2 x 2.0 m/s^2) = 6707.61 / 4.0 = 1677 m, about 1.68 km
Working: Both landing distances (1.40 km to 1.68 km) are longer than the minimum takeoff distance of 1.20 km calculated in Example 2.6.
Answer: Because the landing speed is just as high but the deceleration after touchdown is smaller, the 777 needs a longer distance to stop than it needed to take off; a safe runway must therefore be longer than the takeoff minimum — a longer runway is required for landing due to the smaller deceleration.

Quiz — Distance-Time Graph

Q: Which of these graphs has higher speed?

Ans: Diagram (in words): The box shows a distance-time graph with distance S (m) on the vertical axis and time t (s) on the horizontal axis. Three straight lines rise from the origin: line A rises the least steeply, line B rises more steeply, and line C rises the most steeply.
The slope of a distance-time graph gives the speed, and the steeper the line, the greater the slope.
Line C has the steepest slope of the three.
Answer: Graph C has the higher (highest) speed.

Q: Which of these graphs show increasing speed?

Ans: Diagram (in words): The box shows a second distance-time graph, again with distance S (m) vertical and time t (s) horizontal, carrying two curves. Curve B starts off steep and gradually flattens out, while curve A starts off almost flat and bends upwards, becoming steeper and steeper with time.
On a distance-time graph, the speed at any instant is the slope of the curve; an increasing slope means an increasing speed.
The slope of curve A increases with time, while the slope of curve B decreases with time.
Answer: Graph A shows increasing speed (graph B shows decreasing speed).

Exercise — Numerical Problems

Q: 1. A squash ball makes contact with a squash racket and changes velocity from 15 m/s west to 25 m/s east in 0.10 s. Determine the vector acceleration of the squash ball.

Ans: Given: Initial velocity vi = 15 m/s west, final velocity vf = 25 m/s east, time interval = 0.10 s. Take east as positive, so vi = -15 m/s and vf = +25 m/s
Formula: Acceleration a = (vf - vi) / t
Substitution: a = (25 m/s - (-15 m/s)) / 0.10 s = 40 m/s / 0.10 s
Step: a = 400 m/s^2, in the positive (east) direction
Answer: 400 m/s^2 east

Q: 2. A golf ball that is initially traveling at 25 m/s hits a sand trap and slows down with an acceleration of -20 m/s^2. Find its displacement after 2.0 s.

Ans: Given: Initial velocity vi = 25 m/s, acceleration a = -20 m/s^2, time t = 2.0 s
Formula: Second equation of motion s = vit + 1/2 at^2
Substitution: s = 25 m/s x 2.0 s + 1/2 x (-20 m/s^2) x (2.0 s)^2
Step: s = 50 m - 40 m = 10 m
Answer: 10 m

Q: 3. A bullet accelerates the length of the barrel of a gun 0.750 m long with a magnitude of 5.35 x 10^5 m/s^2. With what speed does the bullet exit the barrel?

Ans: Given: Distance (barrel length) s = 0.750 m, acceleration a = 5.35 x 10^5 m/s^2, initial velocity vi = 0 (bullet starts from rest in the barrel)
Formula: Third equation of motion 2as = vf^2 - vi^2, so vf = square root of (2as)
Substitution: vf^2 = 2 x 5.35 x 10^5 m/s^2 x 0.750 m = 8.025 x 10^5 m^2/s^2
Step: vf = square root of 802,500 = 896 m/s (approx.)
Answer: 896 m/s

Q: 4. A driver is traveling at 18 m/s when she sees a red light ahead. Her car is capable of decelerating at a rate of 3.65 m/s^2. If she applies brakes when she is only 20.0 m from the intersection when she sees the light, will she be able to stop in time?

Ans: Given: Initial velocity vi = 18 m/s, final velocity vf = 0 (stopped), deceleration a = -3.65 m/s^2, distance available = 20.0 m
Formula: Third equation of motion 2as = vf^2 - vi^2, so stopping distance s = (vf^2 - vi^2) / 2a
Substitution: s = (0 - (18 m/s)^2) / (2 x -3.65 m/s^2) = -324 / -7.30
Step: s = 44.4 m
Step: The car needs 44.4 m to stop but the intersection is only 20.0 m away, so it will travel 44.4 m - 20.0 m = 24.4 m past the light
Answer: No, she will not be able to stop in time; the stopping distance is 44.4 m and she will pass about 24.4 m beyond the intersection

Q: 5. An antelope moving with constant acceleration 2 m/s^2 covers crosses a point where its velocity is 5 m/s. After 6.00 s how much distance it has covered and what is its velocity?

Ans: Given: Initial velocity vi = 5 m/s, acceleration a = 2 m/s^2, time t = 6.00 s
Formula: Distance from the second equation of motion s = vit + 1/2 at^2; velocity from the first equation of motion vf = vi + at
Substitution (distance): s = 5 m/s x 6.00 s + 1/2 x 2 m/s^2 x (6.00 s)^2 = 30 m + 36 m = 66 m
Substitution (velocity): vf = 5 m/s + 2 m/s^2 x 6.00 s = 5 m/s + 12 m/s = 17 m/s
Answer: Distance covered 66 m, and velocity 17 m/s

Q: 6. With what speed must a ball be thrown vertically from ground level to rise to a maximum height of 50 m?

Ans: Given: Maximum height h = 50 m; at maximum height vf = 0; acceleration due to gravity g = 10 m/s^2 (value directed for freely falling bodies in the unit checklist), acting downward
Formula: Third equation for free fall 2gh = vf^2 - vi^2 in magnitude, so vi = square root of (2gh)
Substitution: vi = square root of (2 x 10 m/s^2 x 50 m) = square root of 1000
Step: vi = 31.6 m/s
Answer: 31.6 m/s
Note: The book's printed key gives 31.3 m/s, which is the value obtained with g = 9.8 m/s^2; the answer above uses g = 10 m/s^2, as directed for freely falling bodies in the unit checklist.

mcqs.q: Usain Bolt ran 100 m in 9.58 s. His average speed was
mcqs.why: Working: average speed <v> = total distance / total time = s / t. Substitution: 100 m / 9.58 s = 10.44, so his average speed was 10.44 m/s.

mcqs.q: A runner makes one lap of a 270 m circular track in 30 s. His average velocity is
mcqs.why: Working: after one complete lap he returns to the start, so total displacement = 0 m. Average velocity = total displacement / total time = 0 m / 30 s = 0 m/s. His average speed is 270 / 30 = 9 m/s.

mcqs.q: A car speedometer reads 20 km/h in the 4th second and 32 km/h in the 9th second. Its acceleration in this interval is
mcqs.why: Working: convert by dividing by 3.6: vi = 20 / 3.6 = 5.56 m/s, vf = 32 / 3.6 = 8.89 m/s, time interval = 9 - 4 = 5 s. a = (8.89 - 5.56) / 5 = 3.33 / 5 = 0.67 m/s^2.

mcqs.q: A cyclist speed-time graph rises to 8 m/s in 10 s, stays uniform for 20 s, then falls to zero in 20 s. The total distance covered is
mcqs.why: Working: distance = area under speed-time graph. Triangle 1: 1/2 x 8 x 10 = 40 m. Rectangle: 8 x 20 = 160 m. Triangle 2: 1/2 x 8 x 20 = 80 m. Total = 40 + 160 + 80 = 280 m.

mcqs.q: A cyclist with uniform acceleration 1.2 m/s^2 changes velocity from 6 m/s to 12 m/s in a time of
mcqs.why: Working: first equation vf = vi + at, so t = (vf - vi) / a. Substitution: (12 m/s - 6 m/s) / 1.2 m/s^2 = 6 / 1.2 = 5, and the unit is seconds, so t = 5 s. The book printed key gives 5 m/s, which is wrong because the quantity asked for is a time.

mcqs.q: A car at 120 km/h brakes to rest over 30 m. Its deceleration is
mcqs.why: Working: vi = 120 / 3.6 = 33.33 m/s, vf = 0. Third equation: a = (vf^2 - vi^2) / 2s = (0 - 33.33^2) / (2 x 30) = -1111 / 60 = -18.5 m/s^2, so deceleration is 18.5 m/s^2. The book key unit m/s is wrong; acceleration must be in m/s^2.

mcqs.q: A cricket ball goes straight up at 40 m/s. With g = 10 m/s^2, the maximum height it reaches is
mcqs.why: Working: third equation for free fall 2gh = vf^2 - vi^2 in magnitude, h = vi^2 / 2g. Substitution: (40 m/s)^2 / (2 x 10 m/s^2) = 1600 / 20 = 80 m. Time to reach it is t = vi / g = 40 / 10 = 4 s.

mcqs.q: The snail average speed 0.0024 m/s converted to km/h is
mcqs.why: Working: 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h, so multiply by 3.6. Substitution: 0.0024 x 3.6 = 0.00864 km/h. The value 0.000066 km/h printed in the question and example text is wrong, as the source note explains.

mcqs.q: A motorcyclist starts from rest with a = 1.9 m/s^2 and reaches 41.8 m/s. Verified by the third equation, the distance covered is
mcqs.why: Working: third equation 2as = vf^2 - vi^2, so s = (vf^2 - vi^2) / 2a. Substitution: (41.8^2 - 0) / (2 x 1.9) = 1747.24 / 3.8 = 459.8 m, exactly the second-equation result.

mcqs.q: A Boeing 777 lands at 81.9 m/s with weakest braking deceleration -2.0 m/s^2. Its stopping distance is about
mcqs.why: Working: s = vi^2 / (2 x |a|). Substitution: (81.9 m/s)^2 / (2 x 2.0 m/s^2) = 6707.61 / 4.0 = 1677 m, about 1.68 km, longer than the 1.20 km takeoff minimum, so a longer runway is needed for landing.

mcqs.q: A squash ball changes velocity from 15 m/s west to 25 m/s east in 0.10 s. Its vector acceleration is
mcqs.why: Working: take east as positive, vi = -15 m/s, vf = +25 m/s. Formula a = (vf - vi) / t. Substitution: (25 - (-15)) / 0.10 = 40 / 0.10 = 400 m/s^2, in the positive east direction.

mcqs.q: A golf ball travelling at 25 m/s slows with acceleration -20 m/s^2. Its displacement after 2.0 s is
mcqs.why: Working: second equation s = vit + 1/2 at^2. Substitution: s = 25 x 2.0 + 1/2 x (-20) x (2.0)^2 = 50 - 40 = 10 m, so the displacement after 2.0 s is 10 m.

mcqs.q: A bullet accelerates through a 0.750 m barrel with a = 5.35 x 10^5 m/s^2 from rest. Its exit speed is about
mcqs.why: Working: third equation vf^2 = 2as (vi = 0). Substitution: vf^2 = 2 x 5.35 x 10^5 x 0.750 = 8.025 x 10^5 m^2/s^2. Step: vf = square root of 802,500 = 896 m/s approximately.

mcqs.q: A driver at 18 m/s can decelerate at 3.65 m/s^2 and is 20.0 m from an intersection. Will she stop in time, and what is her stopping distance?
mcqs.why: Working: third equation s = (vf^2 - vi^2) / 2a with vf = 0 and a = -3.65. Substitution: (0 - 18^2) / (2 x -3.65) = -324 / -7.30 = 44.4 m. She needs 44.4 m but has only 20.0 m, so she will not stop in time.

mcqs.q: With g = 10 m/s^2, the speed with which a ball must be thrown vertically to rise to a maximum height of 50 m is
mcqs.why: Working: third equation in magnitude vi = square root of (2gh). Substitution: square root of (2 x 10 m/s^2 x 50 m) = square root of 1000 = 31.6 m/s. The book key 31.3 m/s uses g = 9.8 m/s^2; this book directs g = 10 m/s^2 for freely falling bodies.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Weight w = mg: a 30 kg object weighs 30 x 9.8 = 294 N, and tension in its supporting rope equals that weight.
  • Force from Newton's second law F = ma: 0.5 kg at 10 m/s^2 needs 5 N; a car with momentum 22000 kg m/s at 20 m/s has mass 1100 kg.
  • After a collision both balls cannot be at rest, because total momentum is conserved and cannot vanish.
  • An object taken to the Moon keeps the same mass but has less weight, because g is smaller there.
  • The coefficient of friction has no units, because it is a ratio of two forces.
  • Centripetal acceleration ac = v^2 / r: 6 m/s in a circle of radius 3 m gives 12 m/s^2, and doubling the mass doubles the centripetal force.
  • Tension, friction and gravitational force can each act as a centripetal force.
  • Action and reaction do not cancel because they act on different bodies; a suitcase slides forward when a fast bus brakes suddenly, by inertia.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Multiple Choice Questions

Q: 1. A 30 kg object is supported from rope, such that tension in the rope is equal to its weight. the weight of the object is

Options: (a) 30 kg (b) 30 N (c) 294 N (d) 9.8 N/kg

Correct answer: 294 N

Q: 2. Force needed to produce an acceleration of 10 ms^-2 in a ball of mass 0.5 kg is

Options: (a) 20 N (b) 10.5 N (c) 9.5 N (d) 5 N

Correct answer: 5 N

Q: 3. Ball A collide with ball B which is at rest, after the collision which of the following condition is not possible

Options: (a) ball A comes to rest and ball B start moving (b) both balls move in same direction (c) both balls move in opposite directions (d) both balls are at rest

Correct answer: both balls are at rest

Q: 4. What is the mass of a car that is traveling with a velocity of 20 m/s [W] and a momentum of 22000 kg m/s [W]

Options: (a) 440000 kg (b) 21980 kg (c) 22020 kg (d) 1100 kg

Correct answer: 1100 kg

Q: 5. An object at earth and taken to moon should have

Options: (a) less mass/less weight (b) same mass/more weight (c) same mass/less weight (d) less mass/same weight

Correct answer: same mass/less weight

Q: 6. The unit of coefficient of friction is

Options: (a) N (b) kg (c) mu (d) it has no units

Correct answer: it has no units

Q: 7. The centripetal acceleration for an object of mass 1 kg moving with 6 m/s in a circle of radius 3 m is.

Options: (a) 18 ms^-2 (b) 12 ms^-2 (c) 10 ms^-2 (d) 2 ms^-2

Correct answer: 12 ms^-2

Q: 8. How many times the centripetal force will increase if the mass of a body moving with uniform speed in a circle is doubled?

Options: (a) Six time (b) Two times (c) Four times (d) Eight times

Correct answer: Two times

Q: 9. Which of the following forces can act as a centripetal force

Options: (a) tension (b) friction (c) gravitational force (d) All of these

Correct answer: All of these

Q: 10. An empty suitcase is placed in the middle of bus on its floor traveling at high speed. When the bus brake suddenly, the suitcase slide

Options: (a) backwards (b) forward (c) jumps up (d) remains in place

Correct answer: forward

Q: 11. In Newton's third law the action reaction pair does not neutralize each other, because they

Options: (a) act on same body (b) act on different bodies (c) act on third body (d) produce friction

Correct answer: act on different bodies

mcqs.q: A 30 kg object is supported from rope, such that tension in the rope is equal to its weight. the weight of the object is
mcqs.why: Weight w = mg. Working: w = 30 kg x 9.8 m/s^2 = 294 N. Mass is measured in kg, but weight is a force measured in newtons.

mcqs.q: Force needed to produce an acceleration of 10 ms^-2 in a ball of mass 0.5 kg is
mcqs.why: Newton's second law F = ma. Working: F = 0.5 kg x 10 m/s^2 = 5 N, so a force of 5 N produces that acceleration in the 0.5 kg ball.

mcqs.q: Ball A collide with ball B which is at rest, after the collision which of the following condition is not possible
options: ball A comes to rest and ball B start moving
both balls move in same direction
both balls move in opposite directions
mcqs.why: Ball A brings momentum into the collision and total momentum is conserved, so the momentum cannot simply vanish; both balls being at rest afterwards is impossible.

mcqs.q: What is the mass of a car that is traveling with a velocity of 20 m/s [W] and a momentum of 22000 kg m/s [W]
mcqs.why: Momentum P = mv, so m = P / v. Working: m = 22000 kg m/s / 20 m/s = 1100 kg, in the same westward direction as the momentum.

mcqs.q: An object at earth and taken to moon should have
mcqs.why: Mass is the quantity of matter and stays the same everywhere, but weight w = mg is less on the Moon because the Moon's g is smaller than Earth's g.

mcqs.q: The unit of coefficient of friction is
mcqs.why: The coefficient mu is a ratio of two forces, mu = f / FN, so the newton units cancel and the coefficient of friction has no units at all.

mcqs.q: The centripetal acceleration for an object of mass 1 kg moving with 6 m/s in a circle of radius 3 m is.
mcqs.why: Centripetal acceleration ac = v^2 / r. Working: ac = (6 m/s)^2 / 3 m = 36 / 3 = 12 m/s^2. It does not depend on the mass of the object.

mcqs.q: How many times the centripetal force will increase if the mass of a body moving with uniform speed in a circle is doubled?
mcqs.why: Centripetal force Fc = m v^2 / r is directly proportional to mass when speed and radius are fixed, so doubling the mass doubles the force, making it two times.

mcqs.q: Which of the following forces can act as a centripetal force
mcqs.why: Centripetal force is not a new kind of force: tension, friction and gravitational force can each supply it in suitable motion. This replaces the book's 'All of these' option with the explicit combined option, preserving the book's key.

mcqs.q: An empty suitcase is placed in the middle of bus on its floor traveling at high speed. When the bus brake suddenly, the suitcase slide
mcqs.why: By inertia of motion, when the bus suddenly brakes the suitcase tends to keep moving forward at its original speed, so it slides forward on the floor of the bus.

mcqs.q: In Newton's third law the action reaction pair does not neutralize each other, because they
mcqs.why: Action and reaction are equal and opposite but they act on different bodies, so they cannot cancel each other on a single body and each produces its own effect.

mcqs.q: What is the SI unit of linear momentum?
mcqs.why: Linear momentum P = mv has unit kg x m/s = kg m/s, which is also equal to N s, as stated in the comprehensive answer on momentum in this unit.

mcqs.q: For the same surfaces, how does kinetic friction compare with maximum static friction?
options: Kinetic friction is larger than maximum static friction
Kinetic friction equals maximum static friction exactly
Kinetic friction is smaller than maximum static friction
mcqs.why: The source states kinetic (sliding) friction is smaller than the maximum static friction and mu_k is less than mu_s, which is why a crate becomes easier to keep moving once it breaks loose.

mcqs.q: According to Newton's second law in momentum form, the applied force equals
options: the change in mass per second
the rate of change of linear momentum
mcqs.why: From F = m(vf - vi)/t = (mvf - mvi)/t = (Pf - Pi)/t, the applied force equals the rate of change of linear momentum of the body.

mcqs.q: The centripetal force on a body in uniform circular motion is given by
mcqs.why: Centripetal force Fc = m ac and ac = v^2 / r, so Fc = m v^2 / r, directed along the radius toward the centre of the circle.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Dust leaves a beaten carpet and water leaves shaken hands by inertia of rest / inertia of motion under Newton's first law.
  • A balloon flies forward and a fire hose kicks backward by Newton's third law: escaping fluid pushes back on the body.
  • Walking uses static friction: the foot pushes the ground backward and the ground pushes the foot forward.
  • Traction and grip grow with the normal force, since maximum friction f = mu x FN; sitting on a car trunk and rough conveyor belts use this.
  • Locking rear wheels with a parking brake at speed replaces grip with weaker kinetic friction, causing a long, uncontrolled skid.
  • In uniform circular motion speed is constant but velocity and acceleration are not constant vectors, because their directions change continuously; ac = v^2 / r toward the centre.
  • A brick released from a whirling rope flies off along the tangent to the circle at the point of release.
  • Turn speeds are posted lower because the needed centripetal force m v^2 / r grows with the square of speed and must stay within tyre-road friction.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Conceptual Questions

Q: 1. Why does dust fly off, when a hanging carpet is beaten with a stick?

Ans: This is inertia of rest, Newton's first law. The carpet hangs at rest. When it is beaten, the stick suddenly sets the carpet in motion at the struck place, but the dust particles, because of their inertia, tend to remain in their state of rest at their original places. The carpet therefore moves away from under them and the particles are left behind and separate from the carpet; they then fall down under gravity. Repeated beating thus shakes the dust out.

Q: 2. If your hands are wet and no towel is handy, you can remove some of the excess water by shaking them. Why does this work?

Ans: This works because of inertia. When the hands are shaken, they are moved rapidly and then suddenly stopped or thrown back in the opposite direction. The water drops on the hands, because of their inertia, tend to keep moving in the direction in which they were carried and cannot stop or turn with the hands at once. They are therefore flung off the hands, just as dust is flung off a beaten carpet, and repeated shaking removes most of the excess water.

Q: 3. Why a balloon filled with air move forward, when its air is released?

Ans: This is Newton's third law of motion. When the neck of the balloon is released, the air inside rushes out backward with force (action). The air, in return, pushes the balloon forward with an equal force (reaction). The two forces act on different bodies, the escaping air and the balloon, so the balloon moves forward, opposite to the direction in which its air escapes, until the air is exhausted.

Q: 4. Why does a hose pipe tend to move, backward when the fireman directs a powerful stream of water towards fire?

Ans: This is Newton's third law, the recoil effect. The pump forces the water out of the nozzle forward with a large force (action), so the water exerts an equal and opposite force on the pipe, pushing it backward (reaction). In momentum terms, the water carries away forward momentum, so the pipe gains backward momentum. That is why a fire hose kicks backward and the fireman has to hold it very firmly.

Q: 5. Your car is stuck in wet mud. Some students on their way to class see your predicament and help out by sitting on the trunk of your car to increase its traction. Why does this help?

Ans: Traction is friction between the tyres and the ground. Sitting on the trunk increases the weight pressing the driving (rear) wheels onto the ground, so the normal force FN between tyres and mud increases. Since the maximum friction is f = mu x FN, the available friction (grip) increases in the same proportion. The wheels can then push against the ground without slipping and spinning uselessly, and the car can pull itself out of the mud.

Q: 6. How does friction help you walk? Is it kinetic friction or static friction?

Ans: It is static friction. When we walk, the foot pushes the ground backward (action). The ground responds with friction on the foot in the forward direction, and it is this forward friction force that moves us along; without it, for example on ice, the foot simply slips backward. Because the sole of the shoe does not slide over the ground while it is in contact, the friction involved is static friction, not kinetic friction.

Q: 7. The parking brake on a car causes the rear wheels to lock up. What would be the likely consequence of applying the parking brake in a car that is in rapid motion?

Ans: The locked rear wheels stop rotating and begin to slide over the road. Sliding (kinetic) friction is weaker than the static/rolling grip of a turning wheel, so the braking effect is poor and the car needs a much longer distance to stop. Worse, sliding wheels lose all directional control: the rear of the car can swing sideways and the car may skid, slide or spin out of control. Applying the parking brake at speed is therefore dangerous.

Q: 8. Why is the surface of a conveyor belt made rough?

Ans: So that friction between the belt and the objects placed on it is large enough to grip them. The static friction of the rough surface makes each object move along with the belt instead of slipping or sliding backward on it, especially when the belt starts, stops or runs on an incline. A smooth belt would let the load slide and fall.

Q: 9. Why does a boatman tie his boat to a pillar before allowing the passengers to step on the river bank?

Ans: Because of Newton's third law. To step onto the bank, a passenger pushes the boat backward with his feet (action); the boat in turn pushes him forward toward the bank (reaction). If the boat is free, it moves away from the bank into the river under this push, the gap widens and the passengers may fall into the water. Tying the boat to a pillar holds it fixed against the bank, so the passengers can step ashore safely.

Q: 10. In uniform circular motion, is the velocity constant? Is the acceleration constant? Explain.

Ans: Neither is constant as a vector; only their magnitudes are constant. In uniform circular motion the speed is constant, but the direction of motion changes continuously from point to point, and since velocity includes direction, the velocity is not constant. The body is therefore accelerated toward the centre (centripetal acceleration). This acceleration has a constant magnitude, ac = v^2 / r, but its direction also changes continuously, always pointing toward the centre of the circle, so the acceleration vector is not constant either.

Q: 11. You tie a brick to the end of a rope and whirl the brick around you in a horizontal circle. Describe the path of the brick after you suddenly let go of the rope.

Ans: While the rope is held, its tension provides the centripetal force that keeps the brick on the circle. The moment the rope is let go, this force vanishes, so the brick no longer turns; by Newton's first law it flies off in the direction of its velocity at that instant, which is along the tangent to the circle at the point of release. After release it moves as a projectile under gravity along that tangential direction and falls to the ground.

Q: 12. Why is the posted speed for a turn lower than the speed limit on most highways?

Ans: A vehicle on a turn needs a centripetal force Fc = m v^2 / r toward the centre of the turn. On an ordinary road this force is supplied by friction between the tyres and the road, which cannot exceed mu x FN. The required force grows with the square of the speed, so above a certain speed the friction available is not enough and the vehicle skids outward off the road. The posted speed for a turn is therefore kept lower, so that the required centripetal force stays safely within the friction the road can provide.

mcqs.q: Why does dust fly off when a hanging carpet is beaten with a stick?
options: The dust keeps its state of rest by inertia while the carpet moves away
The stick creates a vacuum that sucks the dust out
The dust becomes lighter when beaten
Gravity suddenly increases on the dust
mcqs.why: This is inertia of rest under Newton's first law: the carpet is suddenly set in motion but the dust tends to remain at rest, so the carpet moves away and the dust is left behind and falls.

mcqs.q: Why does shaking wet hands remove excess water?
options: The water keeps moving by inertia when the hands suddenly stop or turn
Shaking increases gravity on the drops
The water is absorbed by the air
mcqs.why: When the hands are moved rapidly and suddenly stopped, the water drops tend by inertia to keep moving in their original direction and are flung off the hands, like dust off a carpet.

mcqs.q: Why does an air-filled balloon move forward when its air is released?
options: The balloon becomes lighter and floats forward
The air pulls the balloon behind it
The escaping air pushes the balloon forward as a reaction
The balloon's rubber contracts forward only
mcqs.why: By Newton's third law, air rushing out backward is the action and the air pushes the balloon forward with an equal reaction, on a different body, so the balloon moves opposite to the escaping air.

mcqs.q: Why does a fire hose pipe tend to move backward when a powerful stream is directed forward?
options: The pipe becomes heavier at the back
Friction with the ground pulls it back
The pump vibrates the pipe backward only
The water exerts an equal and opposite reaction force on the pipe
mcqs.why: The pump forces water forward with a large action force, so the water exerts an equal and opposite reaction on the pipe; in momentum terms the pipe gains backward momentum as water carries forward momentum away.

mcqs.q: Why does sitting on the trunk of a car stuck in mud increase its traction?
options: It increases the normal force and therefore the maximum friction f = mu x FN
It decreases the normal force on the wheels
It reduces the coefficient of friction
It makes the tyres spin faster
mcqs.why: Extra weight presses the driving wheels harder onto the ground, increasing FN. Since maximum friction f = mu x FN increases in the same proportion, the wheels grip instead of spinning uselessly.

mcqs.q: Which kind of friction helps a person to walk?
mcqs.why: The foot pushes the ground backward and the ground's friction pushes the foot forward. The sole does not slide while in contact with the ground, so the friction involved is static friction, not kinetic friction.

mcqs.q: What is the likely consequence of locking the rear wheels with the parking brake in a rapidly moving car?
options: The car stops instantly and safely
The car skids, needs a longer stopping distance and may spin out of control
The braking becomes stronger than normal braking
mcqs.why: Locked wheels slide, and sliding kinetic friction is weaker than the grip of a turning wheel, so stopping takes longer and sliding wheels lose directional control, letting the rear swing sideways.

mcqs.q: Why is the surface of a conveyor belt made rough?
options: So objects slide backward more easily
To make the belt run quieter only
So friction grips objects and carries them with the belt instead of letting them slip
mcqs.why: The static friction of a rough surface makes each object move along with the belt instead of slipping or sliding backward, especially when the belt starts, stops or runs on an incline.

mcqs.q: Why does a boatman tie his boat to a pillar before passengers step onto the bank?
options: Otherwise the passengers' push would move the free boat away from the bank
To keep the boat from floating downstream in the current only
So the pillar pulls the passengers forward
To increase the weight of the boat
mcqs.why: By Newton's third law a passenger pushes the boat backward to step forward; if free, the boat moves away, the gap widens and passengers may fall, so tying it holds it fixed against the bank.

mcqs.q: In uniform circular motion, is the velocity constant?
options: Yes, completely constant in magnitude and direction
No, because its direction changes continuously even though speed is constant
No, because its speed changes continuously
Yes, because the speed is constant
mcqs.why: Velocity includes direction. In uniform circular motion only the speed is constant; the direction changes from point to point, so the velocity vector is not constant and the body is accelerated toward the centre.

mcqs.q: In uniform circular motion, is the acceleration constant as a vector?
options: Yes, both magnitude and direction are constant
No, its magnitude changes but direction is fixed
No, its magnitude is constant but its direction always changes toward the centre
There is no acceleration at all
mcqs.why: The centripetal acceleration has constant magnitude ac = v^2 / r, but it always points toward the centre of the circle, so its direction changes continuously and the acceleration vector is not constant.

mcqs.q: A brick whirled on a rope flies off along which path the moment the rope is let go?
options: Straight toward the centre of the circle
Straight outward away from the centre
It drops vertically with no forward motion
Along the tangent to the circle at the point of release
mcqs.why: Once the rope is released the tension supplying centripetal force vanishes, so by Newton's first law the brick continues in the direction of its velocity at that instant, which is along the tangent, then falls as a projectile.

mcqs.q: Why is the posted speed for a turn lower than the highway speed limit?
options: The required centripetal force grows with v^2 and must stay within the friction available
Because engines cannot turn at high speed
Because centripetal force decreases with speed
Because friction increases without limit at high speed
mcqs.why: A turn needs Fc = m v^2 / r supplied by tyre-road friction, which cannot exceed mu x FN. The required force grows with the square of speed, so a lower posted speed keeps it safely within available friction.

mcqs.q: When walking, in which direction does friction from the ground act on the foot?
options: Forward, in the direction of walking
mcqs.why: The foot pushes the ground backward as an action, and the ground responds with friction on the foot in the forward direction; it is this forward friction force that moves the walker along.

mcqs.q: Sitting on the trunk helps a stuck car because the maximum friction is proportional to
options: the area of the mud only
mcqs.why: The source gives maximum friction as f = mu x FN. Increasing the load on the driving wheels increases FN, so the available friction and traction increase in the same proportion.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Force changes or tends to change a body's state of motion; its SI unit is the newton, 1 N = 1 kg m/s^2. Contact forces include friction and tension; non-contact forces include gravity, magnetic and electric forces.
  • Newton's laws: (1) law of inertia, (2) F = ma, (3) action and reaction are equal, opposite and act on different bodies.
  • Weight w = mg is a vector force in newtons measured by a spring balance; mass is a scalar in kilograms, the same everywhere, measured by a beam balance.
  • Momentum P = mv (unit kg m/s), and force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = (Pf - Pi) / t.
  • In an isolated system no external force acts, so total momentum is conserved: collision m1v1 + m2v2 = m1u1 + m2u2; explosion from rest m1v1 + m2v2 = 0.
  • Friction arises from surface irregularities interlocking and intermolecular attraction at contact points; f = mu FN, with FN = mg on a horizontal surface.
  • mu_s = fs,max / FN and mu_k = fk / FN; both are unitless and mu_k is less than mu_s. Friction is reduced by polishing, lubrication, bearings and streamlining.
  • Atwood machine: acceleration a = (m1 - m2) g / (m1 + m2) and tension T = 2 m1 m2 g / (m1 + m2); banking lets a component of the normal reaction supply centripetal force, and centrifugation moves denser particles outward.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Comprehensive Questions

Q: 1. What is force? What are its unit. Distinguish between contact and non-contact forces?

Ans: Force is an agent that changes or tends to change the state of rest or of uniform motion of a body; it can start or stop motion, change speed or direction, and change the shape of a body. From F = ma, its SI unit is the newton (N): one newton is the force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s^2, so 1 N = 1 kg m/s^2. Types of force: contact forces, which act when bodies are in physical contact, for example friction, tension, the normal force and muscular force; and non-contact (field) forces, which act at a distance without contact, for example gravitational force, magnetic force (the unit's Figure 3.1 shows a magnet attracting an iron piece without touching it) and electric force.

Q: 2. State and explain Newton's three laws of motion. Give one example of each.

Ans: First law (law of inertia): in the absence of an external force, a body at rest will remain at rest and a body in motion will continue its motion in a straight line with uniform velocity. Example: the dust leaves a beaten carpet, and passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly, because bodies resist a change in their state. Second law: when a net external force acts on a body, it produces acceleration in the body in the direction of the force; the acceleration is directly proportional to the force and inversely proportional to the mass, F = ma. Example: the same engine force gives a light car a larger acceleration than a heavy truck, and pushing a trolley harder accelerates it more. Third law: to every action there is always an equal and opposite reaction; the two act on different bodies. Example: a boatman pushes the bank with his oar (action) and the bank pushes the boat forward (reaction); a balloon flies forward as its air rushes out backward.

Q: 3. What is weight? Differentiate between mass and weight.

Ans: Weight is the force with which the Earth attracts a body toward its centre; it is the gravitational force acting on the body. If a body of mass m is at a place where the acceleration due to gravity is g, its weight is w = mg, measured in newtons. Mass and weight differ as follows. Mass is the quantity of matter in a body; weight is a force. Mass is a scalar; weight is a vector directed toward the Earth's centre. Mass is measured in kilograms with a beam balance; weight in newtons with a spring balance. Mass of a body is the same everywhere; weight changes from place to place because g changes (for example it is less on the Moon). Mass can never be zero; weight can be zero, for example in free fall or far from any planet.

Q: 4. Define momentum. Relate force to change in momentum.

Ans: Linear momentum is the product of the mass of a body and its velocity, P = mv. It is a vector quantity in the direction of velocity, with SI unit kg m/s (equal to N s). Derivation: consider a body of mass m moving with initial velocity vi; a constant force F applied for time t changes its velocity to vf. From Newton's second law, F = ma, and acceleration a = (vf - vi) / t, so F = m (vf - vi) / t = (mvf - mvi) / t. The numerator is the change in momentum, Pf - Pi, therefore F = (Pf - Pi) / t = rate of change of momentum. So the applied force equals the rate of change of linear momentum of the body, which is the original form of Newton's second law.

Q: 5. Define isolated system. Explain the law of conservation of momentum.

Ans: An isolated system is a system on which no external force acts and which is completely separated from its surroundings; the unit's example is the gas enclosed in a vessel, whose molecules collide with each other and with the walls, but no force enters from outside. Proof: for any body or system, Newton's second law in momentum form gives F = (Pf - Pi) / t. For an isolated system the external force F = 0, so (Pf - Pi) / t = 0, hence Pf - Pi = 0 and Pf = Pi. The final momentum is equal to the initial momentum, that is, the total momentum of an isolated system remains constant. Internal forces, being action-reaction pairs, cannot change the total momentum.

Q: 6. Define collision and explosion. Explain change in momentum in terms of collision and explosion.

Ans: A collision is an event in which two or more bodies exert strong forces on each other for a short time. With the system isolated during the short impact, momentum is conserved: for two bodies, m1v1 + m2v2 = m1u1 + m2u2 (equation 3.7); for example a striker hitting a carrom disk transfers momentum to it. An explosion is the reverse event: a single body at rest (or moving) breaks into parts that fly apart, the energy coming from inside the system, for example a cannon firing a ball or a bursting cracker. Momentum is still conserved: the total momentum after the explosion equals that before it, so for a body initially at rest m1v1 + m2v2 = 0 (equation 3.8), which is why the cannon recoils with momentum equal and opposite to the ball's. In both events only the internal forces act, so the total momentum of the system does not change.

Q: 7. What is friction. What are microscopic basis of friction? What is normal force, how it affects friction.

Ans: Friction is the force that opposes the relative motion (or tendency of motion) between two surfaces in contact; it acts parallel to the surfaces and opposite to the motion. Its microscopic causes are two. First, no surface is perfectly smooth: under the microscope every surface has irregularities, hills and valleys, which interlock when two surfaces are placed together and resist sliding. Second, at the points of actual contact the molecules of the two surfaces come so close that they attract each other (intermolecular attraction) and tend to stick. A normal force is the force a surface exerts on a body placed on it, directed perpendicular (normal) to the surface; it balances the component of the body's weight pressing into the surface, and on a horizontal surface FN = mg. The friction force is proportional to this normal force, f = mu FN.

Q: 8. Differentiate between static and kinetic friction by giving an example. Find the expression for the coefficient of kinetic and static friction.

Ans: Static friction is the friction between two surfaces when there is no relative motion between them; it acts when a body tends to move, adjusts itself to the applied force, and reaches a maximum value fs,max just before sliding starts. Kinetic (sliding) friction is the friction between surfaces that are actually sliding over each other; it is smaller than the maximum static friction and remains nearly constant during motion. The coefficient of friction mu is the ratio of the friction force to the normal force: mu_s = fs,max / FN for the static case and mu_k = fk / FN for the kinetic case. Since it is a ratio of two forces, the coefficient of friction has no unit; it depends on the nature of the two surfaces in contact, and mu_k is less than mu_s. Example: a heavy crate on the floor resists being started with static friction, but once it breaks loose it slides under the smaller kinetic friction, which is why it suddenly becomes easier to keep it moving.

Q: 9. What are advantages and disadvantages of friction. Also give methods to reduce and improve friction.

Ans: Advantages: friction makes walking and running possible, lets vehicles move and stop (grip of tyres, brakes), holds nails and screws, lets us hold objects and write, and allows belts to drive pulleys. Disadvantages: it wastes energy as heat, wears out moving parts and tyres, reduces the efficiency of machines and limits speed. Methods to reduce friction: polishing and smoothing surfaces; lubrication with oil or grease, which separates the surfaces; using ball or roller bearings, which replace sliding friction by the much smaller rolling friction; and streamlining bodies moving in air or water. Friction is improved (increased) where grip is needed by making surfaces rough, cutting treads in tyres and shoe soles, and pressing the surfaces harder together (increasing the normal force).

Q: 10. What is tension? If two connected bodies of masses m1 and m2 are hanging from the ends of a string which is passing over a pulley, find the values of tension and acceleration in it.

Ans: Diagram (in words): Figure 3.10, the Atwood machine, shows a frictionless pulley with an inextensible string passing over it. The heavier mass m1 hangs on the left and the lighter mass m2 on the right. On m1 two forces are marked: tension T pulling upward and weight W1 = m1g pulling downward; on m2: tension T pulling upward and weight W2 = m2g pulling downward. The system accelerates with m1 going down and m2 going up. Tension is the pulling force exerted by a stretched string (or rope) on the bodies attached to it, acting along the string away from the body; in a light inextensible string over a frictionless pulley the tension is the same throughout. Derivation: for m1, moving downward, m1g - T = m1a; for m2, moving upward, T - m2g = m2a. Adding the two equations: (m1 - m2) g = (m1 + m2) a, so a = (m1 - m2) g / (m1 + m2). Putting this a in the second equation: T = m2 (g + a) = m2 g [1 + (m1 - m2) / (m1 + m2)] = m2 g [(m1 + m2 + m1 - m2) / (m1 + m2)] = 2 m1 m2 g / (m1 + m2). Hence acceleration a = (m1 - m2) g / (m1 + m2) and tension T = 2 m1 m2 g / (m1 + m2).

Q: 11. What is uniform circular motion. What are the factors on which magnitude of acceleration (centripetal acceleration) in uniform circular motion depends.

Ans: Uniform circular motion is the motion of a body moving in a circle with constant speed; its direction changes continuously, so its velocity changes and it is accelerated toward the centre. The centripetal acceleration is ac = v^2 / r, which proves the dependence: for a fixed radius, ac is proportional to v^2, so doubling the speed makes the acceleration four times as great; for a fixed speed, ac is proportional to 1 / r, so a larger circle gives a smaller acceleration. Note that ac does not depend on the mass of the body. (The unit's own numbers illustrate it: a 1 kg body moving at 6 m/s in a circle of radius 3 m has ac = 6^2 / 3 = 12 m/s^2.)

Q: 12. What is centripetal force? Explain how centripetal force is used in banking of roads and centrifugation.

Ans: Centripetal force is the force that keeps a body moving in a circle, acting along the radius toward the centre: Fc = m ac = m v^2 / r. It is not a new kind of force; tension, friction or gravity can supply it. Banking of roads: on a curved road the needed centripetal force is provided by friction between tyres and road, which is limited, so at sharp turns roads are banked, tilted so the outer edge is higher; then a component of the normal reaction points toward the centre of the turn and helps provide the centripetal force, letting vehicles take the turn safely at higher speed without skidding. Centrifugation: a centrifuge spins a mixture rapidly in a circle; the denser particles, needing a larger centripetal force than the machine provides for them at the outside, move outward and settle, while the lighter part stays inward. This principle is used in cream separators and in the spin dryer of a washing machine, where water is thrown out through the holes of the spinning drum.

mcqs.q: What is the SI unit of force and its definition?
options: The newton: the force giving 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s^2
The kilogram: the force giving 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s^2
The newton: the force giving 1 kg a velocity of 1 m/s
mcqs.why: From F = ma, 1 N = 1 kg m/s^2: one newton is the force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s^2, as defined in the comprehensive answer.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a contact force?
mcqs.why: Contact forces act when bodies are in physical contact, for example friction, tension, the normal force and muscular force; gravity, magnetic and electric forces act at a distance without contact.

mcqs.q: Which force is shown in the unit attracting an iron piece without touching it?
mcqs.why: The unit's Figure 3.1 shows a magnet attracting an iron piece without touching it, an example of a non-contact (field) force, like gravitational and electric forces.

mcqs.q: Newton's first law is also called
options: the law of action and reaction
mcqs.why: The first law states that without an external force a body at rest stays at rest and a moving body continues in a straight line at uniform velocity; this resistance to change is inertia.

mcqs.q: Newton's second law is expressed mathematically as
mcqs.why: The second law says acceleration is directly proportional to the net force and inversely proportional to the mass, which is written F = ma, in the direction of the force.

mcqs.q: In the comprehensive answer, the boatman and his oar illustrate
options: Newton's third law: the bank pushes the boat forward in reaction
The law of conservation of energy
mcqs.why: The boatman pushes the bank with his oar (action) and the bank pushes the boat forward (reaction); the pair act on different bodies, illustrating Newton's third law of motion.

mcqs.q: How do mass and weight differ in measurement?
options: Both are measured in kg with a beam balance
Mass in newtons with a spring balance; weight in kg
Mass is measured in kg with a beam balance; weight in newtons with a spring balance
Both are measured in newtons only
mcqs.why: Mass is a scalar quantity of matter in kilograms, while weight w = mg is a vector force toward Earth's centre in newtons; mass is the same everywhere but weight changes where g changes.

mcqs.q: Linear momentum is defined as
options: P = m / v, a scalar with unit kg
P = mv, a vector in the direction of velocity with unit kg m/s
mcqs.why: Linear momentum is the product of mass and velocity, P = mv. It is a vector in the direction of velocity and its SI unit is kg m/s, equal to N s.

mcqs.q: The derivation in the unit shows force equals
options: F = (Pf - Pi) / t, the rate of change of momentum
F = Pf x Pi x t
mcqs.why: With a = (vf - vi)/t, F = ma = m(vf - vi)/t = (mvf - mvi)/t = (Pf - Pi)/t, so force is the rate of change of linear momentum, the original form of the second law.

mcqs.q: An isolated system is one on which
options: a large external force acts continuously
no external force acts, so its total momentum remains constant
momentum is created by internal forces
mcqs.why: For an isolated system F = 0, so (Pf - Pi)/t = 0 and Pf = Pi. The unit's example is gas enclosed in a vessel; internal action-reaction forces cannot change total momentum.

mcqs.q: For a two-body collision in an isolated system, momentum conservation is written
mcqs.why: Equation 3.7 in the unit states m1v1 + m2v2 = m1u1 + m2u2 for a collision, for example a striker transferring momentum to a carrom disk during the short impact.

mcqs.q: For an explosion of a body initially at rest, momentum conservation gives
options: m1v1 + m2v2 = m1u1 + m2u2 with u non-zero
Total momentum becomes twice the initial momentum
Each part must have zero velocity
mcqs.why: Equation 3.8 gives m1v1 + m2v2 = 0 for a body initially at rest breaking apart, which is why a cannon recoils with momentum equal and opposite to the fired ball's momentum.

mcqs.q: Friction on a horizontal surface is calculated from the normal force as
options: f = mu FN, with FN = mg on a horizontal surface
f = mu / FN, with FN = mg
f = mu x mg x v
mcqs.why: The normal force is perpendicular to the surface and on a horizontal surface FN = mg. Friction is proportional to it, f = mu FN, acting parallel to the surfaces opposite to motion.

mcqs.q: The coefficients of static and kinetic friction are
options: mu_s = FN / fs,max, with units of newton
mu_s = fs,max / FN and mu_k = fk / FN, both unitless with mu_k less than mu_s
mcqs.why: Each coefficient is a ratio of friction force to normal force, so it has no unit and depends on the surfaces in contact. Kinetic friction is smaller, so mu_k is less than mu_s.

mcqs.q: For an Atwood machine with masses m1 (heavier) and m2, the acceleration is
mcqs.why: Adding m1g - T = m1a and T - m2g = m2a gives (m1 - m2)g = (m1 + m2)a, so a = (m1 - m2)g/(m1 + m2); the tension is T = 2 m1 m2 g/(m1 + m2).

lessons.title: Numerical Problems and Assignments
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Assignment 3.1: a 3500 N force gives a 600 kg car 5.83 m/s^2 and a 2400 kg truck 1.46 m/s^2.
  • Assignment 3.2: 250 N on the Moon (gM = 1.6 m/s^2) means mass 156.25 kg and Earth weight about 1531 N.
  • Assignment 3.3: a 46 g golf ball at 75.8 m/s has momentum 3.49 kg m/s; Assignment 3.4: stopping in 2 s from 10 m/s needs 6000 N for a 1200 kg car and 45,000 N for a 9000 kg truck.
  • Assignment 3.5: the struck carrom disk moves at 0.6 m/s to the right; Assignment 3.6: a 200 kg cannon firing a 10 kg ball at 90 m/s recoils at 4.5 m/s.
  • Assignment 3.7: a 5 kg bag with mu = 0.1 needs 4.9 N (about 5 N) to start moving; Assignment 3.8: masses 3.5 kg and 1.5 kg give a = 3.92 m/s^2 and T about 20.6 N.
  • Assignment 3.9: the plane's mass is 1112 kg from m = Fc r / v^2. Extension results: 10 N gives a cricket ball 62.5 m/s^2 and a 4 kg metal ball 2.5 m/s^2; equal 1000 kg elevator masses give a = 0 and T = 9800 N.
  • Numerical results: halting a 1580 kg car in 50 m needs 3555 N; a rifle exerts 1000 N on a 10 g bullet; a 500 N crate has mu_s = 0.46 and mu_k = 0.40.
  • Numerical centripetal results: a 45 kg tyre at 30 m/s, r = 0.480 m needs 8.44 x 10^4 N; a 150 kg motorcycle and rider at 10 m/s, r = 5 m need 3000 N; a 1000 kg car at 80 m/s, r = 800 m needs 8000 N.

Solved Exercises

Assignment 3.1 — Truck and Car Accelerations

Q: Find the acceleration produced in engine force of 3500 N in car of mass 600 kg and truck of mass 2400 kg.

Ans: Given: Engine force F = 3500 N; mass of car = 600 kg; mass of truck = 2400 kg
Formula: Newton's second law F = ma, so a = F / m
Substitution (car): a = 3500 N / 600 kg = 5.83 m/s^2
Substitution (truck): a = 3500 N / 2400 kg = 1.46 m/s^2
Answer: Car 5.83 m/s^2, truck 1.46 m/s^2

Assignment 3.2 — Weight of Astronaut

Q: The weight of an astronaut and his space suit on the Moon is only 250 N. How much do they weigh on Earth? What is the mass on the Moon? On Earth? [take acceleration due to gravity for earth as gE = 9.8 ms^-2 and moon as gM = 1.6 ms^-2]

Ans: Given: Weight on Moon wM = 250 N; gM = 1.6 m/s^2; gE = 9.8 m/s^2
Formula: Weight w = mg, so mass m = w / g; mass is the same everywhere, only weight changes with g
Substitution (mass): m = 250 N / 1.6 m/s^2 = 156.25 kg
Substitution (weight on Earth): wE = m x gE = 156.25 kg x 9.8 m/s^2 = 1531 N (approx. 1.53 x 10^3 N)
Answer: Mass is 156.25 kg, the same on the Moon and on Earth; weight on Earth is about 1531 N
Note: The book's printed key gives a mass of 150 kg and an Earth weight of 1.5 x 10^3 N, which is wrong for the values stated in the question, because with the given gM = 1.6 m/s^2 the mass must be 250 / 1.6 = 156.25 kg (the key's figures correspond to using gM of about 1.67 m/s^2 instead of the stated 1.6 m/s^2).

Assignment 3.3 — Fastest Recorded Ball Speed in Any Game

Q: The fastest recorded speed for a golf ball hit by a golfer is 75.8 m/s (273 km/h). If mass of golf ball is 46 g, what is the magnitude of its momentum?

Ans: Given: Mass of golf ball m = 46 g = 0.046 kg, velocity v = 75.8 m/s
Formula: Linear momentum P = mv
Substitution: P = 0.046 kg x 75.8 m/s = 3.4868 kg m/s
Step: P = 3.49 kg m/s (approx.)
Answer: 3.49 kg m/s

Assignment 3.4 — Force Required to Stop a Truck and Car

Q: Calculate the force required to stop a car of mass 1200 kg and a loaded truck of mass 9,000 kg in 2 second, if they are moving with same velocity of 10 ms^-1.

Ans: Given: Car mass = 1200 kg; truck mass = 9000 kg; initial velocity vi = 10 m/s; final velocity vf = 0; time interval = 2 s
Formula: Force = rate of change of momentum, F = m (vf - vi) / t; the magnitude of the stopping force is m x vi / t
Substitution (car): F = 1200 kg x 10 m/s / 2 s = 12,000 / 2 = 6000 N
Substitution (truck): F = 9000 kg x 10 m/s / 2 s = 90,000 / 2 = 45,000 N
Answer: Car 6000 N, truck 45,000 N, in each case directed opposite to the motion

Assignment 3.5 — Carrom Board Collision

Q: In carrom board game the striker of mass having mass 0.015 kg sliding to the right at velocity of 0.40 m/s makes head-on collision with a disk having mass 0.005 kg that is initially at rest. After the collision, striker moves to the right along the direction of disk at 0.20 m/s. Find the final velocity of the disk.

Ans: Given: Striker mass m1 = 0.015 kg, its velocity before collision u1 = 0.40 m/s (to the right, taken positive), its velocity after collision v1 = 0.20 m/s; disk mass m2 = 0.005 kg, its velocity before collision u2 = 0
Formula: Law of conservation of momentum m1v1 + m2v2 = m1u1 + m2u2, so v2 = (m1u1 + m2u2 - m1v1) / m2
Substitution: v2 = (0.015 kg x 0.40 m/s + 0 - 0.015 kg x 0.20 m/s) / 0.005 kg = (0.006 - 0.003) kg m/s / 0.005 kg = 0.003 / 0.005
Step: v2 = 0.6 m/s, positive, so to the right
Answer: 0.6 m/s to the right

Assignment 3.6 — Cannon Recoil

Q: A 200-kg cannon at rest contains a 10-kg cannon ball. When fired, the cannon ball leaves the cannon with a speed of 90 m/s. What is the recoil speed of the cannon?

Ans: Diagram (in words): The figure has two panels of a cannon on wheels. The left panel, labelled before firing, shows the cannon at rest with the 10-kg ball inside it. The right panel, labelled After firing, shows the ball leaving the muzzle to the right while the cannon itself has rolled backward to the left.
Given: Mass of cannon M = 200 kg, mass of ball m = 10 kg, velocity of ball vb = 90 m/s; before firing the system is at rest, so total initial momentum = 0
Formula: Conservation of momentum for the firing (explosion): m x vb + M x vg = 0, so recoil velocity vg = - m x vb / M
Substitution: vg = - (10 kg x 90 m/s) / 200 kg = -900 / 200 = -4.5 m/s
Step: The negative sign shows the cannon moves opposite to the ball
Answer: Recoil speed 4.5 m/s (opposite to the direction of the ball)

Assignment 3.7 — Leather and Wood Friction

Q: A 5 kg heavy leather bag is placed on a horizontal wooden plank. How much force is required to set it in motion if the coefficient of friction between the plank and bag is 0.1.

Ans: Given: Mass of bag m = 5 kg; coefficient of friction mu = 0.1 (taken as the coefficient of static friction, since the bag is to be set in motion); g = 9.8 m/s^2
Formula: The force needed to just set the bag in motion equals the maximum static friction, F = fs,max = mu x FN, where the normal force on a horizontal surface is FN = mg
Substitution: FN = 5 kg x 9.8 m/s^2 = 49 N
Step: F = 0.1 x 49 N = 4.9 N, which rounds to 5 N
Answer: 4.9 N (about 5 N)

Assignment 3.8 — Simple Atwood Machine

Q: Two bodies of mass 3.5 kg and 1.5 kg are tied to ends of string which passes over a pulley. Find a. the acceleration of bodies and b. the tension in string.

Ans: Given: Masses m1 = 3.5 kg (heavier) and m2 = 1.5 kg, tied by a string over a frictionless pulley; g = 9.8 m/s^2 (the value used in the unit's worked Example 3.8)
Formula: For Atwood's machine, acceleration a = (m1 - m2) g / (m1 + m2), and tension T = 2 m1 m2 g / (m1 + m2)
Substitution (a): a = (3.5 kg - 1.5 kg) x 9.8 m/s^2 / (3.5 kg + 1.5 kg) = 2.0 x 9.8 / 5.0 = 19.6 / 5.0 = 3.92 m/s^2
Substitution (b): T = 2 x 3.5 kg x 1.5 kg x 9.8 m/s^2 / 5.0 kg = 102.9 / 5.0 = 20.58 N, about 20.6 N
Answer: (a) 3.92 m/s^2 (b) about 20.6 N (21 N approx.)
Note: The book's printed key gives 9.2 m/s^2 for the acceleration in this assignment, which is wrong because a = (m1 - m2) / (m1 + m2) x g = (2.0 / 5.0) x 9.8 = 3.92 m/s^2; the key's tension of 21 N agrees with the value found here after rounding.

Assignment 3.9 — Mass of Plane

Q: A pilot is flying a small plane at 56.6 m/s in a circular path with a radius of 188.5 m. The centripetal force needed to maintain the plane's circular motion is 1.89 x 10^4 N. What is the plane's mass?

Ans: Given: Speed v = 56.6 m/s, radius r = 188.5 m, centripetal force Fc = 1.89 x 10^4 N
Formula: Centripetal force Fc = m v^2 / r, so m = Fc x r / v^2
Substitution: m = (1.89 x 10^4 N x 188.5 m) / (56.6 m/s)^2 = 3,562,650 / 3203.56
Step: m = 1112 kg (approx.)
Answer: 1112 kg
Note: The book's printed key lists 1112 kg against a non-existent Assignment 3.10 and 11 kg against this Assignment 3.9; only Assignments 3.1 to 3.9 are printed in the unit, and direct calculation, m = Fc r / v^2, gives 1112 kg, so the key's 11 kg entry for 3.9 is wrong (its decimal place is misplaced).

Extension Exercise 3.1

Q: What will be accelerations if you apply the same net force N = 10 N on both cricket ball and metal ball in this example? (Example 3.1: cricket ball of mass 0.16 kg and metal ball for women shot-put game of mass 4 kg.)

Ans: Given: net force F = 10 N on each ball; mass of cricket ball m_c = 0.16 kg; mass of metal ball m_s = 4.00 kg
Formula: From Newton's second law F = m a, so a = F / m (stated before use)
Substitution (cricket ball): a_c = 10 N / 0.16 kg
Working: a_c = 62.5 m/s^2
Substitution (metal ball): a_s = 10 N / 4.00 kg
Working: a_s = 2.5 m/s^2
Answer: Cricket ball: 62.5 m/s^2; metal ball: 2.5 m/s^2 — the same force produces a much larger acceleration in the lighter ball.

Extension Exercise 3.2

Q: Will you want to fire with a rifle of mass 0.008 kg having bullet of 4 kg, ejecting with a muzzle speed of 715 m/s? (The masses of the bullet and the rifle of Example 3.6 are interchanged.)

Ans: Given: mass of bullet m = 4 kg; mass of rifle M = 0.008 kg; muzzle (bullet) speed v = 715 m/s; rifle and bullet are at rest before firing, so total initial momentum is zero.
Formula: By the law of conservation of momentum, m v + M v_g = 0, so the recoil speed of the rifle is v_g = - m v / M
Substitution: v_g = - (4 kg x 715 m/s) / 0.008 kg
Working: v_g = - 2860 / 0.008 = - 357,500 m/s, that is, a recoil speed of 3.575 x 10^5 m/s (the minus sign shows the recoil is opposite to the bullet's motion)
This recoil speed is 500 times the speed of the bullet itself; such a 'rifle', lighter than its own bullet, would be thrown backwards with a destructive speed and could never be held or fired.
Answer: No — the recoil speed of the gun (3.575 x 10^5 m/s) would be far greater than the speed of the bullet, so no one would want to fire such a rifle.

Extension Exercise 3.3

Q: If both mass of elevator cabin and counter weight are equal as 1000 kg. What is the acceleration and tension in the cable. (Example 3.8 treats the elevator as an Atwood machine.)

Ans: Given: mass of counter weight m_1 = 1000 kg; mass of elevator cabin m_2 = 1000 kg; acceleration due to gravity g = 9.8 m/s^2 (the value used in Example 3.8)
Formula (acceleration, Atwood machine): a = ((m_1 - m_2) / (m_1 + m_2)) x g
Substitution: a = ((1000 kg - 1000 kg) / (1000 kg + 1000 kg)) x 9.8 m/s^2
Working: a = (0 / 2000) x 9.8 = 0 m/s^2 — the two equal weights balance each other, so the system does not accelerate.
Formula (tension): T = (2 m_1 m_2 / (m_1 + m_2)) x g
Substitution: T = (2 x 1000 kg x 1000 kg / (1000 kg + 1000 kg)) x 9.8 m/s^2
Working: T = (2,000,000 / 2000) x 9.8 = 1000 x 9.8 = 9800 N — the tension simply supports the weight of either mass.
Answer: Acceleration: 0 m/s^2; tension in the cable: 9800 N.

Exercise — Numerical Problems

Q: 1. 1580-kg car is traveling with a speed of 15.0 m/s. What is the magnitude of the horizontal net force that is required to bring the car to a halt in a distance of 50.0 m?

Ans: Given: Mass m = 1580 kg, initial velocity vi = 15.0 m/s, final velocity vf = 0 (car comes to a halt), stopping distance s = 50.0 m
Formula: Third equation of motion 2as = vf^2 - vi^2 gives the acceleration, then Newton's second law F = ma
Substitution: a = (vf^2 - vi^2) / 2s = (0 - (15.0 m/s)^2) / (2 x 50.0 m) = -225 / 100 = -2.25 m/s^2
Step: F = m x a = 1580 kg x (-2.25 m/s^2) = -3555 N
Step: The magnitude of the force is 3555 N; the negative sign shows it acts opposite to the motion (the braking force of friction)
Answer: 3555 N (about 3.56 x 10^3 N)

Q: 2. A bullet of mass 10 g is fired with a rifle. The bullet takes 0.003 s to move through barrel and leaves with a velocity of 300 ms^-1. What is the force exerted on the bullet by the rifle?

Ans: Given: Mass m = 10 g = 0.010 kg, initial velocity vi = 0, final velocity vf = 300 m/s, time taken in the barrel t = 0.003 s
Formula: Force = rate of change of momentum, F = m (vf - vi) / t
Substitution: F = 0.010 kg x (300 m/s - 0) / 0.003 s = 0.010 x 300 / 0.003 = 3 / 0.003
Step: F = 1000 N
Answer: 1000 N

Q: 3. A 2200-kg vehicle traveling at 94 km/h (26 m/s) can be stopped in 21 s by gently applying the brakes. It can be stopped in 3.8 s if the driver slams on the brakes. What average force is exerted on the vehicle in both of these stops?

Ans: Given: Mass m = 2200 kg, initial velocity vi = 26 m/s, final velocity vf = 0; stopping time (a) 21 s (gentle braking), (b) 3.8 s (slamming)
Formula: Force = rate of change of momentum, F = m (vf - vi) / t; the magnitude is m x vi / t
Substitution (a): F = 2200 kg x 26 m/s / 21 s = 57,200 / 21 = 2724 N, about 2.7 x 10^3 N
Substitution (b): F = 2200 kg x 26 m/s / 3.8 s = 57,200 / 3.8 = 15,053 N, about 1.5 x 10^4 N
Answer: (a) about 2.7 x 10^3 N (b) about 1.5 x 10^4 N, both opposite to the vehicle's motion; the much larger force in (b) shows why slamming the brakes is so violent
Note: The book's printed key lists three values for this problem (-2.7 x 10^3 N, -1.5 x 10^4 N and -2.6 x 10^5 N), but the problem has only two parts; the first two key values agree with the calculation here and the third value, -2.6 x 10^5 N, belongs to no part of the question.

Q: 4. You want to move a 500-N crate across a level floor. To start the crate moving, you have to pull with a 230-N horizontal force. Once the crate "breaks loose" and starts to move, you can keep it moving at constant velocity with only 200 N. What are the co-efficients of static and kinetic friction?

Ans: Given: Weight of crate = 500 N, so on the level floor the normal force FN = 500 N; pull needed to start the crate moving = 230 N, so the maximum static friction fs,max = 230 N; pull that keeps it moving at constant velocity = 200 N, so the kinetic friction fk = 200 N (at constant velocity the pull just balances the friction)
Formula: Coefficient of static friction mu_s = fs,max / FN; coefficient of kinetic friction mu_k = fk / FN
Substitution (static): mu_s = 230 N / 500 N = 0.46
Substitution (kinetic): mu_k = 200 N / 500 N = 0.40
Answer: mu_s = 0.46 and mu_k = 0.40 (both unitless; mu_k is smaller than mu_s, as expected)

Q: 5. Two bodies of masses 3 kg and 5 kg are tied to string which is passed over a pulley. If the pulley has no friction, find the acceleration of the bodies and tension in the string.

Ans: Given: Masses m1 = 5 kg (heavier) and m2 = 3 kg, tied to the ends of a string passing over a frictionless pulley (Atwood machine); g = 9.8 m/s^2 (the value used in the unit's worked Example 3.8)
Formula: Acceleration a = (m1 - m2) g / (m1 + m2); tension T = 2 m1 m2 g / (m1 + m2)
Substitution (a): a = (5 kg - 3 kg) x 9.8 m/s^2 / (5 kg + 3 kg) = 2.0 x 9.8 / 8.0 = 19.6 / 8.0 = 2.45 m/s^2
Substitution (T): T = 2 x 5 kg x 3 kg x 9.8 m/s^2 / 8.0 kg = 294 / 8.0 = 36.75 N
Answer: Acceleration 2.45 m/s^2 (the 5 kg body moves down), tension 36.75 N (about 36.8 N)
Note: The book's printed key gives 2.8 m/s^2 and 42 N for this problem, which is wrong because with g = 9.8 m/s^2 the Atwood formulas give a = (5 - 3) / (5 + 3) x 9.8 = 2.45 m/s^2 and T = 36.75 N; the key's pair of values would require g = 11.2 m/s^2.

Q: 6. Determine the magnitude of the centripetal force exerted by the rim of a car's wheel on a 45.0-kg tyre. The tyre has a 0.480-m radius and is rotating at a speed of 30.0 m/s.

Ans: Given: Mass m = 45 kg, radius r = 0.480 m, speed v = 30 m/s
Formula: Centripetal force Fc = m v^2 / r
Substitution: Fc = 45 kg x (30 m/s)^2 / 0.480 m = 45 x 900 / 0.480 = 40,500 / 0.480
Step: Fc = 84,375 N, about 8.44 x 10^4 N
Answer: 8.44 x 10^4 N

Q: 7. A motorcyclist is moving along a circular wooden track of a circus (death well) of radius 5 m at a speed of 10 ms^-1. If the total mass of motorcycle and the rider is 150 kg find the magnitude of the centripetal force acting on him?

Ans: Given: Mass m = 150 kg, speed v = 10 m/s, radius r = 5 m
Formula: Centripetal force Fc = m v^2 / r
Substitution: Fc = 150 kg x (10 m/s)^2 / 5 m = 150 x 100 / 5 = 15,000 / 5
Step: Fc = 3000 N
Answer: 3000 N (3.0 x 10^3 N), directed toward the centre of the circular track

Q: 8. A car of mass 1000 kg is running on a circular motor way interchange near Swabi with a velocity of 80 ms^-1 the radius of the circular motor way interchange is 800 m. How much centripetal force is required?

Ans: Given: Mass m = 1000 kg, radius r = 800 m, speed v = 80 m/s
Formula: Centripetal force Fc = m v^2 / r
Substitution: Fc = 1000 kg x (80 m/s)^2 / 800 m = 1000 x 6400 / 800 = 6,400,000 / 800
Step: Fc = 8000 N
Answer: 8000 N (8.0 x 10^3 N)

mcqs.q: An engine force of 3500 N acts on a car of mass 600 kg. What is its acceleration?
mcqs.why: Formula: a = F / m from F = ma. Substitution: a = 3500 N / 600 kg. Step: 3500 / 600 = 5.83. Final result: 5.83 m/s^2.

mcqs.q: An astronaut and suit weigh 250 N on the Moon where gM = 1.6 m/s^2. What is their mass?
mcqs.why: Formula: m = w / g. Substitution: m = 250 N / 1.6 m/s^2. Step: 250 / 1.6 = 156.25. Final result: 156.25 kg, the same on Moon and Earth. The book's key gives 150 kg, which is wrong for gM = 1.6 m/s^2; it would need gM of about 1.67 m/s^2.

mcqs.q: A golf ball of mass 46 g is hit at 75.8 m/s. What is the magnitude of its momentum?
mcqs.why: Formula: P = mv. Substitution: m = 46 g = 0.046 kg, so P = 0.046 kg x 75.8 m/s. Step: 0.046 x 75.8 = 3.4868. Final result: about 3.49 kg m/s.

mcqs.q: What force is required to stop a loaded truck of mass 9000 kg moving at 10 m/s in 2 s?
mcqs.why: Formula: F = m(vf - vi)/t, magnitude m x vi / t. Substitution: F = 9000 kg x 10 m/s / 2 s. Step: 90,000 / 2 = 45,000. Final result: 45,000 N opposite to the motion.

mcqs.q: A striker (0.015 kg) moving at 0.40 m/s hits a resting disk (0.005 kg) and continues at 0.20 m/s. What is the disk's final velocity?
mcqs.why: Formula: v2 = (m1u1 + m2u2 - m1v1)/m2 by conservation of momentum. Substitution: v2 = (0.015 x 0.40 + 0 - 0.015 x 0.20)/0.005 = (0.006 - 0.003)/0.005. Step: 0.003/0.005 = 0.6. Final result: 0.6 m/s to the right.

mcqs.q: A 200 kg cannon fires a 10 kg ball at 90 m/s. What is the cannon's recoil speed?
mcqs.why: Formula: vg = -m x vb / M from m x vb + M x vg = 0. Substitution: vg = -(10 kg x 90 m/s)/200 kg = -900/200. Step: vg = -4.5 m/s, the minus showing opposite direction. Final result: recoil speed 4.5 m/s.

mcqs.q: How much force sets a 5 kg leather bag in motion on wood if mu = 0.1?
mcqs.why: Formula: F = mu x FN and FN = mg. Substitution: FN = 5 kg x 9.8 m/s^2 = 49 N, then F = 0.1 x 49 N. Step: 0.1 x 49 = 4.9. Final result: 4.9 N, about 5 N.

mcqs.q: Two masses 3.5 kg and 1.5 kg hang over a pulley. What is their acceleration?
mcqs.why: Formula: a = (m1 - m2)g/(m1 + m2). Substitution: a = (3.5 - 1.5) x 9.8/(3.5 + 1.5) = 2.0 x 9.8/5.0. Step: 19.6/5.0 = 3.92. Final result: 3.92 m/s^2. The book's key gives 9.2 m/s^2, which is wrong for these masses and g = 9.8 m/s^2.

mcqs.q: A plane flies at 56.6 m/s in a circle of radius 188.5 m with centripetal force 1.89 x 10^4 N. What is its mass?
mcqs.why: Formula: m = Fc x r / v^2 from Fc = m v^2 / r. Substitution: m = (1.89 x 10^4 x 188.5)/(56.6)^2 = 3,562,650/3203.56. Step: result is about 1112. Final result: 1112 kg. The book's key lists 11 kg for this assignment, which is wrong; its decimal place is misplaced.

mcqs.q: A net force of 10 N acts on a cricket ball of mass 0.16 kg. What is its acceleration?
mcqs.why: Formula: a = F / m from F = ma. Substitution: a = 10 N / 0.16 kg. Step: 10 / 0.16 = 62.5. Final result: 62.5 m/s^2, much larger than for the 4 kg metal ball under the same force.

mcqs.q: An elevator cabin and counterweight each have mass 1000 kg in an Atwood arrangement. What is the tension in the cable?
mcqs.why: Formula: T = (2 m1 m2/(m1 + m2)) x g. Substitution: T = (2 x 1000 x 1000/2000) x 9.8 = 1000 x 9.8. Step: acceleration is (1000-1000)/2000 x 9.8 = 0. Final result: tension 9800 N, supporting either mass.

mcqs.q: A 1580 kg car travelling at 15.0 m/s must halt in 50.0 m. What is the magnitude of the net force?
mcqs.why: Formula: first a = (vf^2 - vi^2)/2s, then F = ma. Substitution: a = (0 - 15.0^2)/(2 x 50.0) = -225/100 = -2.25 m/s^2, then F = 1580 x (-2.25). Step: F = -3555 N. Final result: magnitude 3555 N opposite to motion.

mcqs.q: A 2200 kg vehicle at 26 m/s is stopped gently in 21 s. What is the average stopping force?
mcqs.why: Formula: F = m x vi / t for the magnitude. Substitution: F = 2200 kg x 26 m/s / 21 s = 57,200/21. Step: 57,200/21 = 2724. Final result: about 2.7 x 10^3 N. Slamming in 3.8 s gives about 1.5 x 10^4 N.

mcqs.q: A 500 N crate needs a 230 N pull to start moving. What is the coefficient of static friction?
mcqs.why: Formula: mu_s = fs,max / FN. Substitution: FN = 500 N on the level floor and fs,max = 230 N, so mu_s = 230 N / 500 N. Step: 230/500 = 0.46. Final result: mu_s = 0.46, unitless; mu_k = 200/500 = 0.40.

mcqs.q: What centripetal force does a wheel rim exert on a 45.0 kg tyre of radius 0.480 m rotating at 30.0 m/s?
mcqs.why: Formula: Fc = m v^2 / r. Substitution: Fc = 45 kg x (30 m/s)^2 / 0.480 m = 45 x 900/0.480 = 40,500/0.480. Step: 40,500/0.480 = 84,375. Final result: about 8.44 x 10^4 N.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Anticlockwise torque is conventionally taken as positive.
  • Torque tau = F x d: a door needing 80 Nm with at most 100 N needs the handle at least 0.8 m from the hinges; 100 N at 0.5 m gives 50 Nm; 25 N at 0.6 m gives 15 Nm.
  • A child leaning inward on a balanced seesaw reduces her moment, so her side rises.
  • A body in equilibrium must not be accelerating, though it may rest, move uniformly or rotate uniformly; a uniformly rotating fan has zero net torque.
  • The shortest distance between two couple forces is the couple arm.
  • The x and y components of a force are equal at 45 degrees, where cos theta = sin theta.
  • Centre of mass differs from centre of gravity when the gravitational force over the body is nonuniform.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Multiple Choice Questions

Q: 1. Conventionally anti clockwise torque is taken as __________

Options: (a) Negative (b) positive (c) parallel (d) zero

Correct answer: positive

Q: 2. A door requires a minimum torque of 80 Nm in order to open it. What is the minimum distance of the handle from the hinges, if the door is to be pulled with a force at the handle not greater than 100N?

Options: (a) 0.6 m (b) 1 m (c) 0.4 m (d) 0.8 m

Correct answer: 0.8 m

Q: 3. Two children are balanced on opposite sides of a seesaw. If one child leans inward toward the pivot point, her side will

Options: (a) rise (b) fall (c) insufficient data (d) neither rise nor fall

Correct answer: rise

Q: 4. A body in equilibrium must not be

Options: (a) at rest (b) moving (c) rotating (d) accelerating

Correct answer: accelerating

Q: 5. The torque in uniformly rotating fan having blade of length 0.5 m is

Options: (a) 0.5 Nm (b) 2 Nm (c) -0.5 Nm (d) 0 Nm

Correct answer: 0 Nm

Q: 6. A force of 100 N is applied perpendicularly at 0.5 m, to turn nut of wheel of a bus. The torque acting on nut is

Options: (a) 500 Nm (b) 50 Nm (c) 5 Nm (d) 0.005 Nm

Correct answer: 50 Nm

Q: 7. The shortest distance between two couple forces is

Options: (a) moment arm (b) couple arm (c) radius (d) double moment

Correct answer: couple arm

Q: 8. A girl pushes to open a door perpendicularly with a force of 25 N at 0.6 m from the hinge, the torque is

Options: (a) 41.6 Nm (b) 25.6 Nm (c) 15 Nm (d) 0 Nm

Correct answer: 15 Nm

Q: 9. The angle at which x and y components of force are equal is

Options: (a) 0° (b) 30° (c) 45° (d) 60°

Correct answer: 45°

Q: 10. CM is different from CG, When we have nonuniform

Options: (a) shape of object (b) mass of object (c) gravitational force (d) none of these

Correct answer: gravitational force

mcqs.q: Conventionally anti clockwise torque is taken as __________
mcqs.why: By convention anticlockwise torque is taken as positive and clockwise torque as negative, as stated in the comprehensive answer on the moment of a force.

mcqs.q: A door requires a minimum torque of 80 Nm in order to open it. What is the minimum distance of the handle from the hinges, if the door is to be pulled with a force at the handle not greater than 100N?
mcqs.why: Formula: tau = F x d, so d = tau / F. Substitution: d = 80 N m / 100 N. Step: 80/100 = 0.8. Final result: 0.8 m from the hinges.

mcqs.q: Two children are balanced on opposite sides of a seesaw. If one child leans inward toward the pivot point, her side will
mcqs.why: Leaning inward reduces her distance from the pivot, so her moment (weight x distance) decreases; her side's moment becomes smaller than the other side's, so her side rises.

mcqs.q: A body in equilibrium must not be
mcqs.why: A body in equilibrium has no change in translational or rotational motion; it may be at rest, moving uniformly or rotating uniformly, but it must not be accelerating.

mcqs.q: The torque in uniformly rotating fan having blade of length 0.5 m is
mcqs.why: A uniformly rotating fan is in dynamic rotational equilibrium, so the net torque on it is zero; the blade length alone does not create a net torque.

mcqs.q: A force of 100 N is applied perpendicularly at 0.5 m, to turn nut of wheel of a bus. The torque acting on nut is
mcqs.why: Formula: tau = F x d. Substitution: tau = 100 N x 0.5 m. Step: 100 x 0.5 = 50. Final result: 50 Nm.

mcqs.q: The shortest distance between two couple forces is
mcqs.why: The shortest (perpendicular) distance between the two equal and opposite forces of a couple is called the couple arm; the moment of a couple is one force multiplied by the couple arm.

mcqs.q: A girl pushes to open a door perpendicularly with a force of 25 N at 0.6 m from the hinge, the torque is
mcqs.why: Formula: tau = F x d. Substitution: tau = 25 N x 0.6 m. Step: 25 x 0.6 = 15. Final result: 15 Nm.

mcqs.q: The angle at which x and y components of force are equal is
mcqs.why: Components are Fx = F cos theta and Fy = F sin theta. They are equal when cos theta = sin theta, which occurs at theta = 45 degrees.

mcqs.q: CM is different from CG, When we have nonuniform
mcqs.why: Centre of mass depends only on mass distribution, while centre of gravity depends on the gravitational field; they differ when the gravitational force is nonuniform over the body. The book's 'none of these' option is replaced here by 'electric force'.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A rectangular component can never exceed the vector itself: Fx = F cos theta and Fy = F sin theta, and F is the hypotenuse of the component triangle.
  • Door handles are placed far from hinges and long spanners are used because torque tau = F x d grows with the moment arm.
  • A small force can beat a larger force in torque: 10 N at 2 m gives 20 N m, while 100 N at 0.1 m gives only 10 N m; equal torques do not imply equal force magnitudes.
  • Gravity exerts no torque on a satellite about Earth's centre because its line of action passes through the centre, giving a zero moment arm.
  • Zero net force does not guarantee equilibrium: a couple (book, steering wheel) gives zero net force but a net torque and rotation.
  • A tightrope walker's long rod lowers the combined centre of mass and provides counter-torque; high heels shift the centre of mass forward and strain the lower back.
  • Leaning backwards is harder because the feet extend little behind the heels, so the line of gravity quickly leaves the base of support.
  • A single force whose line of action misses the centre of mass changes both translational motion (F = ma) and rotational motion (torque) at once.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Conceptual Questions

Q: 1. Can the rectangular component of the vector be greater than the vector itself? Explain.

Ans: No. A force F is resolved into rectangular components F_x = F cos theta and F_y = F sin theta. Since cos theta and sin theta can never be greater than 1, each component is at most equal to F itself (when theta = 0 degrees) and is normally smaller. The same result follows from F = sqrt(F_x^2 + F_y^2): the vector is the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle of its components, and the hypotenuse is always the longest side, so no component can exceed the vector itself.

Q: 2. Explain why door handles are not put near hinges?

Ans: Torque is given by tau = F x d, where d is the perpendicular distance of the force from the axis of rotation (the hinges). If the handle were near the hinges, d would be very small, so even a large force would produce only a small torque and the door would be very hard to open. Putting the handle as far from the hinges as possible makes d maximum, so a small force produces enough torque to open the door easily.

Q: 3. Can a small force ever exert a greater torque than a larger force? Explain.

Ans: Yes. Torque depends on two factors, tau = F x d: the magnitude of the force and its perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation. A small force applied at a large distance can produce more torque than a large force applied close to the axis. For example, a force of 10 N applied at 2 m from the pivot gives a torque of 20 N m, while a force of 100 N applied at only 0.1 m gives just 10 N m.
