This is why long spanners and long door handles work so well.

Q: 4. Why it is better to use a long spanner rather than a short one to loosen a rusty nut?

Ans: A rusty nut needs a large torque to loosen it. Torque tau = F x d increases with the moment arm d. A long spanner gives a larger moment arm, so the same hand force produces a much larger torque on the nut. With a short spanner the moment arm is small, and a very large force would be needed to produce the same torque.

Q: 5. The gravitational force acting on a satellite is always directed towards the centre of the earth. Does this force exert torque on satellite?

Ans: No. Torque is the product of the force and the perpendicular distance of its line of action from the axis (here the centre of the Earth). The gravitational force on the satellite acts along the line joining the satellite to the centre of the Earth, so its line of action passes through the centre and the moment arm is zero. Hence the torque about the centre is zero. Instead of turning the satellite, this force acts as the centripetal force that keeps it in orbit.

Q: 6. Can we have situations in which an object is not in equilibrium, even though the net force on it is zero? Give two examples.

Ans: Yes. Complete equilibrium needs both conditions: net force zero and net torque zero. If the net force is zero but the net torque is not zero, the body does not accelerate translationally but it does start rotating, so it is not in equilibrium. Example 1: two equal and opposite parallel forces (a couple) applied to a book lying on a table along two different lines of action — the forces cancel, yet the book turns. Example 2: two hands applying equal and opposite forces on opposite sides of a steering wheel — the wheel experiences no net force but rotates because the couple produces a net torque.

Q: 7. Why do tightrope walkers carry a long, narrow rod?

Ans: The walker stays balanced only while the vertical line from his centre of mass falls exactly on the rope. The long rod (pole) helps in two ways. First, held low, it lowers the combined centre of mass of walker plus pole towards the rope, which increases stability. Second, if the walker starts tilting to one side, the weights of the long ends of the pole exert a counter-torque about the rope that opposes the tilt, letting him correct his balance. Because torque is force times moment arm, the long pole gives large correcting torques for small movements.

Q: 8. Why does wearing high-heeled shoes sometimes cause lower back pain?

Ans: High heels lift the heels and shift the body's centre of mass forward, so the vertical line of gravity tends to fall in front of the normal base of support. To keep balance, the wearer unconsciously arches the lower back and tenses the back and calf muscles to pull the centre of mass back over the feet. This unnatural posture and the continuous extra strain on the muscles and joints of the lower back cause pain when high heels are worn for a long time. The whole body weight is also carried on a very small area, which adds to the discomfort.

Q: 9. Why is it more difficult to lean backwards. Explain?

Ans: A person remains balanced only while the vertical line from his centre of mass falls within the base of support formed by the feet. The feet extend much further in front (toes) than behind (heels), so the base is large in front and very small at the back. When leaning forward, the line of gravity still falls within the foot base for a considerable lean. When leaning backwards, the line of gravity quickly passes behind the heels, outside the base, and the torque of the weight then topples the person backwards, so backward leaning is much more difficult and limited.

Q: 10. Can a single force applied to a body change both its translational and rotational motion? Explain.

Ans: Yes. If the line of action of a single force does not pass through the centre of mass of the body, the force has two effects at once. As a force acting on the mass, it accelerates the centre of mass and changes the translational motion (F = ma). At the same time, its moment about the centre of mass (force x perpendicular distance) produces a torque and changes the rotational motion. For example, pushing a door at its edge both moves and turns it, and kicking a football off-centre makes it travel forward while spinning.

Q: 11. Two forces produce the same torque. Does it follow that they have the same magnitude? Explain. Describe the path of the brick after you suddenly let go of the rope.

Ans: No, it does not follow. Torque is tau = F x d, the product of the force and its moment arm. Two forces of different magnitudes can produce the same torque if their moment arms differ in the opposite ratio: a smaller force acting at a larger perpendicular distance gives the same torque as a larger force acting at a smaller distance, e.g. 10 N at 2 m and 20 N at 1 m both give 20 N m.
For the second part printed with this question (a brick whirled in a circle at the end of a rope): while the rope is held, its tension provides the centripetal force. The moment the rope is let go, this force vanishes, so the brick flies off in a straight line along the tangent to the circle at the point of release, in the direction of its velocity at that instant. Afterwards, under gravity, it follows the usual curved (projectile) path to the ground.

mcqs.q: Can a rectangular component of a vector be greater than the vector itself?
options: No, each component is at most equal to the vector itself
Yes, whenever the angle is large
Yes, if both components are added
Only the vertical component can exceed it
mcqs.why: Fx = F cos theta and Fy = F sin theta, and cos and sin never exceed 1, so each component is at most F. Also F is the hypotenuse of the component triangle, always its longest side.

mcqs.q: Why are door handles not put near the hinges?
options: Near the hinges the force becomes zero
Near the hinges the moment arm is small, so even a large force gives only a small torque
Handles near hinges increase the torque too much
The hinges absorb all the force
mcqs.why: Torque tau = F x d, where d is the distance from the hinges. A handle far from the hinges makes d maximum, so a small force produces enough torque to open the door easily.

mcqs.q: Can a small force ever exert a greater torque than a larger force?
options: No, torque depends only on force
No, a larger force always wins
Yes, if the small force acts at a much larger distance from the axis
Yes, but only if the small force is vertical
mcqs.why: Torque tau = F x d depends on both force and moment arm: 10 N at 2 m gives 20 N m, while 100 N at only 0.1 m gives just 10 N m, as in the source example.

mcqs.q: Why is a long spanner better for loosening a rusty nut?
options: It increases the hand force itself
It reduces the friction inside the nut to zero
It changes the direction of the force
Its larger moment arm gives a larger torque for the same hand force
mcqs.why: A rusty nut needs a large torque. Since tau = F x d increases with the moment arm d, a long spanner produces much more torque from the same force than a short spanner.

mcqs.q: Does Earth's gravity exert a torque on a satellite about Earth's centre?
options: No, its line of action passes through the centre, so the moment arm is zero
Yes, a large torque that spins the satellite
Yes, equal to the satellite's weight times its altitude
No, because gravity is too weak in orbit
mcqs.why: The gravitational force acts along the line joining the satellite to Earth's centre, so its perpendicular distance from that centre is zero and the torque is zero; the force instead acts as centripetal force.

mcqs.q: Can an object fail to be in equilibrium even though the net force on it is zero?
options: No, zero net force always means equilibrium
Yes, if the net torque is not zero it will start rotating
Yes, but only if it is also accelerating translationally
No, rotation needs a net force
mcqs.why: Complete equilibrium needs net force zero AND net torque zero. A couple on a book, or two hands on opposite sides of a steering wheel, gives zero net force but a net torque that rotates the body.

mcqs.q: Why do tightrope walkers carry a long, narrow rod?
options: It increases the walker's weight so friction doubles
It hides the rope from view
It lowers the combined centre of mass and its ends exert a counter-torque against tilting
It pushes air down to lift the walker
mcqs.why: Held low, the pole lowers the combined centre of mass toward the rope, and if the walker tilts, the long ends exert a correcting counter-torque about the rope because torque grows with moment arm.

mcqs.q: Why can wearing high-heeled shoes cause lower back pain?
options: Heels shift the centre of mass backward
Heels lower the centre of mass to the feet
Heels widen the base of support greatly
Heels shift the centre of mass forward, forcing the back to arch and strain to restore balance
mcqs.why: High heels lift the heels and shift the centre of mass forward, so the wearer arches the lower back and tenses back and calf muscles to pull it back over the feet, straining the lower back over time.

mcqs.q: Why is it more difficult to lean backwards than forwards?
options: The feet extend far in front but very little behind, so the line of gravity soon falls behind the heels
Because gravity is stronger behind the body
Because the centre of mass moves upward when leaning back
Because the toes are weaker than the heels
mcqs.why: Balance requires the vertical line from the centre of mass to fall within the base of the feet. That base is large in front (toes) and very small at the back (heels), so backward lean quickly topples the person.

mcqs.q: Can a single force change both the translational and rotational motion of a body?
options: No, one force can only translate a body
Yes, if its line of action does not pass through the centre of mass
No, one force can only rotate a body
Yes, but only if the force is gravitational
mcqs.why: Such a force accelerates the centre of mass by F = ma and at the same time its moment about the centre of mass produces a torque, for example pushing a door at its edge or kicking a football off-centre.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A force diagram reduces an object to a dot at its centre of mass with forces as arrows; like parallel forces add, unlike parallel forces subtract.
  • Head-to-tail rule: place each next force's tail on the previous head; the resultant joins the first tail to the last head.
  • Torque (moment of a force) tau = F x d, unit N m, anticlockwise positive; it depends on force magnitude, moment arm and line of action, and is zero if the line passes through the axis.
  • Resolution: Fx = F cos theta and Fy = F sin theta; conversely F = sqrt(Fx^2 + Fy^2) and theta = tan^-1(Fy / Fx).
  • A couple is two equal, opposite parallel forces on different lines of action: zero resultant force, pure rotation, moment = force x couple arm (steering wheel, tap, bottle cap).
  • Equilibrium needs both conditions: net force zero and net torque zero; static equilibrium is rest, dynamic equilibrium is uniform translational or rotational motion.
  • Principle of moments: clockwise moments about a pivot equal anticlockwise moments, e.g. 600 N x 1 m balances 400 N x 1.5 m (600 N m each).
  • CM is where mass is balanced; CG is where weight appears to act, found by the plumb-line suspension method. Stability: stable if displacement raises CM, unstable if it falls, neutral if unchanged; lower CM and widen the base to improve it.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Comprehensive Questions

Q: 1. What are force diagrams? Define like and unlike parallel forces with example.

Ans: A force diagram is a diagram that shows all the forces acting on an object. The object is reduced to a dot at its centre (the centre of mass) and each force is drawn as an arrow starting from the dot, with the arrow's length showing the magnitude and its direction showing the direction of the force. For example, for a book resting on a table two arrows are drawn: the weight acting vertically downward and the normal force of the table acting vertically upward; the two are equal and opposite (balanced forces). For a book in free fall only one downward arrow (weight) is drawn.
Parallel forces are forces whose lines of action are parallel to each other. Like parallel forces act in the same direction: for example, when a heavy box is lifted by two supports, or by two persons, both upward forces are like parallel forces, and their resultant is the sum of their magnitudes. Unlike parallel forces act in opposite directions: for example, the two hands on a steering wheel push one side up and the other side down; these unlike parallel forces tend to rotate the wheel, and their resultant is the difference of their magnitudes.

Q: 2. Explain the addition of forces, in connection with head to tail rule.

Ans: Addition of forces means finding a single force, called the resultant force (or net force), which produces the same effect as all the given forces acting together. Because force is a vector, forces are added geometrically by the head-to-tail rule, using these steps: (i) choose a suitable scale and draw the first force vector F_A from an origin, at its correct angle with the x-axis; (ii) place the tail of the second force vector F_B on the head of F_A, drawn to the same scale and in its own direction; (iii) join the tail of F_A (the origin) to the head of F_B — this line, with an arrow pointing away from the origin, is the resultant F_R, so F_R = F_A + F_B; (iv) measure the length of F_R and convert it back through the scale to get its magnitude, and measure its angle theta_R with the x-axis with a protractor to get its direction. The rule extends to any number of forces by placing each next vector's tail on the previous vector's head. For like parallel forces the magnitudes simply add, and for unlike parallel forces they subtract.

Q: 3. Define moment of a force. Give its mathematical description and elaborate the factors on which it depends?

Ans: The turning effect produced in a body about a fixed point (pivot) by an applied force is called the moment of the force, or torque. Torque is the rotational counterpart of force: just as force changes translational motion, torque changes rotational motion. Mathematically, torque = force applied x perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force, i.e. tau = F x d, where d is called the moment arm (or lever arm). Its SI unit is the newton metre (N m). By convention anticlockwise torque is taken as positive and clockwise torque as negative.
The torque depends on these factors: (1) the magnitude of the applied force — greater force gives greater torque; (2) the moment arm — the greater the perpendicular distance from the axis, the greater the torque, which is why door handles are fitted far from the hinges; (3) the direction/line of action of the force — if the force is not perpendicular, only the perpendicular distance from the axis to the (extended) line of action counts, and if the line of action passes through the axis (d = 0) the torque is zero, however large the force.

Q: 4. What is resolution of forces? Explain with an example how forces can be resolved into rectangular components.

Ans: Resolution of forces is the process of splitting a single force vector into two or more component vectors whose combined effect is the same as the original force; it is the reverse of addition of forces. When the components are perpendicular to each other they are called rectangular components. Consider a force F acting at an angle theta with the x-axis, represented by the line OP. Dropping perpendiculars from P to the two axes gives the components along the axes. From the right-angled triangle so formed, cos theta = F_x / F and sin theta = F_y / F, therefore F_x = F cos theta (horizontal component) and F_y = F sin theta (vertical component). Conversely, F = sqrt(F_x^2 + F_y^2) and theta = tan^-1(F_y / F_x).
Example: a boy pulls an ice block with a rope, the force F acting at an angle above the horizontal. The component F_x = F cos theta along the ground actually drags the block forward, while the component F_y = F sin theta acts upward and partly lifts the block, reducing the normal reaction. Resolving forces in this way lets us add forces analytically, without scale drawings.

Q: 5. What is couple? Explain with examples.

Ans: A couple is a pair of two equal and opposite parallel forces acting along different lines of action on a body. Because the two forces are equal and opposite, their resultant force is zero, so a couple produces no translation; it produces only rotation, i.e. a pure moment (torque). The moment of a couple is equal to one force multiplied by the shortest (perpendicular) distance between the two forces, called the couple arm, and it has the same value about every point of the body.
Examples: (1) turning a steering wheel, where the two hands apply equal and opposite forces on opposite sides of the wheel; (2) winding the spring of a toy car or a clock with two fingers; (3) opening or closing the cap of a bottle; (4) turning a water tap; (5) pushing the pedals of a bicycle, where the feet apply a couple to the crank. In each case the body rotates without being pushed bodily in any direction.

Q: 6. Define equilibrium. Explain its types and state the two conditions of equilibrium.

Ans: Equilibrium is the state of a body in which, under the action of several forces acting together, there is no change in its translational motion as well as its rotational motion. The study of objects in equilibrium is called statics.
Types of equilibrium: (A) Static equilibrium — the body is at rest under the action of several forces and torques; for example, a book resting on a table, whose weight is balanced by the normal reaction of the table. (B) Dynamic equilibrium — the body keeps moving with uniform velocity. It is of two kinds: (i) dynamic translational equilibrium, e.g. a paratrooper falling down with constant velocity; (ii) dynamic rotational equilibrium, e.g. a compact disc (CD) rotating in a CD player with constant angular velocity.
Two conditions of equilibrium: First condition — the vector sum of all the forces acting on the body must be zero: F_net = F_1 + F_2 + F_3 + ... + F_n = 0, i.e. the force polygon must close; this prevents translation. Second condition — the vector sum of all the torques acting on the body must be zero: tau_net = tau_1 + tau_2 + ... + tau_n = 0; this prevents rotation. Both conditions must be satisfied together for complete equilibrium.

Q: 7. State and explain principle of moments with examples.

Ans: The principle of moments is another statement of the second condition of equilibrium. It states: for an object in equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments taken about the pivot must be equal to the sum of the anti-clockwise moments taken about the same pivot. In other words, the total torque about the pivot is zero.
Explanation: each moment is calculated as force x perpendicular distance from the pivot. Moments trying to turn the body clockwise are balanced by moments trying to turn it anticlockwise. Example 1 (seesaw): a child of weight 600 N sitting 1 m from the pivot produces an anticlockwise moment of 600 N x 1 m = 600 N m; a second child of weight 400 N sitting 1.5 m on the other side produces a clockwise moment of 400 N x 1.5 m = 600 N m. The moments are equal, so the seesaw balances. Example 2 (metre rule on a pivot): a weight of 3 N hung 0.2 m to one side of the pivot (moment 0.6 N m) is balanced by a weight of 1 N hung 0.6 m to the other side (moment 0.6 N m). The principle is used in beam balances and in finding the weight of an unknown object.

Q: 8. What is center of mass or center of gravity. Explain how CM/CG can be determined? Is there any difference between CM and CG?

Ans: The centre of mass (CM) of a body is the point about which its mass is equally distributed in all directions; the whole mass of the body may be imagined to be concentrated at this point, and it is the point that moves like a single particle under a net force. The centre of gravity (CG) is the point at which the whole weight of the body appears to act; the distributed pull of gravity on all parts of the body can be replaced by a single force (the weight) acting at the CG.
Determination: for a homogeneous (uniform) symmetric object the CM/CG lies at its geometric centre — the centre of a sphere, cube or circular disc, and on the axis of a cylinder or cone. For an irregular object it is found by the suspension (plumb-line) method: hang the object freely from one point and draw the vertical plumb line through that point; repeat by hanging it from at least two or three other points. The point where all the plumb lines intersect is the centre of gravity (and centre of mass), as is done for a bicycle in the book. The CM/CG may even lie outside the material of the body, e.g. for a banana or a bent leg.
Difference: strictly, CM depends only on the distribution of mass, while CG depends on the distribution of weight, i.e. on the gravitational field. Since g decreases with altitude, for a very large body the CG is slightly different from the CM; but for ordinary small objects the variation of g over the body is negligible, so the CG and CM coincide and the two terms are used interchangeably.

Q: 9. Explain the stability of the objects with reference to position of center of mass.

Ans: Stability is a measure of how hard it is to displace an object from equilibrium, and it is governed by what happens to the centre of mass when the object is slightly displaced. There are three states. (a) Stable equilibrium: on slight displacement the centre of mass rises, and on release the weight acts with a moment about the point of contact that restores the object to its original position — e.g. a cone standing on its wide base, or a ball at the bottom of a bowl. (b) Unstable equilibrium: on slight displacement the centre of mass falls, and the moment of the weight increases the displacement, so the object topples — e.g. a cone balanced on its tip, or a ball on top of an upturned bowl. (c) Neutral equilibrium: on displacement the centre of mass neither rises nor falls and the object stays in its new position — e.g. a cone lying on its side, or a ball on a flat surface.
An object remains stable as long as the vertical line from its centre of mass falls inside the area of its base; once a disturbance pushes this line outside the base, the object topples. Stability is therefore improved by (i) lowering the centre of mass and (ii) increasing the area of support (base). That is why racing cars are built low with wide tyres, and why the bases of tall glasses and reading lamps are made heavy and wide.

mcqs.q: In a force diagram for a book resting on a table, which arrows are drawn from the dot?
options: Weight downward and the table's normal force upward, equal and opposite
mcqs.why: A force diagram reduces the object to a dot at its centre of mass with each force as an arrow. A resting book has weight vertically downward balanced by the normal force vertically upward.

mcqs.q: Like parallel forces act in the same direction, so their resultant is
mcqs.why: Like parallel forces act in the same direction, for example two persons lifting a heavy box upward, and their resultant is the sum of their magnitudes; unlike parallel forces give the difference.

mcqs.q: In the head-to-tail rule, the resultant is drawn
options: from the head of the first force to its tail
between the two force heads only
from the tail of the first force to the head of the last force
mcqs.why: Draw the first force, place the second force's tail on its head, then join the tail of the first to the head of the last; that line is the resultant FR = FA + FB, measured for magnitude and angle.

mcqs.q: The moment of a force (torque) is given by
options: tau = F x v, in joules
tau = F x d, in newton metres, with anticlockwise taken as positive
mcqs.why: Torque is force times the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action, tau = F x d, with SI unit N m. By convention anticlockwise torque is positive and clockwise is negative.

mcqs.q: A force F at angle theta to the x-axis resolves into rectangular components
options: Fx = F cos theta and Fy = F sin theta
Fx = F sin theta and Fy = F cos theta
Fx = F / cos theta and Fy = F / sin theta
Fx = F theta and Fy = F / theta
mcqs.why: From the right-angled triangle of components, cos theta = Fx/F and sin theta = Fy/F, giving Fx = F cos theta and Fy = F sin theta, with F = sqrt(Fx^2 + Fy^2).

mcqs.q: A couple produces
options: only rotation, with zero resultant force
mcqs.why: A couple is two equal and opposite parallel forces on different lines of action; their resultant force is zero so there is no translation, only a pure moment equal to one force times the couple arm.

mcqs.q: The two conditions of equilibrium are
options: net force zero and net torque zero
mcqs.why: First condition: the vector sum of all forces is zero, preventing translation. Second condition: the vector sum of all torques is zero, preventing rotation. Both must hold together for complete equilibrium.

mcqs.q: The principle of moments states that for a body in equilibrium
options: all moments about the pivot are zero individually
clockwise moments are twice anticlockwise moments
moments depend only on the forces, not their distances
the sum of clockwise moments about the pivot equals the sum of anticlockwise moments
mcqs.why: Each moment is force x perpendicular distance from the pivot. In the seesaw example, 600 N x 1 m = 600 N m anticlockwise balances 400 N x 1.5 m = 600 N m clockwise, so the seesaw balances.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between centre of mass and centre of gravity?
options: CM depends on mass distribution; CG depends on the gravitational field, and they coincide for ordinary small objects
There is never any difference for any body
CG depends on mass only; CM depends on gravity only
CM is always outside the body; CG is always inside
mcqs.why: Strictly, CM depends only on how mass is distributed, while CG depends on weight distribution, i.e. on g, which decreases with altitude. For small objects the variation of g is negligible, so CM and CG coincide.

mcqs.q: In stable equilibrium, a slight displacement
options: lowers the centre of mass, and the object topples
raises the centre of mass, and the weight's moment restores the object
leaves the centre of mass at the same height
removes the centre of mass from the base
mcqs.why: A cone on its wide base is in stable equilibrium: displacement raises its centre of mass and the restoring moment returns it. Stability improves by lowering the centre of mass and widening the base of support.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems and Assignments
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Assignment 4.1: forces 25 N at 20 degrees and 10 N at 60 degrees give Rx = 28.49 N, Ry = 17.21 N, resultant 33.3 N at 31 degrees with the x-axis.
  • Assignment 4.2: components Fx = 85 N and Fy = 13 N give a force of 86 N at 8.7 degrees above the horizontal.
  • Assignment 4.3: a 20 N m torque with a 0.1 m opener arm needs a force of 200 N; Assignment 4.4: masses at 0.4 m and 0.5 m balance when m1 = 2 kg if m2 = 1.6 kg.
  • Extension 4.1: drawing FB before FA makes no difference, because vector addition is commutative. Extension 4.2: Sanaan (400 N) has mass 40.8 kg and Romaisa (600 N) has mass 61.2 kg.
  • Self Assessment: a sledgehammer's centre of mass is on the handle just below the massive head. Concept Test: the largest torque comes from a perpendicular force farthest from the axis.
  • Numerical 1: 15 N at 30 degrees resolves to Fx about 13 N and Fy = 7.5 N. Numerical 2: a 40 N m torque with a 0.25 m wrench needs 160 N.
  • Numerical 3: Faiz (52 kg) balances Sana (43 kg at 1.8 m) at about 1.5 m. Numerical 4: a 250 N third kid sits 0.6 m from the centre on the 300 N kid's side. Numerical 5: the second child must push with 24 N at 0.50 m.
  • Numerical 6: lifting 1500 kg (weight 14,700 N) gives a moment of 294,000 N m at a 20 m arm and 176,400 N m at a 12 m arm.

Solved Exercises

Assignment 4.1 — HEAD TO TAIL RULE

Q: Two forces are applied one force is 25 N [20° with x-axis] and the other force is 10 N [60° with x-axis], find the net resultant force.

Ans: Given: F_A = 25 N at 20 degrees with the x-axis, F_B = 10 N at 60 degrees with the x-axis.
Resolve each force into rectangular components.
Formula: F_x = F cos theta and F_y = F sin theta.
For F_A: F_Ax = 25 x cos 20° = 25 x 0.940 = 23.49 N.
For F_A: F_Ay = 25 x sin 20° = 25 x 0.342 = 8.55 N.
For F_B: F_Bx = 10 x cos 60° = 10 x 0.500 = 5.00 N.
For F_B: F_By = 10 x sin 60° = 10 x 0.866 = 8.66 N.
Add the components: R_x = 23.49 + 5.00 = 28.49 N.
Add the components: R_y = 8.55 + 8.66 = 17.21 N.
Formula: R = sqrt(R_x^2 + R_y^2).
Substitution: R = sqrt(28.49^2 + 17.21^2) = sqrt(811.7 + 296.2) = sqrt(1107.9).
So R = 33.3 N.
Formula for direction: theta = tan^-1(R_y / R_x).
Substitution: theta = tan^-1(17.21 / 28.49) = tan^-1(0.604) = 31 degrees with the x-axis.
Answer: 33.3 N at 31 degrees with the x-axis

Q: Note on Assignment 4.1

Ans: The book's printed key gives 30 N; the correct answer is 33.3 N at 31 degrees with the x-axis, because resolving the two forces into rectangular components and adding them (as done above) gives R_x = 28.49 N and R_y = 17.21 N, whose resultant is 33.3 N. The key's value appears to be a rough estimate from a scale (head-to-tail) drawing.

Assignment 4.2 — TILLING GARDEN

Q: While tilling your garden, you exert a force on the handles of the tiller that has components F_x = 85 N and F_y = 13 N. The x-axis is horizontal and the y-axis points up. What are the magnitude and direction of this force?

Ans: Given: F_x = 85 N, F_y = 13 N.
Formula: F = sqrt(F_x^2 + F_y^2).
Substitution: F = sqrt(85^2 + 13^2) = sqrt(7225 + 169) = sqrt(7394).
So F = 86 N.
Formula for direction: theta = tan^-1(F_y / F_x).
Substitution: theta = tan^-1(13 / 85) = tan^-1(0.153) = 8.7 degrees above the horizontal.
Answer: 86 N at 8.7 degrees above the x-axis

Assignment 4.3 — FORCE ON BOTTLE OPENER

Q: 20 Nm torque is required to open a soda bottle. A boy with a bottle opener apply a force perpendicularly at 0.1 m, what is the magnitude of force required.

Ans: Given: torque tau = 20 N m, moment arm d = 0.1 m, force applied perpendicularly.
Formula: tau = F x d, so F = tau / d.
Substitution: F = 20 N m / 0.1 m.
F = 200 N.
Answer: 200 N

Assignment 4.4 — CALCULATING MASSES

Q: With a beam two masses m_1 and m_2 are suspended at distance 0.4 m and 0.5 m respectively from suspension point as shown in the figure. Ignoring the weight of the balance, if m_2 = 1.6 kg, what is the mass m_1?

Ans: Diagram (in words): A horizontal beam is suspended from a point marked near its middle. A mass m_1 = ? kg hangs from the beam on the left of the suspension point at distance d_1 = 0.4 m. A mass m_2 = 1.6 kg hangs from the beam on the right of the suspension point at distance d_2 = 0.5 m. The beam is balanced horizontally.
Given: d_1 = 0.4 m, d_2 = 0.5 m, m_2 = 1.6 kg.
For balance, the principle of moments applies: anticlockwise moment = clockwise moment.
Formula: m_1 x g x d_1 = m_2 x g x d_2, so m_1 = m_2 x d_2 / d_1 (g cancels).
Substitution: m_1 = 1.6 kg x 0.5 m / 0.4 m.
m_1 = 0.8 / 0.4 = 2.0 kg.
Answer: 2 kg

Extension Exercise 4.1

Q: Will it make any difference if you first draw F_B and then F_A to find the resultant? (In the text the resultant of forces F_A and F_B is found by the head to tail rule, giving F_R = 31 N at 30 degrees with the x-axis.)

Ans: No, it will make no difference.
Vector addition is commutative: F_A + F_B = F_B + F_A. In the head to tail rule, whether we draw F_A first and place the tail of F_B on its head, or draw F_B first and place the tail of F_A on its head, the arrow drawn from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last vector is the same.
The resultant is therefore unchanged, with the same magnitude and the same direction (in the text's measurement, F_R = 31 N at 30 degrees with the x-axis).
Answer: No difference — the resultant force is the same.

Extension Exercise 4.2

Q: Find the mass of Sanaan and Romaisa. (Example 4.4: Romaisa's weight is 600 N and Sanaan's weight, found from the balanced seesaw, is 400 N.)

Ans: Given: weight of Romaisa W_R = 600 N; weight of Sanaan W_S = 400 N; acceleration due to gravity g = 9.8 m/s^2
Formula: weight W = m g, so mass m = W / g
Substitution (Sanaan): m_S = 400 N / 9.8 m/s^2
Working: m_S = 40.8 kg
Substitution (Romaisa): m_R = 600 N / 9.8 m/s^2
Working: m_R = 61.2 kg
Answer: Mass of Sanaan: 40.8 kg; mass of Romaisa: 61.2 kg.

Self Assessment

Q: A sledgehammer has a massive metal head attached to a much lighter wooden handle. Which location is most likely to be the sledgehammer's center of mass?

Ans: Diagram (in words): The figure shows three identical sledgehammers standing upright side by side, each labelled at the left 'massive head' (the heavy metal head at the top) and 'lighter handle' (the long wooden handle below it). A red cross mark X shows a candidate position on each hammer: on hammer (a) the X is about halfway down the handle; on hammer (b) the X is in the middle of the massive head itself; on hammer (c) the X is on the handle just below the head.
The center of mass lies closer to the part of the body that carries more mass. Most of the sledgehammer's mass is in its metal head, so the center of mass must be near the head — position (a), halfway down the handle, is far too low.
But the handle is not massless: its mass is spread along the whole handle and pulls the balance point a little way down from the centre of the head itself, so the center of mass sits just below the head, not inside it.
Answer: Location (c) — on the handle just below the massive head.

Concept Test

Q: Which force of equal magnitude will produce larger torque?

Ans: Diagram (in words): The box shows two diagrams of the same horizontal bar, each with its 'axis of rotation' marked at the left-hand end and an empty tick box beside it. In the UPPER diagram three upward arrows of equal length, labelled F_1, F_2 and F_3, push up on the bar at increasing distances from the axis (F_1 nearest the axis, F_3 at the far end), and all three forces act perpendicular to the bar. In the LOWER diagram the same three forces act at the same three points, but F_1 and F_3 are slanted at an angle to the bar and only F_2 acts perpendicular to it.
Formula: torque = force x moment arm, where the moment arm is the perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force.
In the upper diagram every force acts perpendicular to the bar, so each moment arm is the full distance of its point from the axis, and the torques are as large as possible.
In the lower diagram the slanted forces F_1 and F_3 have only a part of their magnitude acting perpendicular to the bar, so their effective moment arms are shortened and their torques are smaller.
Within either diagram, F_3 — applied farthest from the axis — has the largest moment arm and so produces the largest single torque.
Answer: The upper arrangement produces the larger torque (tick the upper box): forces of equal magnitude produce the largest torque when they act perpendicular to the bar and farthest from the axis of rotation, as F_3 does there.

Exercise — Numerical Problems

Q: 1. To open a door force of 15 N is applied at 30° to the horizontal, find the horizontal and vertical components of force.

Ans: Given: force F = 15 N, angle theta = 30 degrees with the horizontal.
Formula: horizontal component F_x = F cos theta.
Substitution: F_x = 15 N x cos 30° = 15 x 0.866 = 12.99 N, about 13 N.
Formula: vertical component F_y = F sin theta.
Substitution: F_y = 15 N x sin 30° = 15 x 0.500 = 7.5 N.
Answer: horizontal component 13 N, vertical component 7.5 N

Q: 2. A bolt on a car engine needs to be tightened with a torque of 40 Nm. You use a 25-cm-long wrench and pull on the end of the wrench perpendicularly. How much force do you have to exert?

Ans: Given: torque tau = 40 N m, moment arm d = 25 cm = 0.25 m, force applied perpendicularly at the end of the wrench.
Formula: tau = F x d, so F = tau / d.
Substitution: F = 40 N m / 0.25 m.
F = 160 N.
Answer: 160 N

Q: 3. Sana, whose mass is 43 kg, sits 1.8 m from the center of a seesaw. Faiz, whose mass is 52 kg, wants to balance Sana. How far from the center of the seesaw should Faiz sit?

Ans: Given: Sana's mass m_S = 43 kg at distance d_S = 1.8 m; Faiz's mass m_F = 52 kg at distance d_F = ?
For balance, apply the principle of moments about the centre: clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment.
Formula: m_F x g x d_F = m_S x g x d_S, so d_F = m_S x d_S / m_F (g cancels).
Substitution: d_F = 43 kg x 1.8 m / 52 kg.
d_F = 77.4 / 52 = 1.49 m, about 1.5 m.
Answer: 1.5 m from the center

Q: 4. Two kids of weighing 300 N and 350 N are sitting at the ends of 6 m long see-saw. The seesaw is pivoted at its centre. Where would a third kid sit so that the see-saw is in equilibrium in the horizontal position? The weight of third kid is 250 N. (Ignore the weight of see-saw)

Ans: Given: kid 1 weight W_1 = 300 N at one end, kid 2 weight W_2 = 350 N at the other end; seesaw length 6 m, pivoted at centre, so each end is 3 m from the pivot; third kid weight W_3 = 250 N.
Moment of the 300 N kid about the pivot: 300 N x 3 m = 900 N m (anticlockwise).
Moment of the 350 N kid about the pivot: 350 N x 3 m = 1050 N m (clockwise).
Excess clockwise moment = 1050 - 900 = 150 N m.
The third kid must sit on the side of the 300 N kid to supply an opposing moment of 150 N m.
Formula: W_3 x d = 150 N m, so d = 150 / W_3.
Substitution: d = 150 N m / 250 N = 0.6 m.
Answer: 0.6 m from the centre, on the side of the 300 N kid

Q: 5. Two children push on opposite sides of a door during play. Both push horizontally and perpendicular to the door. One child pushes with a force of 20 N at a distance of 0.60 m from the hinges, and the second child pushes at a distance of 0.50 m. What force must the second child exert to keep the door from moving? Assume friction is negligible.

Ans: Given: first force F_1 = 20 N at d_1 = 0.60 m from the hinges; second child pushes at d_2 = 0.50 m with force F_2 = ?
For the door to stay still, the opposing torques must balance (second condition of equilibrium).
Formula: F_2 x d_2 = F_1 x d_1, so F_2 = F_1 x d_1 / d_2.
Substitution: F_2 = 20 N x 0.60 m / 0.50 m.
F_2 = 12 / 0.50 = 24 N.
Answer: 24 N

Q: 6. A construction crane lifts building material of mass 1500 kg by moving its crane arm, calculate moment of force when moment arm is 20 m. After lifting the crane arm, which reduces moment arm to 12 m calculate moment.

Ans: Given: mass m = 1500 kg, g = 9.8 m/s^2, moment arms 20 m and 12 m.
First find the weight (force) of the material.
Formula: W = m x g.
Substitution: W = 1500 kg x 9.8 m/s^2 = 14,700 N.
Case 1: moment arm d = 20 m.
Formula: moment = W x d.
Substitution: moment = 14,700 N x 20 m = 294,000 N m.
Case 2: moment arm reduced to d = 12 m.
Formula: moment = W x d.
Substitution: moment = 14,700 N x 12 m = 176,400 N m.
Answer: 294,000 N m at 20 m arm, and 176,400 N m at 12 m arm

mcqs.q: Two forces, 25 N at 20 degrees and 10 N at 60 degrees to the x-axis, act together. What is the magnitude of their resultant?
mcqs.why: Formula: resolve, Rx = 25 cos20 + 10 cos60, Ry = 25 sin20 + 10 sin60, then R = sqrt(Rx^2 + Ry^2). Substitution: Rx = 23.49 + 5.00 = 28.49 N, Ry = 8.55 + 8.66 = 17.21 N, R = sqrt(811.7 + 296.2) = sqrt(1107.9). Final result: 33.3 N. The book's key gives 30 N, which is wrong; it appears to be a rough scale-drawing estimate.

mcqs.q: For the same two forces (25 N at 20 degrees and 10 N at 60 degrees), what is the resultant's direction?
mcqs.why: Formula: theta = tan^-1(Ry / Rx). Substitution: with Rx = 28.49 N and Ry = 17.21 N, theta = tan^-1(17.21 / 28.49) = tan^-1(0.604). Step: tan^-1(0.604) is about 31 degrees. Final result: 31 degrees with the x-axis.

mcqs.q: A tiller force has components Fx = 85 N and Fy = 13 N. What is the magnitude of the force?
mcqs.why: Formula: F = sqrt(Fx^2 + Fy^2). Substitution: F = sqrt(85^2 + 13^2) = sqrt(7225 + 169) = sqrt(7394). Step: sqrt(7394) is about 86. Final result: 86 N, at 8.7 degrees above the horizontal.

mcqs.q: A torque of 20 N m is needed to open a bottle. The opener applies force perpendicularly at 0.1 m. What force is required?
mcqs.why: Formula: tau = F x d, so F = tau / d. Substitution: F = 20 N m / 0.1 m. Step: 20 / 0.1 = 200. Final result: 200 N.

mcqs.q: Masses hang at 0.4 m (m1, unknown) and 0.5 m (m2 = 1.6 kg) from a beam's suspension point and balance. What is m1?
mcqs.why: Formula: principle of moments m1 x g x d1 = m2 x g x d2, so m1 = m2 x d2 / d1 with g cancelling. Substitution: m1 = 1.6 kg x 0.5 m / 0.4 m = 0.8 / 0.4. Step: 0.8 / 0.4 = 2.0. Final result: 2 kg.

mcqs.q: Will drawing FB first and then FA, instead of FA then FB, change the resultant found by the head-to-tail rule?
options: No, vector addition is commutative, so the resultant is the same
No, but only if the forces are equal
mcqs.why: Vector addition is commutative: FA + FB = FB + FA. In the head-to-tail rule either order gives the same arrow from the first tail to the last head, with the same magnitude and direction.

mcqs.q: Romaisa weighs 600 N and Sanaan weighs 400 N (g = 9.8 m/s^2). What are their masses?
options: Sanaan 40 kg and Romaisa 60 kg exactly from these divisions
mcqs.why: Formula: m = W / g from W = mg. Substitution: Sanaan m = 400 N / 9.8 m/s^2 = 40.8 kg; Romaisa m = 600 N / 9.8 m/s^2 = 61.2 kg. Step: each division is carried out as shown. Final result: Sanaan 40.8 kg, Romaisa 61.2 kg.

mcqs.q: Where is the centre of mass of a sledgehammer (massive metal head, much lighter wooden handle) most likely to be?
options: In the middle of the massive head itself
At the bottom end of the handle
On the handle just below the massive head
mcqs.why: Most of the mass is in the head, so the centre of mass is near the head, but the handle's mass spread along its length pulls the balance point a little below the head, onto the handle just below it (position c).

mcqs.q: Forces of equal magnitude act on a bar. Which arrangement produces the largest torque?
options: Forces acting perpendicular to the bar, farthest from the axis of rotation
Forces slanted to the bar, nearest the axis
Forces acting along the bar itself
Forces applied at the axis of rotation
mcqs.why: Torque equals force times moment arm, the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of action. Perpendicular forces use the full distance as moment arm, and the farthest force (F3) has the largest arm, so the upper, perpendicular arrangement gives the largest torque.

mcqs.q: A force of 15 N is applied at 30 degrees to the horizontal to open a door. What is its horizontal component?
mcqs.why: Formula: Fx = F cos theta. Substitution: Fx = 15 N x cos 30 degrees = 15 x 0.866. Step: 15 x 0.866 = 12.99. Final result: about 13 N. The vertical component is Fy = 15 x sin30 = 7.5 N.

mcqs.q: A bolt needs a torque of 40 N m. A 25 cm wrench is pulled perpendicularly at its end. How much force is needed?
mcqs.why: Formula: tau = F x d, so F = tau / d. Substitution: d = 25 cm = 0.25 m, so F = 40 N m / 0.25 m. Step: 40 / 0.25 = 160. Final result: 160 N.

mcqs.q: Sana (43 kg) sits 1.8 m from a seesaw's centre. How far from the centre must Faiz (52 kg) sit to balance her?
mcqs.why: Formula: principle of moments mF x g x dF = mS x g x dS, so dF = mS x dS / mF with g cancelling. Substitution: dF = 43 kg x 1.8 m / 52 kg = 77.4 / 52. Step: 77.4 / 52 = 1.49. Final result: about 1.5 m from the centre.

mcqs.q: Kids of 300 N and 350 N sit at the ends of a 6 m seesaw pivoted at its centre. Where must a 250 N kid sit to balance it?
options: 0.6 m from the centre, on the side of the 300 N kid
0.6 m from the centre, on the side of the 350 N kid
3 m from the centre, on the side of the 300 N kid
At the centre of the seesaw
mcqs.why: Formula: moments about the pivot: 300 x 3 = 900 N m and 350 x 3 = 1050 N m, excess clockwise 150 N m, then d = 150 / W3. Substitution: d = 150 N m / 250 N. Step: 150 / 250 = 0.6. Final result: 0.6 m from the centre on the 300 N kid's side.

mcqs.q: One child pushes a door with 20 N at 0.60 m from the hinges. A second child pushes at 0.50 m on the other side. What force keeps the door still?
mcqs.why: Formula: balancing torques F2 x d2 = F1 x d1, so F2 = F1 x d1 / d2. Substitution: F2 = 20 N x 0.60 m / 0.50 m = 12 / 0.50. Step: 12 / 0.50 = 24. Final result: 24 N.

mcqs.q: A crane lifts 1500 kg of material with a moment arm of 20 m (g = 9.8 m/s^2). What is the moment of the force?
mcqs.why: Formula: first W = m x g, then moment = W x d. Substitution: W = 1500 kg x 9.8 m/s^2 = 14,700 N, then moment = 14,700 N x 20 m. Step: 14,700 x 20 = 294,000. Final result: 294,000 N m; at a 12 m arm it is 176,400 N m.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Newton's law of gravitation: F = G m_1 m_2 / r^2, with G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2.
  • Doubling both masses multiplies the gravitational force by 4; doubling the distance divides it by 4.
  • The radius of Earth r_E is 6.4 x 10^6 m and the mass of Earth is 6 x 10^24 kg.
  • Mass is the same everywhere; an object weighing 784 N on Earth has mass 784 / 9.8 = 80.0 kg on Mercury too.
  • The value of g on the Moon's surface is 1.63 m/s^2, about one-sixth of Earth's 9.8 m/s^2.
  • The value of g decreases with altitude and is smaller at the equator than at the poles.
  • Orbital speed v = sqrt(G m_E / r): if the planet's mass increases 4 times at the same radius, the orbital speed doubles.
  • Moving a body from sea level to a mountain top changes its weight, not its mass.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Multiple Choice Questions

Q: 1. Two masses are separated by a distance r. If both masses are doubled, the force of interaction between the two masses changes by a factor

Options: (a) 2 (b) 4 (c) 1/2 (d) 1/4

Correct answer: 4

Q: 2. The radius of earth r_E is

Options: (a) 9.8 m (b) 6.67 x 10^-11 m (c) 6 x 10^24 m (d) 6.4 x 10^6 m

Correct answer: 6.4 x 10^6 m

Q: 3. The S.I. unit for gravitational constant 'G' is

Options: (a) N kg^2 (b) N m^2 kg^-2 (c) N m^2 kg^2 (d) N m^-2 kg^2

Correct answer: N m^2 kg^-2

Q: 4. What is the mass on planet Mercury of an object that weighs 784 N on the earth's surface?

Options: (a) 80.0 kg (b) 118 (c) 784 kg (d) More information needed

Correct answer: 80.0 kg

Q: 5. An object is orbiting a planet with orbital speed v, if the radius is same and mass is increased 4 times, by what factor orbital speed will change

Options: (a) 2 (b) 4 (c) 1/2 (d) 1/4

Correct answer: 2

Q: 6. The value of 'g' at the surface of the moon is;

Options: (a) 9.8 m/s^2 (b) 1.63 m/s^2 (c) 4.9 m/s^2 (d) 8.9 m/s^2

Correct answer: 1.63 m/s^2

Q: 7. The value of 'g' __________ with altitude

Options: (a) increases (b) decreases (c) gets ZERO (d) remains the same

Correct answer: decreases

Q: 8. When a body is moved from sea level to the top of a mountain, There is change in the body's

Options: (a) mass (b) weight (c) none (d) both mass and weight

Correct answer: weight

Q: 9. The value of 'g' at equator is

Options: (a) Same at poles (b) Larger at poles (c) Smaller at poles (d) none

Correct answer: Smaller at poles

mcqs.q: Two masses are separated by a distance r. If both masses are doubled, the force of interaction between the two masses changes by a factor
mcqs.why: F = G m_1 m_2 / r^2 is proportional to the product of the masses. Doubling each mass makes the product 2 x 2 = 4 times larger, so the force changes by a factor of 4.

mcqs.q: The radius of earth r_E is
mcqs.why: The radius of Earth used throughout this unit is r_E = 6.4 x 10^6 m. The other values are g (9.8 m/s^2), the constant G and the mass of Earth, not its radius.

mcqs.q: The S.I. unit for gravitational constant 'G' is
mcqs.why: From F = G m_1 m_2 / r^2, G = F r^2 / (m_1 m_2), so its unit is N x m^2 / kg^2, written N m^2 kg^-2.

mcqs.q: What is the mass on planet Mercury of an object that weighs 784 N on the earth's surface?
mcqs.why: Mass does not change from planet to planet. On Earth, m = W / g = 784 N / 9.8 m/s^2 = 80.0 kg, and the mass on Mercury is the same 80.0 kg; only the weight would change there.

mcqs.q: An object is orbiting a planet with orbital speed v, if the radius is same and mass is increased 4 times, by what factor orbital speed will change
mcqs.why: Orbital speed v = sqrt(G M / r). At the same radius, v is proportional to sqrt(M). Increasing the mass 4 times multiplies v by sqrt(4) = 2.

mcqs.q: The value of 'g' at the surface of the moon is;
mcqs.why: The Moon's small mass gives a surface gravity of only 1.63 m/s^2, about one-sixth of Earth's 9.8 m/s^2, as also found in Assignment 5.3 (1.62 m/s^2).

mcqs.q: The value of 'g' __________ with altitude
mcqs.why: g_h = g x r_E^2 / (r_E + h)^2. As altitude h grows, the denominator grows, so g decreases steadily, though it never becomes exactly zero at any finite height.

mcqs.q: When a body is moved from sea level to the top of a mountain, There is change in the body's
mcqs.why: Mass is a fixed property of the body and does not change with place. Weight W = m g changes because g is slightly smaller at the top of a mountain than at sea level.

mcqs.q: The value of 'g' at equator is
mcqs.why: Earth is flattened at the poles and rotating, so g at the equator (about 9.78 m/s^2) is smaller than at the poles (about 9.83 m/s^2): the value at the equator is smaller than at the poles.

mcqs.q: What is the value of the universal gravitational constant G?
mcqs.why: Every calculation in this unit uses G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2. It is called universal because it has this same value for all pairs of masses anywhere in the universe.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • We do not feel attraction towards buildings because G is tiny: a 70 kg person 1 m from a 10^6 kg building feels only about 4.7 x 10^-3 N, masked by weight and friction.
  • The Sun pulls Earth with exactly the same force as Earth pulls the Sun (action-reaction pair); only the accelerations differ because the masses differ.
  • G is universal (6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2 everywhere) and is needed for forces, planetary masses, g on other bodies and orbital speeds; it is hard to measure because attraction between laboratory masses is of order 10^-7 N or less - Cavendish used a sensitive torsion balance.
  • Weight follows g: at fixed Earth mass, doubling Earth's radius cuts weight to one-fourth (g varies as 1 / r_E^2); doubling Earth's mass at the same radius doubles g to 19.6 m/s^2 and doubles every weight, while masses stay unchanged.
  • All objects fall at the same rate because a = F / m = G m_E / r_E^2 = g: the falling body's own mass cancels out.
  • g varies only slightly over Earth, about 9.78 m/s^2 at the equator and 9.83 m/s^2 at the poles, so 9.8 m/s^2 is used for ordinary calculations.
  • The Moon keeps missing Earth: it falls continuously under gravity but its tangential velocity carries it around, gravity acting as the centripetal force.
  • At the same height all satellites have the same orbital speed v = sqrt(G m_E / r), because the satellite's own mass cancels out.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Conceptual Questions

Q: 1. If there is an attractive force between all objects, why don't we feel ourselves gravitating toward nearby massive buildings?

Ans: The gravitational force between ordinary objects is extremely small because the gravitational constant G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2 is very small. Even for a person of 70 kg standing 1 m from a building of, say, 10^6 kg, the force F = G m_1 m_2 / r^2 works out to only about 5 x 10^-6 N, which is far too weak to notice. It is also completely masked by two much larger effects: the enormous gravitational pull of the Earth (our weight, hundreds of newtons) and the friction between our feet and the ground, which easily resists such a tiny sideways pull. Only bodies of planetary mass produce noticeable gravitational attraction.

Q: 2. Does the sun exert a larger force on the Earth than that exerted on the sun by the Earth? Explain.

Ans: No. By Newton's law of gravitation the force depends on the product of the two masses and the distance between them, and these are the same whichever body we consider first. The Sun pulls the Earth with exactly the same magnitude of force with which the Earth pulls the Sun; the two forces form an action-reaction pair (Newton's third law), equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. Their effects are very different only because the masses are very different: the same force produces a large acceleration of the light Earth (which keeps it in orbit) but a negligibly small acceleration of the enormously massive Sun.

Q: 3. What is the importance of gravitational constant 'G'? Why is it difficult to calculate?

Ans: The gravitational constant G is needed in every quantitative use of the law of gravitation, F = G m_1 m_2 / r^2. Without knowing G we could not calculate the gravitational force between two bodies, the mass of the Earth or of other planets (m_E = g r_E^2 / G), the value of g on other bodies, or the orbital speeds of satellites. Its value, G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2, is universal — the same for all pairs of masses anywhere in the universe.
It is difficult to measure because gravity is an extremely weak force: the attraction between laboratory-sized masses is fantastically small (of the order of 10^-7 N or less), far below what ordinary balances can detect. Cavendish first measured it with a very sensitive torsion balance, in which the tiny twist of a fine wire caused by the attraction of lead spheres had to be measured, while air currents, vibrations and the attraction of surrounding objects all disturbed the experiment.

Q: 4. If Earth somehow expanded to a larger radius, with no change in mass, how would your weight be affected? How would it be affected if Earth instead shrunk?

Ans: Weight is W = m g, and on the surface g = G m_E / r_E^2, so g (and hence weight) varies inversely with the square of the Earth's radius when the mass stays the same. If the Earth expanded to a larger radius, we would be farther from its centre, g would decrease, and our weight would decrease; for example, doubling the radius would reduce g, and our weight, to one-fourth. If the Earth instead shrank to a smaller radius with the same mass, we would be closer to the centre, g would increase, and our weight would increase; halving the radius would make the weight four times greater. Our mass would remain unchanged in both cases.

Q: 5. What would happen to your weight on earth if the mass of the earth doubled, but its radius stayed the same?

Ans: Weight is W = m g with g = G m_E / r_E^2. The value of g is directly proportional to the mass of the Earth. If the Earth's mass doubled while its radius stayed the same, g would double from 9.8 m/s^2 to 19.6 m/s^2, and our weight would also double. A person weighing 600 N would then weigh 1200 N, although his own mass would be exactly the same as before.

Q: 6. Why lighter and heavier objects fall at the same rate toward the earth?

Ans: The acceleration of a falling body does not depend on its own mass. From the law of gravitation, the force on a body of mass m near the Earth's surface is F = G m_E m / r_E^2, and by Newton's second law a = F / m = G m_E / r_E^2 = g. The body's mass m cancels out: a heavier body is pulled with a proportionally greater force, but it also has proportionally greater inertia (resistance to acceleration), so the two effects exactly balance. Hence all objects, light or heavy, fall with the same acceleration g (about 9.8 m/s^2), provided air resistance is negligible.

Q: 7. The value of 'g' changes with location on earth, however we take same value of 'g' as 9.8 m/s^2 for ordinary calculations. Why?

Ans: The value of g varies only slightly over the Earth's surface: it is about 9.78 m/s^2 at the equator and about 9.83 m/s^2 at the poles, because the Earth is not a perfect sphere and because of its rotation. This total variation is only about half a percent, which is negligible for ordinary school-level calculations and for most practical purposes. Using the single standard value g = 9.8 m/s^2 everywhere keeps calculations simple while introducing an error too small to matter, except in very precise scientific work where the local value must be used.

Q: 8. Moon is attracted by the earth, why it does not fall on earth?

Ans: The Moon is in fact continuously falling towards the Earth under gravity, but it never reaches the Earth because it also has a large sideways (tangential) velocity. As it falls, the curved surface of the Earth falls away beneath it by the same amount, so the Moon keeps 'missing' the Earth and goes around it instead. The Earth's gravitational force acts as the centripetal force that continuously bends the Moon's path into a (nearly) circular orbit. If the Moon's tangential velocity were removed, it would indeed fall straight onto the Earth.

Q: 9. Why for same height larger and smaller satellites must have same orbital speeds?

Ans: The orbital speed is v = sqrt(G m_E / r), where r is the distance from the centre of the Earth. The satellite's own mass does not appear in this formula: in the derivation, the gravitational force G m_E m_s / r^2 provides the centripetal force m_s v^2 / r, and the satellite's mass m_s cancels from both sides. Therefore at the same height (same r) every satellite, large or small, heavy or light, must travel at the same orbital speed to stay in a circular orbit.

mcqs.q: A 70 kg person stands 1 m from a building of mass 10^6 kg. About how large is the gravitational force between them?
mcqs.why: Formula: F = G m_1 m_2 / r^2. Substitution: F = (6.67 x 10^-11) x 70 x 10^6 / (1)^2. Step by step: 70 x 10^6 = 7 x 10^7; 6.67 x 10^-11 x 7 x 10^7 = 46.7 x 10^-4 = 4.7 x 10^-3 N. Note: the source solution prints about 5 x 10^-6 N, which is an arithmetic slip (1000 times too small); the correct value is 4.7 x 10^-3 N, still far too weak to feel.

mcqs.q: Does the Sun exert a larger force on Earth than Earth exerts on the Sun?
options: Yes, because the Sun is much more massive
No, the two forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
Yes, because Earth is the one that orbits
No, because Earth exerts no force on the Sun
mcqs.why: In F = G m_1 m_2 / r^2 the product of the masses and the distance are the same whichever body is considered first, so both forces have the same magnitude. They form a Newton's third law action-reaction pair; only their effects differ because the masses differ.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the gravitational constant G is correct?
options: Its value changes from planet to planet
It is needed only for finding the mass of Earth
It equals 9.8 m/s^2 on Earth's surface
It is universal, G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2, the same everywhere
mcqs.why: G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2 is a universal constant, the same for all pairs of masses anywhere in the universe. Without it we could not calculate gravitational forces, planetary masses, g on other bodies or orbital speeds.

mcqs.q: Why is G so difficult to measure accurately?
options: Because gravity between laboratory masses is extremely weak, of order 10^-7 N or less
Because G changes during the experiment
Because no balance has ever been built
Because the masses must be placed in space
mcqs.why: The attraction between laboratory-sized masses is fantastically small, far below what ordinary balances detect. Cavendish first measured G with a very sensitive torsion balance, where air currents, vibrations and nearby objects all disturbed the tiny twist of the wire.

mcqs.q: If Earth expanded to twice its radius with no change in mass, your weight would become
mcqs.why: On the surface g = G m_E / r_E^2, so g varies as 1 / r_E^2. Doubling the radius gives g' = g / (2)^2 = g / 4. Since W = m g, your weight also falls to one-fourth, while your mass stays the same.

mcqs.q: If Earth's mass doubled while its radius stayed the same, a person weighing 600 N would weigh
mcqs.why: g = G m_E / r_E^2 is directly proportional to Earth's mass. Doubling m_E doubles g from 9.8 m/s^2 to 19.6 m/s^2. Weight W = m g therefore doubles: 2 x 600 N = 1200 N. The person's own mass is unchanged.

mcqs.q: Why do lighter and heavier objects fall towards Earth at the same rate?
options: Because air resistance is always zero
Because the heavier object is pulled less strongly
Because the object's mass cancels: a = F / m = G m_E / r_E^2 = g
Because both objects have the same weight
mcqs.why: The force on a body is F = G m_E m / r_E^2, and by Newton's second law a = F / m = G m_E / r_E^2 = g. The mass m cancels: a heavier body is pulled harder but has proportionally more inertia, so all objects fall with the same acceleration g when air resistance is negligible.

mcqs.q: Why is the single value g = 9.8 m/s^2 used for ordinary calculations even though g varies over Earth?
options: Because g is actually exactly the same everywhere
Because the variation is only about half a percent, 9.78 m/s^2 at the equator to 9.83 m/s^2 at the poles
Because calculators cannot handle other values
Because the variation is about 50 percent but is ignored
mcqs.why: g changes only slightly over Earth's surface, from about 9.78 m/s^2 at the equator to about 9.83 m/s^2 at the poles, a variation of only about 0.5 percent. That error is negligible for ordinary calculations, so the standard value 9.8 m/s^2 is used everywhere.

mcqs.q: The Moon is attracted by Earth, yet it does not fall onto Earth. Why?
options: Because no gravitational force acts on the Moon
Because the Moon is too far away to fall
Because the Moon's mass is too small to fall
Because it is continuously falling but its tangential velocity makes it keep missing Earth, gravity acting as centripetal force
mcqs.why: The Moon is in fact falling towards Earth all the time, but it also has a large sideways velocity. As it falls, Earth's curved surface falls away beneath it by the same amount, so it goes around instead. Gravity provides the centripetal force; remove the tangential velocity and it would fall straight onto Earth.

mcqs.q: Why must a large and a small satellite at the same height have the same orbital speed?
options: Because both are pulled by the same total force
Because the satellite's mass cancels in v = sqrt(G m_E / r), so speed depends only on the orbital radius
Because air resistance equalises their speeds
Because larger satellites are launched more slowly
mcqs.why: Setting the gravitational force equal to the centripetal force, G m_E m_s / r^2 = m_s v^2 / r, the satellite mass m_s cancels from both sides, leaving v = sqrt(G m_E / r). At the same height r is the same, so every satellite, large or small, needs the same orbital speed.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Law of universal gravitation: every body attracts every other body with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres.
  • The law obeys Newton's third law: the formula is symmetric in m_1 and m_2, so F_12 = -F_21, an equal and opposite action-reaction pair.
  • Mass of Earth from gravitation: m_E = g r_E^2 / G = 9.8 x (6.4 x 10^6)^2 / (6.67 x 10^-11) = 6.0 x 10^24 kg.
  • The gravitational field is the region around a mass where another mass experiences a force; field strength g = F_g / m, unit N/kg, directed towards the centre.
  • Weight W = m g changes with location because g changes: less on mountains, slightly less at the equator, and only about one-sixth on the Moon where g is about 1.6 m/s^2.
  • g at height h: g_h = g x r_E^2 / (r_E + h)^2; g is about 7.33 m/s^2 at 1000 km and only about 0.22 m/s^2 at 35,900 km, never exactly zero at finite height.
  • Orbital speed derivation: setting G m_E m_s / r^2 = m_s v^2 / r gives v = sqrt(G m_E / r); near Earth's surface the maximum orbital speed is about 7.9 x 10^3 m/s.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Comprehensive Questions

Q: 1. State and explain the law of Universal Gravitation. Also show that the law obeys Newton's third law of motion.

Ans: Newton's law of universal gravitation states: every body in the universe attracts every other body with a force which is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres. For two bodies of masses m_1 and m_2 separated by distance r, the force is F = G m_1 m_2 / r^2, where G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2 is the universal gravitational constant. The force acts along the line joining the centres of the two bodies. The law is called 'universal' because it applies to all bodies everywhere, from falling apples to planets and galaxies.
Obedience to Newton's third law: the formula is symmetric in the two masses — the product m_1 m_2 and the distance r are the same for both bodies. So the force with which body 1 attracts body 2 has exactly the same magnitude as the force with which body 2 attracts body 1, while the two forces point in opposite directions along the line joining them: F_12 = -F_21. They form an action-reaction pair acting on different bodies, which is exactly Newton's third law. For example, the Earth pulls the Moon towards itself with the same force with which the Moon pulls the Earth towards itself.

Q: 2. Determine the mass of Earth by applying law of gravitation.

Ans: Consider a small object of mass m_o resting on the surface of the Earth, whose mass is m_E and radius is r_E. The distance of the object from the centre of the Earth is r_E.
Step 1: The gravitational force between the Earth and the object is, by the law of gravitation, F = G m_E m_o / r_E^2.
Step 2: This force is simply the weight of the object, so F = m_o g.
Step 3: Equating the two expressions: m_o g = G m_E m_o / r_E^2.
Step 4: The object's mass m_o cancels, giving g = G m_E / r_E^2.
Step 5: Rearranging for the mass of the Earth: m_E = g r_E^2 / G.
Step 6: Substituting g = 9.8 m/s^2, r_E = 6.4 x 10^6 m and G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2: m_E = 9.8 x (6.4 x 10^6)^2 / (6.67 x 10^-11) = 9.8 x 4.096 x 10^13 / 6.67 x 10^-11 = 4.014 x 10^14 / 6.67 x 10^-11 = 6.0 x 10^24 kg.
Thus the mass of the Earth is about 6 x 10^24 kg, obtained without leaving the Earth's surface.

Q: 3. What is gravitational field and gravitational field strength? Show that the weight of an object changes with location.

Ans: The gravitational field of a body is the region (space) around it in which another mass experiences a gravitational force. A mass placed anywhere in this field is pulled towards the body creating the field. The gravitational field strength at a point is the gravitational force experienced by a unit mass placed at that point: g = F_g / m. It is a vector quantity, directed towards the centre of the attracting body, with unit N/kg (equivalently m/s^2). At the Earth's surface the field strength is g = G m_E / r_E^2 = 9.8 m/s^2.
Weight changes with location: since weight W = m g, and g is not the same everywhere, the weight of an object changes from place to place even though its mass stays constant. (i) g decreases with altitude, g_h = g r_E^2 / (r_E + h)^2, so a body weighs less on a mountain top than at sea level. (ii) g is slightly smaller at the equator than at the poles because the Earth is flattened and rotating. (iii) g is very different on other bodies: on the Moon g is only about 1.6 m/s^2, so the same object weighs about one-sixth of its Earth weight there, while on a more massive planet it would weigh more.

Q: 4. How is the value of 'g' changing by going to higher altitude? Write the relevant formula.

Ans: The value of g decreases as we go to higher altitude above the Earth's surface, because our distance from the centre of the Earth increases and gravity follows an inverse-square law.
Derivation: at the surface, g = G m_E / r_E^2. At a height h above the surface, the distance from the centre is (r_E + h), so g_h = G m_E / (r_E + h)^2. Dividing the second equation by the first: g_h / g = r_E^2 / (r_E + h)^2, hence g_h = g x r_E^2 / (r_E + h)^2.
So g falls steadily with height: at h = 1000 km it is about 7.33 m/s^2, and at the geostationary height of about 35,900 km it is only about 0.22 m/s^2. It never becomes exactly zero at any finite height, it only becomes weaker and weaker.

Q: 5. Derive the formula for the orbital speed of an artificial satellite.

Ans: Consider an artificial satellite of mass m_s moving in a circular orbit of radius r around the Earth (mass m_E), where r = r_E + h, h being the height of the satellite above the Earth's surface.
Step 1: The only force on the satellite is the gravitational attraction of the Earth: F = G m_E m_s / r^2.
Step 2: For circular motion this force must provide the centripetal force: F = m_s v^2 / r, where v is the orbital speed.
Step 3: Equating the two: G m_E m_s / r^2 = m_s v^2 / r.
Step 4: The satellite's mass m_s cancels, and one factor of r cancels: G m_E / r = v^2.
Step 5: Taking the square root: v = sqrt(G m_E / r) = sqrt(G m_E / (r_E + h)).
This shows that the orbital speed depends only on the mass of the Earth and the orbital radius: the higher the orbit, the smaller the speed needed. Near the Earth's surface (h negligible) this gives the maximum orbital speed of about 7.9 x 10^3 m/s.

mcqs.q: According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the force between two bodies is
options: Directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres
Directly proportional to the distance between them
Inversely proportional to the product of their masses
mcqs.why: The law states F = G m_1 m_2 / r^2: double either mass and the force doubles (direct proportion to the product), while doubling the distance quarters the force (inverse-square law). It applies to all bodies everywhere, which is why it is called universal.

mcqs.q: How does the law of gravitation show obedience to Newton's third law of motion?
options: It does not obey the third law
The heavier body always exerts the larger force
The formula is symmetric in the two masses, so F_12 = -F_21: equal magnitudes, opposite directions, on different bodies
The forces act in the same direction
mcqs.why: The product m_1 m_2 and the distance r are the same for both bodies, so the force of body 1 on body 2 equals in magnitude the force of body 2 on body 1, while pointing the opposite way along the line joining them. That is exactly an action-reaction pair, as with Earth and the Moon.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the mass of Earth from the law of gravitation?
mcqs.why: Equating weight with gravitational force, m_o g = G m_E m_o / r_E^2, the object's mass cancels giving g = G m_E / r_E^2. Rearranging for Earth's mass gives m_E = g r_E^2 / G.

mcqs.q: Using g = 9.8 m/s^2, r_E = 6.4 x 10^6 m and G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2, the mass of Earth is
The gravitational field of a body is
options: The solid region inside the body
The region of space around the body in which another mass experiences a gravitational force
A field that exists only on Earth's surface
The path followed by an orbiting satellite
mcqs.why: By definition, the gravitational field is the space around a mass where another mass is pulled towards it. A mass placed anywhere in this field experiences a gravitational force directed towards the body creating the field.

mcqs.q: Gravitational field strength at a point is defined as
options: The mass placed at that point
The distance from the centre of Earth
The total weight of all objects at that point
The gravitational force experienced by a unit mass placed at that point, g = F_g / m
mcqs.why: Field strength is force per unit mass, g = F_g / m, a vector directed towards the centre of the attracting body. Its unit is N/kg, equivalent to m/s^2; at Earth's surface it equals G m_E / r_E^2 = 9.8 m/s^2.

mcqs.q: An object is taken from Earth to the Moon, where g is about 1.6 m/s^2. What happens to its weight and mass?
options: Both weight and mass fall to about one-sixth
Weight falls to about one-sixth of its Earth value; mass stays the same
Weight stays the same; mass falls to one-sixth
mcqs.why: Weight W = m g follows the local g. On the Moon g is about 1.6 m/s^2 compared with 9.8 m/s^2 on Earth, a ratio of about 1/6, so the weight becomes about one-sixth. Mass is a property of the object itself and does not change with location.

mcqs.q: The correct formula for g at a height h above Earth's surface is
mcqs.why: At height h the distance from Earth's centre is (r_E + h), so g_h = G m_E / (r_E + h)^2. Dividing by the surface value g = G m_E / r_E^2 gives g_h = g x r_E^2 / (r_E + h)^2, which decreases as h increases.

mcqs.q: At the geostationary height of about 35,900 km, the value of g is about
In deriving a satellite's orbital speed, equating gravity with the centripetal force gives
options: v = sqrt(G m_E / r), with r = r_E + h
mcqs.why: Step by step: gravity gives F = G m_E m_s / r^2 and circular motion needs F = m_s v^2 / r. Equating them, the satellite mass m_s cancels and one r cancels, leaving v^2 = G m_E / r, so v = sqrt(G m_E / r). Near Earth's surface this gives the maximum orbital speed, about 7.9 x 10^3 m/s.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems and Assignments
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Force exerted by Earth on the Moon: F = G m_1 m_2 / r^2 = 2 x 10^20 N (Earth 6 x 10^24 kg, Moon 7.4 x 10^22 kg, r = 3.84 x 10^8 m); force between Pluto and Charon is 4.1 x 10^18 N.
  • Moon results: mass from m = g r^2 / G is 7.3 x 10^22 kg, and free-fall acceleration is 1.62 m/s^2, so a 65.0 kg astronaut weighing 637 N on Earth weighs only 105 N on the Moon.
  • g falls with height: 7.33 m/s^2 at 1000 km, 0.22 m/s^2 at 35,900 km, and 4.9 m/s^2 at a height of 0.414 r_E, about 2650 km above Earth's surface.
  • g = G m / r^2 on other bodies: Jupiter 24.7 m/s^2 (m = 1.89 x 10^27 kg, r = 7.15 x 10^7 m), Mars 3.69 m/s^2 and Titan 1.36 m/s^2.
  • Orbital speeds from v = sqrt(G m_E / r): 6.9 x 10^3 m/s for a satellite 2000 km up, 7.77 x 10^3 m/s at 225 km up, and 1.03 x 10^3 m/s for the Moon.
  • The Hubble telescope at 7.6 x 10^3 m/s orbits at radius 6.93 x 10^6 m, an altitude of about 529 km.

Solved Exercises

Assignment 5.1 — GRAVITATIONAL FORCE ON MOON

Q: The mass of earth is 6 x 10^24 kg and that of the moon is 7.4 x 10^22 kg. If the distance between the earth and the moon is 3.84 x 10^5 km, calculate the force exerted by the earth on the moon.

Ans: Given: mass of Earth m_1 = 6 x 10^24 kg, mass of Moon m_2 = 7.4 x 10^22 kg, distance r = 3.84 x 10^5 km = 3.84 x 10^8 m, G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2.
Formula: F = G x m_1 x m_2 / r^2.
Substitution: F = (6.67 x 10^-11) x (6 x 10^24) x (7.4 x 10^22) / (3.84 x 10^8)^2.
Numerator: 6.67 x 6 x 7.4 x 10^(-11 + 24 + 22) = 296.2 x 10^35 = 2.962 x 10^37.
Denominator: (3.84 x 10^8)^2 = 14.75 x 10^16 = 1.475 x 10^17.
F = 2.962 x 10^37 / 1.475 x 10^17 = 2.0 x 10^20 N.
Answer: 2 x 10^20 N

Assignment 5.2 — MASS OF MOON

Q: If the radius of the moon is 1.74 x 10^6 m and have acceleration due to gravity on its surface as 1.6 m/s^2. Calculate the mass of moon.

Ans: Given: radius of Moon r = 1.74 x 10^6 m, g on Moon's surface = 1.6 m/s^2, G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2.
Formula: g = G x m / r^2, so m = g x r^2 / G.
Substitution: m = 1.6 x (1.74 x 10^6)^2 / (6.67 x 10^-11).
(1.74 x 10^6)^2 = 3.0276 x 10^12.
Numerator: 1.6 x 3.0276 x 10^12 = 4.844 x 10^12.
m = 4.844 x 10^12 / 6.67 x 10^-11 = 7.3 x 10^22 kg.
Answer: 7.3 x 10^22 kg

Assignment 5.3 — FREE FALL AT MOON

Q: An astronaut of mass 65.0 kg (weighing 637 N on earth) is walking on the surface of the Moon, which has a mean radius of 1.74 x 10^6 m and a mass of 7.35 x 10^22 kg. What is the weight of the astronaut on moon? What is the free-fall acceleration at the surface of the moon?

Ans: Given: astronaut's mass m = 65.0 kg, Moon's mass M = 7.35 x 10^22 kg, Moon's radius r = 1.74 x 10^6 m, G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2.
First find the free-fall acceleration on the Moon.
Formula: g = G x M / r^2.
Substitution: g = (6.67 x 10^-11) x (7.35 x 10^22) / (1.74 x 10^6)^2.
Numerator: 6.67 x 7.35 x 10^(-11 + 22) = 49.02 x 10^11 = 4.902 x 10^12.
Denominator: (1.74 x 10^6)^2 = 3.0276 x 10^12.
g = 4.902 x 10^12 / 3.0276 x 10^12 = 1.62 m/s^2.
Now find the weight on the Moon.
Formula: W = m x g.
Substitution: W = 65.0 kg x 1.62 m/s^2 = 105 N.
Answer: weight on Moon 105 N, free-fall acceleration 1.62 m/s^2

Assignment 5.4 — Value Of g At Specific Height

Q: Calculate the value of g at 1000 km and 35900 km above the earth surface.

Ans: Given: g at Earth's surface = 9.8 m/s^2, radius of Earth r_E = 6.4 x 10^6 m = 6400 km.
Formula: g_h = g x r_E^2 / (r_E + h)^2.
Case 1: h = 1000 km, so r_E + h = 6400 + 1000 = 7400 km.
Substitution: g_h = 9.8 x (6400 / 7400)^2 = 9.8 x (0.8649)^2 = 9.8 x 0.748 = 7.33 m/s^2.
Case 2: h = 35900 km, so r_E + h = 6400 + 35900 = 42,300 km.
Substitution: g_h = 9.8 x (6400 / 42300)^2 = 9.8 x (0.1513)^2 = 9.8 x 0.0229 = 0.22 m/s^2.
Answer: 7.33 m/s^2 at 1000 km height, and 0.22 m/s^2 at 35900 km height

Assignment 5.5 — ORBITAL SPEED OF A SATELLITE

Q: If a satellite orbits the earth at 2,000 km above sea level, how fast must the orbiting satellite travel to maintain a circular orbit?

Ans: Given: height h = 2000 km = 2 x 10^6 m, radius of Earth r_E = 6.4 x 10^6 m, mass of Earth m_E = 6 x 10^24 kg, G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2.
Orbital radius: r = r_E + h = 6.4 x 10^6 + 2 x 10^6 = 8.4 x 10^6 m.
Formula: v = sqrt(G x m_E / r).
Substitution: v = sqrt[(6.67 x 10^-11) x (6 x 10^24) / (8.4 x 10^6)].
Numerator: 6.67 x 6 x 10^(-11 + 24) = 40.02 x 10^13 = 4.002 x 10^14.
Inside the root: 4.002 x 10^14 / 8.4 x 10^6 = 4.76 x 10^7.
v = sqrt(4.76 x 10^7) = 6.9 x 10^3 m/s.
Answer: 6.9 x 10^3 m/s

Extension Exercise 5.1

Q: Confirm the value of 'g' for Jupiter given in Example 5.2. Using equation 5.5 (Example 5.2 uses g = 24.7 N/kg for Jupiter and finds the mass of Jupiter as 1.89 x 10^27 kg; radius of Jupiter is 7.15 x 10^7 m.)

Ans: Given: mass of Jupiter m_J = 1.89 x 10^27 kg (found in Example 5.2); radius of Jupiter r_J = 7.15 x 10^7 m; gravitational constant G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2
Formula: The value of g on the surface of a planet is g = G m / r^2 (equation 5.4 of the unit; the confirmation the book asks for is made with this relation)
Substitution: g = (6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2 x 1.89 x 10^27 kg) / (7.15 x 10^7 m)^2
Working: numerator = 1.26 x 10^17; denominator = 5.11 x 10^15; g = 1.26 x 10^17 / 5.11 x 10^15 = 24.7 m/s^2
Answer: g = 24.7 m/s^2 (24.7 N/kg) — the value of g for Jupiter used in Example 5.2 is confirmed.

Exercise — Numerical Problems

Q: 1. Pluto's moon Charon is unusually large considering Pluto's size, giving them the character of a double planet. Their masses are 1.25 x 10^22 kg and 1.9 x 10^21 kg, and their average distance from one another is 1.96 x 10^4 km. What is the gravitational force between them?

Ans: Given: masses m_1 = 1.25 x 10^22 kg and m_2 = 1.9 x 10^21 kg, distance r = 1.96 x 10^4 km = 1.96 x 10^7 m, G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2.
Formula: F = G x m_1 x m_2 / r^2.
Substitution: F = (6.67 x 10^-11) x (1.25 x 10^22) x (1.9 x 10^21) / (1.96 x 10^7)^2.
Numerator: 6.67 x 1.25 x 1.9 x 10^(-11 + 22 + 21) = 15.84 x 10^32 = 1.584 x 10^33.
Denominator: (1.96 x 10^7)^2 = 3.8416 x 10^14.
F = 1.584 x 10^33 / 3.8416 x 10^14 = 4.1 x 10^18 N.
Answer: 4.1 x 10^18 N
