Q: 2. The mass of Mars is 6.4 x 10^23 kg and having radius of 3.4 x 10^6 m. Calculate the gravitational field strength (g) on Mars surface.

Ans: Given: mass of Mars m = 6.4 x 10^23 kg, radius of Mars r = 3.4 x 10^6 m, G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2.
Formula: g = G x m / r^2.
Substitution: g = (6.67 x 10^-11) x (6.4 x 10^23) / (3.4 x 10^6)^2.
Numerator: 6.67 x 6.4 x 10^(-11 + 23) = 42.69 x 10^12 = 4.269 x 10^13.
Denominator: (3.4 x 10^6)^2 = 11.56 x 10^12 = 1.156 x 10^13.
g = 4.269 x 10^13 / 1.156 x 10^13 = 3.69 m/s^2.
Answer: 3.69 m/s^2

Q: 3. Titan is the largest moon of Saturn and the only moon in the solar system known to have a substantial atmosphere. Find the acceleration due to gravity on Titan's surface, given that its mass is 1.35 x 10^18 and its radius is 2570 km.

Ans: Note: the mass of Titan printed in the question, 1.35 x 10^18 kg, is a misprint; Titan's mass is 1.35 x 10^23 kg (the book's own answer key, 1.352 m/s^2, also uses 10^23). The problem is solved with the correct mass.
Given: mass of Titan m = 1.35 x 10^23 kg, radius r = 2570 km = 2.57 x 10^6 m, G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2.
Formula: g = G x m / r^2.
Substitution: g = (6.67 x 10^-11) x (1.35 x 10^23) / (2.57 x 10^6)^2.
Numerator: 6.67 x 1.35 x 10^(-11 + 23) = 9.0045 x 10^12.
Denominator: (2.57 x 10^6)^2 = 6.6049 x 10^12.
g = 9.0045 x 10^12 / 6.6049 x 10^12 = 1.36 m/s^2.
Answer: 1.36 m/s^2

Q: 4. At which altitude above Earth's surface would the gravitational acceleration be 4.9 m/s^2?

Ans: Given: g = 9.8 m/s^2 at the surface, required g_h = 4.9 m/s^2, radius of Earth r_E = 6.4 x 10^6 m.
Formula: g_h = g x r_E^2 / (r_E + h)^2.
Substitution: 4.9 = 9.8 x (r_E / (r_E + h))^2, so (r_E / (r_E + h))^2 = 4.9 / 9.8 = 1/2.
Taking square roots: r_E / (r_E + h) = 1 / sqrt(2) = 0.707.
So r_E + h = r_E / 0.707 = 1.414 x r_E.
h = 1.414 r_E - r_E = 0.414 x r_E.
h = 0.414 x 6.4 x 10^6 m = 2.65 x 10^6 m, about 2650 km.
Answer: 2.65 x 10^6 m (about 2650 km) above the surface

Q: 5. Assume that a satellite orbits Earth 225 km above its surface. Given that the mass of Earth is 6 x 10^24 kg and the radius of Earth is 6.4 x 10^6 m, what is the satellite's orbital speed?

Ans: Given: height h = 225 km = 2.25 x 10^5 m, mass of Earth m_E = 6 x 10^24 kg, radius of Earth r_E = 6.4 x 10^6 m, G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2.
Orbital radius: r = r_E + h = 6.4 x 10^6 + 0.225 x 10^6 = 6.625 x 10^6 m.
Formula: v = sqrt(G x m_E / r).
Substitution: v = sqrt[(6.67 x 10^-11) x (6 x 10^24) / (6.625 x 10^6)].
Numerator: 6.67 x 6 x 10^(-11 + 24) = 40.02 x 10^13 = 4.002 x 10^14.
Inside the root: 4.002 x 10^14 / 6.625 x 10^6 = 6.04 x 10^7.
v = sqrt(6.04 x 10^7) = 7.77 x 10^3 m/s.
Answer: 7.77 x 10^3 m/s

Q: 6. The distance from center of earth to center of moon is 3.8 x 10^8 m. Mass of earth is 6 x 10^24 kg. What is the orbital speed of moon?

Ans: Given: orbital radius r = 3.8 x 10^8 m, mass of Earth m_E = 6 x 10^24 kg, G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2.
Formula: v = sqrt(G x m_E / r).
Substitution: v = sqrt[(6.67 x 10^-11) x (6 x 10^24) / (3.8 x 10^8)].
Numerator: 6.67 x 6 x 10^(-11 + 24) = 40.02 x 10^13 = 4.002 x 10^14.
Inside the root: 4.002 x 10^14 / 3.8 x 10^8 = 1.053 x 10^6.
v = sqrt(1.053 x 10^6) = 1.03 x 10^3 m/s.
Answer: 1.03 x 10^3 m/s

Q: 7. The Hubble space telescope orbits Earth (m_E = 6 x 10^24 kg) with an orbital speed of 7.6 x 10^3 m/s. Calculate its altitude above Earth's surface.

Ans: Given: mass of Earth m_E = 6 x 10^24 kg, orbital speed v = 7.6 x 10^3 m/s, radius of Earth r_E = 6.4 x 10^6 m, G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2.
Formula: v = sqrt(G x m_E / r), so r = G x m_E / v^2.
Substitution: r = (6.67 x 10^-11) x (6 x 10^24) / (7.6 x 10^3)^2.
Numerator: 6.67 x 6 x 10^(-11 + 24) = 40.02 x 10^13 = 4.002 x 10^14.
Denominator: (7.6 x 10^3)^2 = 57.76 x 10^6 = 5.776 x 10^7.
r = 4.002 x 10^14 / 5.776 x 10^7 = 6.93 x 10^6 m.
Altitude: h = r - r_E = 6.93 x 10^6 - 6.4 x 10^6 = 0.53 x 10^6 m = 530 km (about 529 km).
Answer: about 529 km above Earth's surface

Q: Note on 3

Ans: The question prints Titan's mass as 1.35 x 10^18 kg, which is a misprint. The book's printed key gives 1.352 m/s^2, which is obtained only with Titan's real mass, 1.35 x 10^23 kg. The solution above therefore uses 1.35 x 10^23 kg and gives g = 1.36 m/s^2.

Q: Note on 7

Ans: The book's printed key gives 547 km; the correct answer is about 529 km, because from the stated data (m_E = 6 x 10^24 kg, r_E = 6.4 x 10^6 m, v = 7.6 x 10^3 m/s) the orbital radius is r = G m_E / v^2 = 6.93 x 10^6 m, so the altitude is r - r_E = 0.53 x 10^6 m, about 529 km.

mcqs.why: Formula: v = sqrt(G m_E / r), so r = G m_E / v^2. Substitution: r = (6.67 x 10^-11) x (6 x 10^24) / (7.6 x 10^3)^2. Step by step: numerator = 4.002 x 10^14; denominator = 5.776 x 10^7; r = 6.93 x 10^6 m. Altitude h = r - r_E = 6.93 x 10^6 - 6.4 x 10^6 = 0.53 x 10^6 m, about 529 km. Note: the book's printed key gives 547 km, which does not follow from the stated data; 529 km is correct.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Work is zero when the angle between force and displacement is 90 degrees, because W = F S cos theta and cos 90 degrees = 0.
  • Work done by a 30 N force moving a trolley 5 m in the direction of the force: W = F x S = 30 x 5 = 150 J.
  • Kinetic energy varies with the square of speed: halving the speed reduces kinetic energy to 1/4.
  • Gravitational potential energy gained by a 10 kg object lifted 5 m: E_GPE = m g h = 10 x 9.8 x 5 = 490 J.
  • Efficiency = useful work output / total energy input: an engine doing 20 J of useful work per 100 J supplied is 20 percent efficient.
  • The kilowatt hour (kWh) is a unit of energy; 1 hp = 746 W.
  • Hira (weight 500 N) climbing 18 m in 90 s develops average power (500 x 18) / 90 = 100 W.
  • A machine lifting a 200 N slab through 30 m in 50 s develops average power (200 x 30) / 50 = 120 W.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Multiple Choice Questions

Q: 1. Work done will be zero when the angle between force and displacement is

Options: (a) 30° (b) 45° (c) 60° (d) 90°

Correct answer: 90°

Q: 2. 30 N force is exerted and the trolley moves a distance of 5 m in the direction of the force, the work done is

Options: (a) 6 J (b) 25 J (c) 150 J (d) 0.17 N

Correct answer: 150 J

Q: 3. If the speed of a car decreases by half, The kinetic energy change by factor

Options: (a) 4 (b) 2 (c) 1/2 (d) 1/4

Correct answer: 1/4

Q: 4. An object of mass 10 kg is lifted vertically through a height of 5 m. The gravitational potential energy gained by the object is

Options: (a) 0.5 J (b) 2 J (c) 50 J (d) 490 J

Correct answer: 490 J

Q: 5. If a petrol engine does 20 J of useful work for every 100 J of energy supplied to it, then its efficiency is

Options: (a) 80 % (b) 60 % (c) 40 % (d) 20 %

Correct answer: 20 %

Q: 6. kWh is unit for

Options: (a) Energy (b) Power (c) Efficiency (d) None

Correct answer: Energy

Q: 7. 1 hp =

Options: (a) 476 W (b) 550 W (c) 746 W (d) 1 ft.lb/s

Correct answer: 746 W

Q: 8. Hira weighing 500 N takes 90 s to reach the top of a hill 18 m high. Her average muscle power is

Options: (a) 2500 W (b) 100 W (c) 32.8 W (d) 3.24 W

Correct answer: 100 W

Q: 9. A machine is able to lift 200 N of concrete slab vertically up to a height of 30 m above the ground in 50 s. The average power of the machine is

Options: (a) 1.33 W (b) 60 W (c) 120 W (d) 6000 W

Correct answer: 120 W

mcqs.q: Work done will be zero when the angle between force and displacement is
mcqs.why: Work is W = F S cos theta. At theta = 90 degrees, cos 90 degrees = 0, so the work done is zero no matter how large the force or displacement, as for a centripetal force.

mcqs.q: 30 N force is exerted and the trolley moves a distance of 5 m in the direction of the force, the work done is
mcqs.why: Formula: W = F x S. Substitution: W = 30 N x 5 m = 150 J. Step by step: the force acts along the displacement, so the full force does work: 30 x 5 = 150, and the unit of work is the joule.

mcqs.q: If the speed of a car decreases by half, The kinetic energy change by factor
mcqs.why: Kinetic energy E_K = 1/2 m v^2 is proportional to v^2. Halving the speed gives (1/2)^2 = 1/4 of the original kinetic energy, so it changes by a factor of 1/4.

mcqs.q: An object of mass 10 kg is lifted vertically through a height of 5 m. The gravitational potential energy gained by the object is
mcqs.why: Formula: E_GPE = m x g x h. Substitution: E_GPE = 10 kg x 9.8 m/s^2 x 5 m. Step by step: 10 x 9.8 = 98; 98 x 5 = 490 J.

mcqs.q: If a petrol engine does 20 J of useful work for every 100 J of energy supplied to it, then its efficiency is
mcqs.why: Formula: Efficiency (%) = (Useful output / Total input) x 100. Substitution: (20 J / 100 J) x 100. Step by step: 20 / 100 = 0.20; 0.20 x 100 = 20 %. The remaining 80 J is wasted, mainly as heat.

mcqs.q: kWh is unit for
mcqs.why: The kilowatt hour is the energy converted by a 1000 W device working for one hour: 1 kWh = 1000 W x 3600 s = 3.6 x 10^6 J, so it is a unit of energy, used on electricity bills.

mcqs.q: 1 hp =
mcqs.why: The horsepower is a unit of power still used for engines and motors, and 1 hp = 746 W. So a 2 hp motor, for example, is a 1492 W motor.

mcqs.q: Hira weighing 500 N takes 90 s to reach the top of a hill 18 m high. Her average muscle power is
mcqs.why: Formula: work against gravity W = F x h, then P = W / t. Substitution: W = 500 N x 18 m = 9000 J. Step by step: P = 9000 J / 90 s = 100 W.

mcqs.q: A machine is able to lift 200 N of concrete slab vertically up to a height of 30 m above the ground in 50 s. The average power of the machine is
mcqs.why: Formula: work W = F x h, then P = W / t. Substitution: W = 200 N x 30 m = 6000 J. Step by step: P = 6000 J / 50 s = 120 W. Note 6000 is the work in joules, not the power.

mcqs.q: What is the SI unit of work?
mcqs.why: Work W = F x S is measured in joules: 1 joule is the work done when a force of 1 newton displaces a body by 1 metre in its own direction. The watt measures power and the newton measures force.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A centripetal force never does work: it is always perpendicular to the displacement (theta = 90 degrees), so W = F S cos 90 degrees = 0; it changes direction, never speed.
  • A bullet stopping in a sand bag loses its kinetic energy mainly as heat, plus some sound and energy spent tearing and displacing the sand; total energy is conserved.
  • A meteor burning in the atmosphere converts its kinetic energy into heat and light through air friction.
  • For equal kinetic energies, speed varies as 1 / sqrt(m): the bullet with half the mass has sqrt(2) (about 1.41) times the speed; both bullets can do the same work.
  • Gravitational potential energy depends on the chosen reference level, so the same object at the same elevation can have different GPE values; only differences of GPE are fixed.
  • Winding mountain roads do the same total work mgh against gravity but with a smaller force over a longer distance, because the slope is gentler.
  • Doubling velocity quadruples kinetic energy (x 4), while doubling mass only doubles it (x 2); tripling speed multiplies kinetic energy by 9.
  • Lifting a beam twice as high in half the time needs 4 times the power: P' = 2W / (t/2) = 4P.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Conceptual Questions

Q: 1. Can a centripetal force ever do work on an object? Explain.

Ans: No. Work is W = F x S x cos theta, where theta is the angle between the force and the displacement. A centripetal force always acts towards the centre of the circular path, while the displacement of the object at every instant is along the tangent to the path. The force is therefore always perpendicular to the displacement (theta = 90 degrees), and cos 90 degrees = 0, so the work done is zero at every instant. This is why the Moon's speed (and kinetic energy) stays constant in its orbit: Earth's gravity, acting as centripetal force, does no work on it. A centripetal force changes only the direction of motion, never the speed.

Q: 2. What happens to the kinetic energy of a bullet when it penetrates into a sand bag?

Ans: As the bullet pushes its way into the sand bag, the sand exerts a large opposing frictional force on it. The bullet does work against this friction and slows down, so its kinetic energy decreases continuously until the bullet stops inside the bag. The lost kinetic energy is not destroyed: it is converted mainly into heat (the bullet and the sand around the path warm up), some into sound, and some into the energy used in tearing and displacing the sand grains (deformation). The total energy remains conserved, only its form changes.

Q: 3. A meteor enters into earth's atmosphere and burns. What happens to its kinetic energy?

Ans: A meteor enters the atmosphere with a very high speed, so it has a large kinetic energy. As it rushes through the air, air resistance (friction with the air) does negative work on it. Its kinetic energy is converted into heat energy and light energy: the meteor and the air around it become so hot that the meteor glows and burns up. If it is completely burnt, all of its kinetic energy is transferred to the atmosphere as heat and light; only large meteors survive with some kinetic energy remaining to strike the ground as meteorites.

Q: 4. Two bullets are fired at the same time with the same kinetic energy. If one bullet has twice the mass of the other, which has the greater speed and by what factor? Which can do the most work?

Ans: Since E_K = 1/2 m v^2, for a fixed kinetic energy the speed is inversely proportional to the square root of the mass, v = sqrt(2 E_K / m). The lighter bullet (half the mass of the other) therefore has the greater speed. If the heavier bullet has mass 2m and speed v, the lighter bullet of mass m must have speed sqrt(2) x v, i.e. about 1.41 times greater, so that 1/2 m (sqrt(2) v)^2 = 1/2 (2m) v^2. Both bullets, however, can do exactly the same amount of work, because the work a moving body can do in coming to rest equals its kinetic energy, and their kinetic energies are equal.

Q: 5. Can an object have different amounts of gravitational potential energy if it remains at the same elevation?

Ans: Yes. Gravitational potential energy is measured relative to a chosen reference level (the level where E_GPE is taken as zero), and that choice is arbitrary. The same object at the same elevation has E_GPE = mgh with different values of h when different reference levels are chosen: for example, a piano on a floor has zero GPE with respect to that floor but about 3.7 x 10^4 J with respect to the basement floor 1.9 m below (see Numerical Problem 3). The GPE also differs if the value of g differs at that elevation. Only differences of GPE between two points have a fixed physical meaning, not the absolute value.

Q: 6. Why do roads leading to the top of a mountain wind back and forth?

Ans: To climb a mountain of height h, a vehicle must gain gravitational potential energy mgh, i.e. it must do a fixed amount of work against gravity, whatever route it takes. A straight, steep road would require a very large driving force (the component of weight along the slope is large), which engines may not provide and tyres may not grip. A winding road makes the path much longer and the slope much gentler, so the same total work (force x distance) is done with a smaller force over a longer distance. The climb becomes possible and comfortable, at the cost of travelling farther.

Q: 7. Which would have a greater effect on the kinetic energy of an object, doubling the mass or doubling the velocity?

Ans: Doubling the velocity has the greater effect. Kinetic energy is E_K = 1/2 m v^2: it is directly proportional to the mass but proportional to the square of the velocity. Doubling the mass doubles the kinetic energy (x 2), whereas doubling the velocity makes it four times as great (x 2^2 = 4). This is also why high-speed collisions are so much more destructive, and why braking distances grow rapidly with speed.

Q: 8. If the speed of a particle triples, by what factor does its kinetic energy increase?

Ans: Kinetic energy is proportional to the square of the speed, E_K = 1/2 m v^2. If the speed triples (v becomes 3v), the kinetic energy becomes 1/2 m (3v)^2 = 9 x (1/2 m v^2). So the kinetic energy increases by a factor of 9.

Q: 9. The motor of a crane uses power P to lift a steel beam. By what factor must the motor's power increase to lift the beam twice as high in half the time?

Ans: Power is the rate of doing work, P = W / t, and the work needed to lift the beam is W = mgh. Lifting the beam twice as high doubles the work (2W). Doing this doubled work in half the time gives a required power of P' = 2W / (t/2) = 4 x (W/t) = 4P. So the motor's power must increase by a factor of 4.

mcqs.q: Can a centripetal force ever do work on an object?
options: Yes, whenever the object speeds up
Yes, because the object keeps moving
No, because it is always perpendicular to the displacement, so W = F S cos 90 degrees = 0
Only when the circle is very large
mcqs.why: A centripetal force points towards the centre while the displacement at every instant is along the tangent, so theta = 90 degrees at all times. Since cos 90 degrees = 0, W = F S cos theta = 0. That is why the Moon's speed and kinetic energy stay constant in orbit: the force changes only the direction of motion.

mcqs.q: What happens to the kinetic energy of a bullet when it penetrates into a sand bag?
options: It is converted mainly into heat, with some sound and energy used in tearing and displacing the sand
It turns entirely into potential energy
It stays stored in the bullet unchanged
mcqs.why: The sand exerts a large frictional force opposing the bullet, which does work against it and slows to rest. Energy is never destroyed: the lost kinetic energy becomes mainly heat in the bullet and sand, some sound, and the work of tearing and displacing sand grains.

mcqs.q: A meteor enters Earth's atmosphere and burns. What happens to its kinetic energy?
options: It is stored as chemical energy
It is converted into heat energy and light energy by air friction
mcqs.why: The fast meteor does work against air resistance, which does negative work on it. Its large kinetic energy is transferred to the atmosphere as heat and light, which is why the meteor glows and burns up; only large meteors keep some kinetic energy and reach the ground as meteorites.

mcqs.q: Two bullets fired with the same kinetic energy: one has twice the mass of the other. Which has the greater speed, and by what factor?
options: The heavier bullet, by a factor of 2
The lighter bullet, by a factor of sqrt(2), about 1.41
The lighter bullet, by a factor of 4
mcqs.why: From E_K = 1/2 m v^2, v = sqrt(2 E_K / m), so at fixed E_K the speed goes as 1 / sqrt(m). If the heavy bullet has mass 2m and speed v, the light bullet of mass m needs speed sqrt(2) x v, about 1.41 v, so that 1/2 m (sqrt(2) v)^2 = 1/2 (2m) v^2.

mcqs.q: For the two bullets of equal kinetic energy but different masses, which can do the most work in coming to rest?
options: Both can do exactly the same work
mcqs.why: The work a moving body can do in coming to rest equals its kinetic energy. The two bullets were fired with the same kinetic energy, so despite their different masses and speeds, each can do exactly the same amount of work.

mcqs.q: Can an object have different amounts of gravitational potential energy while remaining at the same elevation?
options: Yes, because GPE is measured from an arbitrarily chosen reference level
No, GPE at a given height is always unique
mcqs.why: E_GPE = m g h, and h is measured from a reference level where GPE is taken as zero; that choice is arbitrary. A piano has 0 J relative to its own floor but about 3.7 x 10^4 J relative to a basement 1.9 m below. Only differences of GPE between two points have a fixed meaning.

mcqs.q: Why do roads leading to the top of a mountain wind back and forth?
options: To increase the total work done against gravity
Because a winding road is cheaper to build
Because the same work mgh is then done with a smaller force over a longer distance on a gentler slope
mcqs.why: Climbing height h always needs the same work, mgh, whatever the route. A straight steep road would need a very large driving force along the slope. The winding road lengthens the path and gentles the slope, so the same work (force x distance) is done with a smaller force over a longer distance.

mcqs.q: Which has the greater effect on an object's kinetic energy: doubling the mass or doubling the velocity?
options: Doubling the mass, which quadruples it
Doubling the velocity, which makes it four times as great
Both have exactly the same effect
Doubling the mass, which makes it eight times as great
mcqs.why: E_K = 1/2 m v^2 is proportional to m but to v^2. Doubling the mass gives 2 x E_K, while doubling the velocity gives (2)^2 = 4 times the kinetic energy. This is why high-speed collisions are so much more destructive.

mcqs.q: If the speed of a particle triples, by what factor does its kinetic energy increase?
mcqs.why: Kinetic energy is proportional to the square of the speed. Tripling the speed gives E_K' = 1/2 m (3v)^2 = 9 x (1/2 m v^2), so the kinetic energy increases by a factor of 9.

mcqs.q: A crane motor of power P lifts a steel beam. To lift it twice as high in half the time, the power must increase by a factor of
mcqs.why: Power P = W / t and the lifting work is W = m g h. Twice the height doubles the work to 2W, and doing it in half the time gives P' = 2W / (t / 2) = 4 x (W / t) = 4P. So the motor's power must increase by a factor of 4.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Work is done when a force displaces a body in its direction: W = F x S; it is a scalar with SI unit the joule, 1 J being the work of 1 N over 1 m. For a force at angle theta, W = F S cos theta: maximum at 0 degrees, zero at 90 degrees, negative (-F S) at 180 degrees, as with friction.
  • Kinetic energy derivation: W = F S = m a S with a S = v^2 / 2 gives E_K = 1/2 m v^2, the work needed to bring the body from rest to speed v.
  • Gravitational potential energy proof: lifting mass m slowly through height h needs force m g over distance h, so the stored energy is E_GPE = m g h.
  • Law of conservation of energy: energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed; the total energy of an isolated system remains constant.
  • Mass-energy relation E = m c^2 with c = 3 x 10^8 m/s: even 1 g of mass equals 9 x 10^13 J, the basis of nuclear energy.
  • Major sources: fossil fuels (non-renewable, polluting), wind, solar, biomass, nuclear fission and geothermal (thermal) energy, plus hydroelectric energy from falling water.
  • Efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input, usually as a percentage; an ordinary bulb is only about 5 percent efficient, a fluorescent tube about 20 percent.
  • Power is the rate of doing work, P = W / t, unit watt (1 W = 1 J/s); 1 kW = 1000 W, 1 hp = 746 W and 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Comprehensive Questions

Q: 1. Define work and explain how work is calculated if force is applied at an angle.

Ans: Work is said to be done when a force acts on a body and the body moves (is displaced) in the direction of the force. Work is the product of the force and the displacement in the direction of the force: W = F x S. Work is a scalar quantity; its SI unit is the joule (J), where 1 J is the work done when a force of 1 N displaces a body by 1 m in its own direction.
When the force is applied at an angle theta to the displacement, only the component of the force along the displacement does work. This component is F cos theta, so the work is W = F cos theta x S = (F x S) cos theta. Special cases: if theta = 0 degrees (force along the displacement), cos theta = 1 and the work is maximum, W = F S. If theta = 90 degrees (force perpendicular to the displacement, e.g. centripetal force or carrying a load horizontally), cos theta = 0 and no work is done. If theta = 180 degrees (force opposite to the displacement, e.g. friction or braking), cos theta = -1 and the work is negative, W = -F S, meaning work is done against the motion.

Q: 2. Define kinetic energy. Derive the expression used for kinetic energy.

Ans: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its motion. A moving body can do work in coming to rest, and the kinetic energy equals the work done to bring the body from rest to its present speed.
Derivation: consider a body of mass m initially at rest (v_i = 0). A constant force F is applied over a distance S, accelerating it to final velocity v_f.
Step 1: The work done by the force is W = F x S.
Step 2: By Newton's second law, F = m a, so W = m a S.
Step 3: From the equation of motion 2 a S = v_f^2 - v_i^2, with v_i = 0, we get a S = v_f^2 / 2.
Step 4: Substituting: W = m x (v_f^2 / 2) = 1/2 m v_f^2.
This work is stored in the body as its kinetic energy, so E_K = 1/2 m v^2, where v is the speed of the body. Kinetic energy is a scalar, measured in joules.

Q: 3. What is potential energy? Prove that the gravitational potential energy of a body of mass m at a height h above the surface of earth is given by mgh.

Ans: Potential energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its position or configuration; it is the stored energy that can be converted into work when the body is released. Its gravitational form is the energy a body has because of its height above the ground (reference level).
Proof: consider a body of mass m lying on the ground. To raise it slowly to a height h at constant speed, an upward force equal to its weight must be applied.
Step 1: The force required is F = weight = m g.
Step 2: The displacement in the direction of the force is S = h.
Step 3: Work done = F x S = m g x h.
Step 4: This work is stored in the body as its gravitational potential energy (nothing is spent on kinetic energy because the speed is constant).
Therefore E_GPE = m g h. It is measured relative to the chosen reference level, and its unit is the joule.

Q: 4. State the law of conservation of energy and mass energy conversion relation.

Ans: Law of conservation of energy: energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be transformed from one form into another. The total energy of an isolated system always remains constant. For example, in a pole vault the athlete's kinetic energy changes into elastic potential energy of the bending pole and then into gravitational potential energy; a diver standing on a springboard has gravitational potential energy which becomes kinetic energy during the fall and then energy of the splashing water; and in electricity generation, the potential energy of stored water becomes kinetic energy, then mechanical energy of turbines, and finally electrical energy.
Mass-energy conversion relation: Einstein showed that mass and energy are inter-convertible, i.e. mass is a concentrated form of energy. The relation is E = m c^2, where E is the energy equivalent of a mass m and c = 3 x 10^8 m/s is the speed of light. Because c^2 is a huge number, even a tiny mass converts into an enormous amount of energy: 1 g of mass is equivalent to 9 x 10^13 J. This conversion is the source of nuclear energy in the Sun, in nuclear reactors and in nuclear weapons.

Q: 5. Explain briefly major sources of energy. Such fossil fuel, wind, solar, biomass, nuclear and thermal energy.

Ans: The major sources of energy are: (1) Fossil fuels — coal, oil and natural gas formed from the remains of plants and animals buried millions of years ago. They are burnt in power stations and engines to produce heat, electricity and motion. They are cheap and widely used but are non-renewable, and burning them releases carbon dioxide and other pollutants that cause air pollution and global warming. (2) Wind energy — the kinetic energy of moving air turns the blades of wind turbines to generate electricity; it is renewable and clean but depends on suitable windy sites and variable weather. (3) Solar energy — energy from the Sun, used directly for heating (solar water heaters, solar cookers) and converted into electricity by solar (photovoltaic) cells; it is renewable and pollution-free but needs sunlight and large areas of panels. (4) Biomass — energy obtained from plant and animal material such as wood, crop waste and animal dung, burnt directly for heat or converted into biogas and biofuels; it is renewable as long as plants are regrown. (5) Nuclear energy — energy released by fission of uranium nuclei in reactors, used to produce steam and generate electricity; a small amount of fuel gives a huge amount of energy, but the radioactive waste is dangerous and must be stored safely for a very long time. (6) Thermal (geothermal) energy — heat from inside the Earth, where hot water and steam from underground reservoirs are used for heating and to generate electricity; it is renewable and reliable but available in only some regions. (The unit also describes hydroelectric energy, obtained from falling water in dams.)

Q: 6. Define and explain efficiency.

Ans: Efficiency of a machine or system is the ratio of the useful energy (or work) output to the total energy input: Efficiency = Useful energy output / Total energy input. It has no unit, and is usually expressed as a percentage: Efficiency (%) = (Useful output / Total input) x 100.
No real machine can be 100% efficient, because some of the input energy is always wasted, mainly as heat due to friction between moving parts, and also as sound. For example, of every 100 J of electrical energy supplied to an ordinary (incandescent) bulb, only about 5 J appears as useful light and 95 J is wasted as heat, so its efficiency is about 5%; a fluorescent tube is better, at about 20%. Improving efficiency — by reducing friction, using lubrication and better designs — saves fuel and money and reduces pollution, which is why efficient appliances are encouraged.

Q: 7. Define and explain power.

Ans: Power is the rate of doing work, i.e. the work done per unit time: P = W / t. A machine that does the same work in less time is more powerful. Power is a scalar quantity and its SI unit is the watt (W): 1 watt = 1 joule per second (1 W = 1 J/s), so a 100 W bulb converts 100 J of electrical energy every second.
Other units: the kilowatt (1 kW = 1000 W) and the horsepower (1 hp = 746 W), still used for engines and motors. Electrical energy consumed is commonly measured in kilowatt hours: 1 kWh = 1000 W x 3600 s = 3.6 x 10^6 J, the 'unit' of electricity billing. For lifting a load at constant speed, power can also be written as P = F x v, force times velocity.

mcqs.q: Work is said to be done when
options: A force acts on a body and the body is displaced in the direction of the force
Any force acts on a body, moving or not
A body moves without any force on it
A force is applied perpendicular to the motion only
mcqs.why: Work is the product of the force and the displacement in the direction of the force, W = F x S. If there is no displacement, or no component of force along the displacement, no work is done. Work is a scalar measured in joules.

mcqs.q: When a force is applied at an angle theta to the displacement, the work done is
mcqs.why: Only the component of the force along the displacement does work, and that component is F cos theta, so W = F cos theta x S = (F x S) cos theta. At theta = 0 degrees this gives the maximum W = F S; at 90 degrees it gives zero.

mcqs.q: A force acting opposite to the displacement, such as friction or braking, does work equal to
options: Negative work, W = -F S, because cos 180 degrees = -1
mcqs.why: For theta = 180 degrees, cos theta = -1, so W = F S cos theta = -F S. The negative sign means work is done against the motion: friction and braking forces remove kinetic energy from a moving body.

mcqs.q: The expression for kinetic energy is derived by combining W = F S with F = m a and 2 a S = v_f^2 - v_i^2, giving
mcqs.why: Step by step: W = F x S = m a S. From 2 a S = v_f^2 - v_i^2 with the body starting from rest (v_i = 0), a S = v_f^2 / 2. Substituting, W = m x v_f^2 / 2 = 1/2 m v^2. This work is stored as kinetic energy, the energy a body has due to its motion.

mcqs.q: The gravitational potential energy of a body of mass m at height h is mgh because
options: Gravity pulls it down with force m g h
Raising it slowly needs an upward force equal to its weight m g acting through the distance h, and that work is stored in the body
Its kinetic energy at height h equals m g h
The height multiplies the mass directly
mcqs.why: Step by step: the force needed to lift the body slowly at constant speed is F = weight = m g; the displacement in the force's direction is S = h; work done = F x S = m g h. Since the speed is constant, none of this work becomes kinetic energy - all of it is stored as gravitational potential energy, E_GPE = m g h.

mcqs.q: The law of conservation of energy states that
options: Energy is created whenever a machine runs
Energy can only be destroyed, never created
Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be transformed from one form to another, and the total energy of an isolated system stays constant
Energy and mass can never change into each other
mcqs.why: In every process energy only changes form: a diver's gravitational potential energy becomes kinetic energy and then energy of splashing water, and stored water's potential energy becomes kinetic energy, turbine mechanical energy and finally electrical energy. The total always remains constant.

mcqs.q: How much energy is equivalent to a mass of 1 g, using E = m c^2 with c = 3 x 10^8 m/s?
mcqs.why: Formula: E = m c^2, with m = 1 g = 0.001 kg. Substitution: E = 0.001 x (3 x 10^8)^2. Step by step: (3 x 10^8)^2 = 9 x 10^16; E = 0.001 x 9 x 10^16 = 9 x 10^13 J. Because c^2 is huge, a tiny mass equals an enormous energy - the source of nuclear energy.

mcqs.q: Which description of fossil fuels is correct?
options: They are renewable and produce no pollution
They formed from remains of plants and animals buried millions of years ago, are non-renewable, and burning them releases carbon dioxide and pollutants
They are obtained from moving air
They come from fission of uranium nuclei
mcqs.why: Coal, oil and natural gas are fossil fuels formed from buried plant and animal remains. They are cheap and widely used in power stations and engines, but they are non-renewable and their burning causes air pollution and global warming - unlike wind and solar energy, which are renewable and clean.

mcqs.q: The efficiency of a machine is defined as
options: Total energy input divided by useful energy output
Useful energy output divided by total energy input
Useful output multiplied by total input
The power of the machine in watts
mcqs.why: Efficiency = Useful energy output / Total energy input, with no unit, usually given as a percentage: Efficiency (%) = (Useful output / Total input) x 100. No real machine reaches 100 percent because some input energy is always wasted, mainly as heat from friction. Example: an ordinary bulb gives only about 5 J of light per 100 J supplied, an efficiency of (5 / 100) x 100 = 5 percent; a fluorescent tube reaches about 20 percent.

mcqs.q: Power is defined as the rate of doing work, P = W / t. Which statement about its units is correct?
options: 1 watt = 1 joule per second, 1 kW = 1000 W and 1 hp = 746 W
1 kWh is a unit of power
mcqs.why: Since P = W / t, its SI unit is the watt: 1 W = 1 J/s, so a 100 W bulb converts 100 J every second. Larger units are the kilowatt (1 kW = 1000 W) and the horsepower (1 hp = 746 W); the kilowatt hour, 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J, measures energy, not power.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems and Assignments
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Work cases (W = F x S): tug of war, 1100 N through 2.0 m gives 2200 J = 2.2 x 10^3 J; kicking a ball with 40 N over 0.15 m gives 6 J; lifting a 50 kg barbell 1.95 m gives about 9.6 x 10^2 J.
  • Kinetic energy cases (E_K = 1/2 m v^2): a 30 g bullet at 400 m/s has 2400 J; an 800 kg car with 3150 J moves at only 2.8 m/s; a 1.2 kg meteorite with 5.5 x 10^8 J travels at about 3 x 10^4 m/s.
  • Gravitational potential energy (E_GPE = m g h): lifting 10 kg through 5 m gains 490 J; a 2000 kg piano has 0 J relative to its own floor but 3.7 x 10^4 J relative to a basement floor 1.9 m below.
  • Mass-energy (E = m c^2): complete conversion of 1 g gives 0.001 x (3 x 10^8)^2 = 9 x 10^13 J; a 50 kg person's mass equals 4.5 x 10^18 J.
  • A 250 W heater running for 10 minutes generates E = P x t = 250 x 600 = 1.5 x 10^5 J = 150 kJ of heat.
  • Power results (P = W / t): an elevator raising 5000 N through 15.0 m in 10.0 s develops 7500 W; a chair lift carrying 500 people up 1200 m in one hour needs 1.06 x 10^5 W.
  • A 2750 W motor lifts a 385 kg sofa set 16.0 m in about 22 s; a 2.0 hp motor does about 5.4 x 10^6 J of work in 1.0 h.

Solved Exercises

Assignment 6.1 — TUG OF WAR

Q: During a tug-of-war, team A pulls on team B by applying a force of 1100 N to the rope between them. The rope remains parallel to the ground. How much work does team A do if they pull team B toward's them a distance of 2.0 m?

Ans: Given: force F = 1100 N, displacement S = 2.0 m in the direction of the force (rope parallel to the ground).
Formula: W = F x S.
Substitution: W = 1100 N x 2.0 m.
W = 2200 J = 2.2 x 10^3 J.
Answer: 2.2 x 10^3 J

Assignment 6.2 — BULLET KINETIC ENERGY

Q: A bullet of mass 30 g travels at a speed of 400 ms^-1. Calculate its kinetic energy.

Ans: Given: mass m = 30 g = 30 / 1000 = 0.03 kg, speed v = 400 m/s.
Formula: E_K = 1/2 x m x v^2.
Substitution: E_K = 1/2 x 0.03 kg x (400 m/s)^2.
(400)^2 = 160,000.
E_K = 0.5 x 0.03 x 160,000 = 0.5 x 4800 = 2400 J.
Answer: 2400 J

Assignment 6.3 — GAIN IN GRAVITATIONAL POTENTIAL ENERGY

Q: An object of mass 10 kg is lifted vertically through a height of 5 m at a constant speed. What is the gravitational potential energy gained by the object?

Ans: Given: mass m = 10 kg, height h = 5 m, g = 9.8 m/s^2.
Formula: E_GPE = m x g x h.
Substitution: E_GPE = 10 kg x 9.8 m/s^2 x 5 m.
E_GPE = 490 J.
Answer: 490 J

Assignment 6.4 — ONLY 1g OF ENERGY

Q: How much energy is generated when mass of 1g is completely converted into energy?

Ans: Given: mass m = 1 g = 1 / 1000 = 0.001 kg, speed of light c = 3 x 10^8 m/s.
Formula: E = m x c^2 (Einstein's mass-energy equation).
Substitution: E = 0.001 kg x (3 x 10^8 m/s)^2.
(3 x 10^8)^2 = 9 x 10^16.
E = 0.001 x 9 x 10^16 = 9 x 10^13 J.
Answer: 9 x 10^13 J

Assignment 6.5 — ELECTRIC HEATER

Q: An electric heater is heated at 250 W. Calculate the quantity of heat generated in 10 minutes.

Ans: Given: power P = 250 W, time t = 10 minutes = 10 x 60 = 600 s.
Formula: energy (heat) E = P x t.
Substitution: E = 250 W x 600 s.
E = 150,000 J = 1.5 x 10^5 J = 150 kJ.
Answer: 150 kJ (1.5 x 10^5 J)

Extension Exercise 6.1

Q: If a car of mass 800 kg is having same kinetic energy, what will be its speed? (Example 6.2: the bullet has kinetic energy of 3150 J.)

Ans: Given: mass of car m = 800 kg; kinetic energy of the car E_K = 3150 J (the same as the bullet in Example 6.2)
Formula: E_K = (1/2) m v^2, so v = sqrt(2 E_K / m)
Substitution: v = sqrt(2 x 3150 J / 800 kg)
Working: v = sqrt(6300 / 800) = sqrt(7.875) = 2.81 m/s
Answer: 2.8 m/s — because the car is far more massive than the bullet, the same kinetic energy gives it only a very small speed.

Extension Exercise 6.2

Q: Find your mass and convert it into energy.

Ans: This exercise is to be done with your own mass, so the final answer is different (variable) for every student; the method is as follows, worked out for a mass of 50 kg as in Example 6.4.
Given: your mass m (in kg, measured on a balance); speed of light c = 3 x 10^8 m/s
Formula: Einstein's mass-energy equation E = m c^2
Substitution (for m = 50 kg): E = 50 kg x (3 x 10^8 m/s)^2
Working: E = 50 x 9 x 10^16 = 4.5 x 10^18 J
In general, for your own mass m in kilograms, E = m x 9 x 10^16 J.
Answer: Variable — for a 50 kg person the mass is equivalent to 4.5 x 10^18 J of energy; insert your own mass in E = m c^2 to get your own value.

Exercise — Numerical Problems

Q: 1. Determine the work done in each of the following cases: a) Kicking a soccer ball forward with a force of 40 N over a distance of 15 cm b) Lifting a 50-kg barbell straight up 1.95 m

Ans: a) Kicking a soccer ball:
Given: force F = 40 N, distance S = 15 cm = 0.15 m.
Formula: W = F x S.
Substitution: W = 40 N x 0.15 m = 6 J.
Answer (a): 6 J
b) Lifting a barbell:
Given: mass m = 50 kg, height h = 1.95 m, g = 9.8 m/s^2.
The force needed equals the weight, F = m g = 50 x 9.8 = 490 N.
Formula: W = F x h = m g h.
Substitution: W = 490 N x 1.95 m = 955.5 J, about 9.6 x 10^2 J.
Answer (b): 9.6 x 10^2 J

Q: 2. Calculate the velocity of a 1.2 kg falling star (meteorite) with 5.5 x 10^8 J of energy.

Ans: Given: mass m = 1.2 kg, kinetic energy E_K = 5.5 x 10^8 J.
Formula: E_K = 1/2 x m x v^2, so v = sqrt(2 x E_K / m).
Substitution: v = sqrt(2 x 5.5 x 10^8 / 1.2) = sqrt(1.1 x 10^9 / 1.2).
Inside the root: 1.1 x 10^9 / 1.2 = 9.17 x 10^8.
v = sqrt(9.17 x 10^8) = 3.03 x 10^4 m/s, about 3.0 x 10^4 m/s.
Answer: 3 x 10^4 m/s

Q: 3. Calculate the gravitational potential energy of a 2000 kg piano a) resting on the floor b) with respect to the basement floor, 1.9 m below.

Ans: Given: mass m = 2000 kg, g = 9.8 m/s^2.
a) Resting on the floor: taking the floor as the reference level, the height is h = 0.
Formula: E_GPE = m x g x h.
Substitution: E_GPE = 2000 x 9.8 x 0 = 0 J.
Answer (a): 0 J
b) With respect to the basement floor, the piano is h = 1.9 m above the reference level.
Formula: E_GPE = m x g x h.
Substitution: E_GPE = 2000 kg x 9.8 m/s^2 x 1.9 m = 37,240 J, about 3.7 x 10^4 J.
Answer (b): 3.7 x 10^4 J

Q: 4. An elevator weighing 5000N is raised to a height of 15.0 m in 10.0 s, how much power is developed?

Ans: Given: weight (force) F = 5000 N, height h = 15.0 m, time t = 10.0 s.
First find the work done against gravity.
Formula: W = F x h.
Substitution: W = 5000 N x 15.0 m = 75,000 J.
Now find the power.
Formula: P = W / t.
Substitution: P = 75,000 J / 10.0 s = 7500 W.
Answer: 7500 W

Q: 5. What power is required for a ski-hill chair lift that transports 500 people (average mass 65 kg) per hour to an increased elevation of 1200 m?

Ans: Given: number of people = 500, average mass of one person = 65 kg, height h = 1200 m, time t = 1 hour = 3600 s, g = 9.8 m/s^2.
Total mass lifted: m = 500 x 65 kg = 32,500 kg.
Work done against gravity:
Formula: W = m x g x h.
Substitution: W = 32,500 x 9.8 x 1200 = 3.822 x 10^8 J.
Power required:
Formula: P = W / t.
Substitution: P = 3.822 x 10^8 J / 3600 s = 1.06 x 10^5 W.
Answer: 1.06 x 10^5 W

Q: 6. How long will it take a 2750-W motor to lift a 385-kg sofa set to a sixth-story window 16.0 m above?

Ans: Given: power P = 2750 W, mass m = 385 kg, height h = 16.0 m, g = 9.8 m/s^2.
Work needed to lift the sofa set:
Formula: W = m x g x h.
Substitution: W = 385 x 9.8 x 16.0 = 60,368 J.
Time taken:
Formula: P = W / t, so t = W / P.
Substitution: t = 60,368 J / 2750 W = 21.95 s, about 22 s.
Answer: 22 s

Q: 7. How much work can a 2.0-hp motor do in 1.0 h?

Ans: Given: power P = 2.0 hp, time t = 1.0 h = 3600 s.
Convert horsepower to watts: 1 hp = 746 W, so P = 2.0 x 746 = 1492 W.
Formula: W = P x t.
Substitution: W = 1492 W x 3600 s = 5,371,200 J, about 5.4 x 10^6 J.
Answer: 5.4 x 10^6 J

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Mass from density: m = rho x V, so a 6 m^3 liquid of density 30 kg m^-3 has mass 180 kg.
  • Liquids and gases are collectively categorized as fluids because both can flow.
  • Pressure can be measured in atm, Pa and bar, but kg m^-3 is a unit of density, not pressure.
  • Pressure at a depth in a fluid increases as the depth increases.
  • The unit used for pressure in weather maps is the bar (millibar on weather maps).
  • A rock weighing 25.7 N in air and 21.8 N in water experiences a buoyant force of 3.9 N.
  • Strain has no unit because it is a ratio of two lengths, while Young modulus is measured in Pa.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Multiple Choice Questions

Q: 1. A container having volume of 6 m^3 is full with a liquid, having density of 30 kg m^-3. The mass of the liquid is

Options: (a) 180 kg (b) 24 kg (c) 5 kg (d) 0.2 kg

Correct answer: 180 kg

Q: 2. Liquids and gases and collectively categorized as

Options: (a) Liquids (b) Pascals (c) Fluids (d) None

Correct answer: Fluids

Q: 3. Which of the following cannot be used to measure pressure

Options: (a) Atm (b) Pa (c) bar (d) kg m^-3

Correct answer: kg m^-3

Q: 4. Pressure at depth in fluid

Options: (a) increases (b) decreases (c) none (d) stays the same

Correct answer: increases

Q: 5. The unit used for pressure in weather maps is

Options: (a) Atm (b) Pa (c) bar (d) N m^-2

Correct answer: bar

Q: 6. A rock weighs 25.7 N in air and 21.8 N in water. What is the buoyant force of the water

Options: (a) 4.1 N (b) 3.9 N (c) 1.18 N (d) 0.84 N

Correct answer: 3.9 N

Q: 7. Which of the following objects, submerged in water, experiences the largest magnitude of the buoyant force?

Options: (a) 1-kg helium balloon (b) 1 kg of wood (c) 1 kg of iron (d) all the same

Correct answer: 1-kg helium balloon

Q: 8. The unit of strain is

Options: (a) kg m^-3 (b) Pa (c) N m^-2 (d) none

Correct answer: none

Q: 9. Young modulus is measured in units of

Options: (a) kg m^-3 (b) Pa (c) N (d) none

Correct answer: Pa

mcqs.q: A container having volume of 6 m^3 is full with a liquid, having density of 30 kg m^-3. The mass of the liquid is
mcqs.why: Using m = rho x V, substitution gives m = 30 kg m^-3 x 6 m^3 = 180 kg, so the mass of the liquid is 180 kg.

mcqs.q: Liquids and gases and collectively categorized as
mcqs.why: Liquids and gases can both flow, and substances that can flow are collectively categorized as fluids in the book.

mcqs.q: Which of the following cannot be used to measure pressure
mcqs.why: Atm, Pa and bar are all units of pressure, whereas kg m^-3 is the unit of density (mass per unit volume), so it cannot measure pressure.

mcqs.q: Pressure at depth in fluid
mcqs.why: Pressure in a fluid is P = rho g h, so as depth h increases the pressure increases in direct proportion to the depth.

mcqs.q: The unit used for pressure in weather maps is
mcqs.why: The book states that the unit used for pressure in weather maps is the bar, with millibar used for the plotted isobar values.

mcqs.q: A rock weighs 25.7 N in air and 21.8 N in water. What is the buoyant force of the water
mcqs.why: Buoyant force equals loss of weight: formula Fb = weight in air - weight in water, substitution Fb = 25.7 N - 21.8 N = 3.9 N as the final result.

mcqs.q: Which of the following objects, submerged in water, experiences the largest magnitude of the buoyant force?
mcqs.why: For the same 1 kg mass, the helium balloon has the lowest density and therefore the largest volume, so it displaces the most water and experiences the largest buoyant force.

mcqs.q: The unit of strain is
mcqs.why: Strain = extension / original length is a ratio of two lengths, so the units cancel and strain has no unit at all.

mcqs.q: Young modulus is measured in units of
mcqs.why: Young modulus = stress / strain; strain has no unit, so Young modulus has the unit of stress, the pascal (Pa).

mcqs.q: At sea level, the average value of atmospheric pressure is
mcqs.why: The book gives atmospheric pressure at sea level as 1.013 x 10^5 Pa, defined as one atmosphere (1 atm), supporting a mercury column of about 760 mm.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A mercury barometer column decreases as you climb a mountain because atmospheric pressure falls with height.
  • Two walnuts squeezed together crack because the force acts on a very small contact area, giving a very large pressure P = F / A.
  • A knife cutting edge is made very thin so a small area gives a very large pressure and cuts easily.
  • Water tanks are kept at the highest level so depth h gives large pressure P = rho g h at the taps.
  • A needle sinks because solid steel is denser than water, while a hollow ship has average density less than water and floats when upthrust equals its weight.
  • Camels have large, broad, flat feet so their weight is spread over a large area and the pressure on sand is small.
  • Ears pop when air equalizes the pressure difference across the eardrum during rapid height changes; a sealed balloon filled on a mountain contracts on descending.
  • Steel is more elastic than rubber: its Young modulus is about 2.0 x 10^11 Pa, far greater than that of rubber.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Conceptual Questions

Q: 1. If you climbed a mountain carrying a mercury barometer, would the level of the mercury column in the glass tube of the barometer increase or decrease as you climb the mountain? Explain.

Ans: It would decrease. Atmospheric pressure falls as we go higher above the surface of the Earth, because there is less air above us pressing down. The mercury column is supported by the atmospheric pressure acting on the mercury in the bowl, so a smaller pressure can support only a shorter column. The height of the column therefore drops as we climb.

Q: 2. Walnuts can be broken in the hand by squeezing two together but not one. Why?

Ans: When two walnuts are squeezed together, the force of the hand is concentrated on the very small area where the two hard shells touch each other. Since pressure = force / area, the small contact area produces a very large pressure and the shell cracks. A single walnut rests against the broad palm of the hand; the same force is spread over a much larger area, the pressure is small, and the shell does not break.

Q: 3. Why is the cutting edge of the knife made very thin?

Ans: A thin edge has a very small area. When we push the knife, our force acts on this small area, so the pressure (force per unit area) becomes very large. This large pressure separates the material being cut, so the knife cuts easily. A thick, blunt edge spreads the force over a larger area and gives much less pressure.

Q: 4. Why water tanks are constructed at the highest level in our houses?

Ans: Pressure in a liquid increases with depth, P = rho g h. Keeping the tank at the highest level gives the water a large height h above the taps, so the pressure at the taps is large. This pressure pushes the water through the pipes to every part of the house. A low tank would give weak pressure and the water would not reach the upper taps properly.

Q: 5. Why a small needle sinks in water and huge ships travel easily in water without sinking?

Ans: Floating depends on density and upthrust, not on size or total weight. A needle is solid steel, denser than water; the small volume of water it displaces weighs less than the needle, so the upthrust is less than its weight and it sinks. A ship is hollow, so its average density, including the air inside it, is less than that of water. It displaces a very large volume of water, and when the weight of the displaced water becomes equal to the total weight of the ship, the upthrust balances its weight and it floats.

Q: 6. Explain how and why camels have adapted to allow them to walk more easily in desert conditions?

Ans: A camel has large, broad, flat feet. Its weight (the force) is spread over a large area, so the pressure exerted on the sand, P = F / A, is small. The feet therefore do not sink deep into the soft sand and the camel can walk easily in the desert. Narrow feet would give a large pressure and would sink at every step.

Q: 7. You would have probably experienced your ears 'popping' while driving in the mountains. Why ears 'pop'?

Ans: As we go up or come down a mountain, the atmospheric pressure outside changes quickly, but the air pressure in the middle ear, behind the eardrum, changes more slowly. The pressure difference pushes the eardrum in or out, which feels uncomfortable. When air finally passes through the narrow tube joining the middle ear to the throat, the pressures on the two sides become equal, the eardrum returns to its normal position, and we hear and feel a 'pop'.

Q: 8. If you filled an airtight balloon at the top of a mountain, would the balloon expand or contract as you descend the mountain? Explain.

Ans: It would contract. At the top of the mountain the outside atmospheric pressure is low, so the air sealed inside the balloon keeps it fully expanded. As we descend, the atmospheric pressure around the balloon increases. This greater outside pressure squeezes the balloon, the air inside is compressed into a smaller volume, and the balloon contracts until the inside and outside pressures balance again.

Q: 9. A rowboat is floating in a swimming pool when the anchor is dropped over the side. When the anchor is dropped, will the water level in the swimming pool increase, decrease, or remain the same? Explain.

Ans: The water level will decrease. While the anchor is in the boat, the floating boat displaces a volume of water whose weight equals the weight of the boat plus the anchor. When the anchor is dropped into the pool it sinks, because it is denser than water, and then it displaces only its own volume of water. The weight of that volume of water is less than the weight of the anchor, so the total volume of water displaced becomes smaller and the pool level falls slightly.

Q: 10. Which material is more elastic, steel or rubber and why?

Ans: Steel is more elastic than rubber. Elasticity is judged by how completely a material recovers and by its Young's modulus, not by how much it stretches. For the same load a steel wire stretches very little, that is, it shows a very small strain for a large stress, and it returns completely to its original length when the load is removed; its Young's modulus is about 2.0 x 10^11 Pa, far greater than that of rubber. Rubber stretches a great deal under a small force, which shows a small modulus, so in the physics sense rubber is less elastic than steel.

mcqs.q: If you climb a mountain carrying a mercury barometer, what happens to the mercury column?
options: It decreases because atmospheric pressure falls with height
It empties completely at any height
mcqs.why: Atmospheric pressure falls as we go higher because there is less air above pressing down, so the smaller pressure can support only a shorter mercury column.

mcqs.q: Why can two walnuts be broken by squeezing them together in the hand, but not one walnut alone?
options: Two walnuts are softer than one
The hand force doubles with two walnuts
The force is concentrated on a very small contact area, giving very large pressure
The palm produces no force on one walnut
mcqs.why: Pressure = force / area. Where the two hard shells touch the area is very small, so the same hand force produces a very large pressure that cracks the shell.

mcqs.q: Why is the cutting edge of a knife made very thin?
options: To make the knife lighter only
A thin edge increases the force of the hand
A thin edge reduces pressure so material is not damaged
A thin edge gives a small area and therefore a very large pressure for the applied force
mcqs.why: With P = F / A, a very small edge area makes the pressure from the pushing force very large, and this large pressure separates the material being cut.

mcqs.q: Why are water tanks constructed at the highest level in houses?
options: To give a large height h so pressure P = rho g h at the taps is large
To reduce the density of water
To stop water flowing to upper taps
mcqs.why: Pressure in a liquid increases with depth, P = rho g h. A high tank gives a large h above the taps, so the pressure pushes water through pipes to every part of the house.

mcqs.q: Why does a small needle sink in water while a huge ship floats?
options: Floating depends only on total weight
The needle is heavier than the ship
The needle is denser than water, while the hollow ship has average density less than water and upthrust balances its weight
Ships are pushed up by their engines
mcqs.why: The needle displaces little water so upthrust is less than its weight. The hollow ship displaces a large volume until the weight of displaced water equals the ship weight, so it floats.

mcqs.q: How have camels adapted to walk easily in desert sand?
options: Large, broad, flat feet that spread weight over a large area and reduce pressure
Narrow feet that dig into sand
Very heavy feet that compact the sand
Feet that increase pressure on sand
mcqs.why: From P = F / A, spreading the camel weight over a large foot area makes the pressure on soft sand small, so the feet do not sink deeply at every step.

mcqs.q: Why do ears pop while driving in the mountains?
options: Air pressure in the middle ear changes faster than outside
The eardrum breaks and repairs itself
Air passes through the tube to the throat and equalizes pressure on both sides of the eardrum
mcqs.why: Outside pressure changes quickly with height while middle-ear pressure lags, pushing the eardrum. When air passes through the narrow tube, pressures equalize, the eardrum returns to normal and a pop is felt.

mcqs.q: A balloon filled airtight at the top of a mountain is brought down. What happens to it?
options: It expands because outside pressure rises
It contracts because the greater outside pressure squeezes it
It bursts at once on descending
mcqs.why: At the top the outside pressure is low. On descending, atmospheric pressure increases and squeezes the sealed air into a smaller volume until inside and outside pressures balance again.

mcqs.q: A rowboat floats in a swimming pool and its anchor is dropped over the side into the pool. What happens to the pool water level?
mcqs.why: In the boat the anchor displaces water equal to its weight. Sunk in the pool it displaces only its own volume, whose water weight is less than the anchor weight, so total displaced volume falls and the level decreases.

mcqs.q: Which material is more elastic, steel or rubber, and why?
options: Rubber, because it stretches the most
Steel, because it has a far greater Young modulus and recovers completely
Rubber, because its Young modulus is larger
Both are equally elastic in physics
mcqs.why: Elasticity is judged by recovery and Young modulus, not by amount of stretch. Steel shows very small strain for large stress, recovers completely, and its Young modulus is about 2.0 x 10^11 Pa, far greater than rubber.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • In solids molecules vibrate about fixed positions; in liquids they slide over each other; in gases they move randomly at high speed; plasma is a fourth state found at very high temperatures.
  • Density rho = m / V has SI unit kg/m^3; iron is 7900 kg/m^3 and air is 1.3 kg/m^3.
  • Pressure P = F / A has SI unit the pascal: 1 Pa = 1 N / 1 m^2.
  • Atmospheric pressure at sea level averages 1.013 x 10^5 Pa (1 atm); a mercury barometer column stands about 760 mm and lines of equal pressure on weather maps are isobars.
  • Pascal principle: external pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted unchanged to every point; in a hydraulic lift F2 = (A2 / A1) x F1.
  • Pressure in a liquid is P = rho g h, depending only on depth, density and g.
  • Archimedes principle: buoyant force equals the weight of fluid displaced, Fb = weight of displaced fluid.
  • Hooke law: within the elastic limit extension is proportional to force, F(res) = -k x with k in N/m; Young modulus Y = stress / strain = F l / (A x), about 20 x 10^10 Pa for steel.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Comprehensive Questions

Q: 1. Using kinetic molecular model of matter, explain three states of matter.

Ans: In the kinetic molecular model, matter is made of molecules in motion, and the three states differ in the arrangement of the molecules, the strength of the forces between them and the kind of motion they have. In solids the molecules are arranged closely in a fixed pattern, the attractive forces between them are strong, and they only vibrate about their mean positions; a solid therefore has a definite shape and volume. In liquids the molecules are close together but the pattern is not fixed and does not extend far; the molecules can move about and slide over each other and the attractive forces are weaker than in solids, so a liquid has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container. In gases the molecules are far apart compared with their size, they move constantly and randomly at high speed, collide elastically with each other and with the walls of the container, and the forces between them are negligible except during collisions; a gas therefore has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume and fills its container. Because liquids and gases can flow, they are together called fluids. There is also a fourth state, plasma, consisting of free electrons and atoms from which electrons have been removed, found at very high temperatures, for example in the Sun.

Q: 2. Define and explain density and pressure.

Ans: Density is the mass of a substance per unit volume, rho = m / V. It tells how heavy a material is for its size; for example iron, with density 7900 kg/m^3, has much more mass in the same volume than air, 1.3 kg/m^3. Its SI unit is kg/m^3. Pressure is the force acting normally (perpendicularly) per unit area, P = F / A. The same force produces a large pressure when it acts on a small area and a small pressure when it acts on a large area, which is why a needle pricks easily while a finger only makes a dent in a balloon. The SI unit of pressure is the newton per square metre, N/m^2, given the special name pascal (Pa): 1 Pa = 1 N / 1 m^2.

Q: 3. What is atmospheric pressure? How is it measured by using a mercury barometer? Also describe how weather changes with atmospheric pressure?

Ans: The Earth is covered by a deep layer of air, the atmosphere, and the pressure exerted by this air on everything is called atmospheric pressure. At sea level its average value is 1.013 x 10^5 Pa, defined as one atmosphere (1 atm). It is measured with a mercury barometer, invented by Torricelli: a long glass tube, closed at one end, is filled with mercury and inverted into a bowl of mercury. The mercury in the tube falls until the column stands about 760 mm above the level in the bowl. The atmosphere presses on the mercury in the bowl and this pressure supports the column, so the height h of the column measures the atmospheric pressure, and any change in h means the atmospheric pressure has changed. Barometers kept at one place show small day-to-day changes, which are plotted on weather maps; lines joining places of equal pressure are called isobars and the unit used is the millibar. Falling pressure generally warns of unsettled or stormy weather and rising pressure indicates fair weather; winds blow from high-pressure regions to low-pressure regions, so changes in atmospheric pressure in a region indicate a change in the weather.

Q: 4. State Pascal's principle and explain with example?

Ans: Pascal's principle (Pascal's law) states: an external pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted unchanged to every point within the fluid. Example, the hydraulic lift: two cylinders of cross-sectional areas A1 (small) and A2 (large), each fitted with a piston, are connected and filled with oil (hydraulic fluid). A small force F1 on the small piston produces pressure P1 = F1 / A1. By Pascal's principle the same pressure acts under the large piston, P2 = P1, so F2 / A2 = F1 / A1 and F2 = (A2 / A1) x F1. If A2 is 100 times A1, the force is magnified 100 times, so a small effort can lift a car. Hydraulic brakes work on the same principle: pressing the brake pedal creates pressure in the brake fluid, which is transmitted equally to the pistons at the wheels and forces the brake shoes against the wheels to stop the car.

Q: 5. How pressure varies with depth in liquids? Explain.

Ans: Pressure in a liquid increases directly with depth below the surface. Consider a disc of area A at depth h in a liquid of density rho. The force on the disc is the weight of the cylindrical column of liquid above it: F = m g, with m = rho V and V = A h, so F = rho A h g. Dividing by the area, P = F / A = rho g h. Thus the pressure at a point depends only on the depth h, the density rho of the liquid and g, not on the shape of the container or the total volume of liquid. From this law follow the properties of liquid pressure: pressure increases with depth, so water spurts fastest and furthest from the lowest hole in a can; at the same depth the pressure is the same in all directions; and a liquid finds its own level, standing at the same height in connected tubes of different shapes, because points at the same depth beneath the surface are at the same pressure.

Q: 6. What is meant by buoyant force or upthrust in fluids?

Ans: When an object is immersed in a fluid, the fluid pressure on its lower surface is greater than the pressure on its upper surface, because pressure increases with depth. The difference of these pressures produces a net upward force on the object. This upward force exerted by a fluid on a body immersed in it is called the upthrust, or buoyant force, and the phenomenon is called buoyancy. We feel it when we try to push a piece of cork under water: the buoyant force pushes the cork back up. The upthrust reduces the apparent weight of an immersed body, which is why it is relatively easy to lift someone in a swimming pool.

Q: 7. State and explain Archimedes principle.

Ans: Archimedes' principle states: the buoyant force acting on an object fully or partially submerged in a fluid is equal to the weight of the fluid displaced by the object, Fb = weight of displaced fluid = m(fluid) x g. It can be understood with a brick lowered into a container of water that has a spout at the surface: as the brick sinks, water flows out through the spout into a smaller container, and the volume collected is the displaced volume, equal to the volume of the submerged part of the brick. The weight of this displaced water equals the upthrust on the brick, which is also the brick's apparent loss of weight. The principle is used to find the density of a body: weighing the body in air (W) and in water gives Fb = W - apparent weight, and W / Fb = density of body / density of water, from which the density of the body follows. Whether a body floats or sinks depends on its density relative to the fluid: denser than the fluid it sinks, less dense it floats.

Q: 8. What is elasticity? Explain.

Ans: Elasticity is the property of solid materials by which they return to their original shape and size after the deforming force is removed. A rubber band, an archer's bow and the strings of a tennis racket are deformed by a force and recover when the force is removed; when a tennis ball is hit, its shape is distorted but it regains its original shape as it bounces off the racket. Materials that do not return to their original shape after being distorted, such as plasticine, clay and dough, are called inelastic. Most materials are elastic only up to a certain limit, the elastic limit: beyond this limit the material does not recover, but breaks or remains permanently deformed when the deforming force is removed.

Q: 9. State and explain Hooke's law.

Ans: Hooke's law states that within the elastic limit, the extension (or compression) x of a spring or wire is directly proportional to the applied force. For a spring it is written in terms of the restoring force as F(res) proportional to -x, or F(res) = -k x, where k is the force constant, with unit N/m, and the negative sign shows that the restoring force is directed against the displacement. On the stress-strain curve the law is obeyed up to the limit of proportionality (point A); up to the nearby elastic limit (point B) the material still behaves elastically, but beyond it the material is permanently deformed, passes the maximum stress at point C and finally breaks at the breaking point D. The same relation holds for a wire under tension.

Q: 10. Define and explain, Stress, Strain and Young's modulus

Ans: When a wire of length l and cross-sectional area A is stretched by a force F, producing an extension x: (i) Stress is the force applied per unit area of cross-section to produce deformation, stress = F / A; its unit is N/m^2 or pascal. (ii) Strain is the extension per unit original length, strain = x / l; being a ratio of two lengths, it has no unit. (iii) Within the limit of proportionality the strain produced in a stretched wire is proportional to the stress within it, and the constant ratio is called Young's modulus of the material, Y = stress / strain = (F / A) / (x / l) = F l / (A x). Young's modulus depends only on the material: it is large for stiff materials such as steel, about 20 x 10^10 Pa, and much smaller for easily stretched materials. Its unit is the same as that of stress, N/m^2 or Pa.

mcqs.q: In the kinetic molecular model, how do molecules behave in a solid?
options: They move randomly at high speed far apart
They are arranged closely in a fixed pattern and only vibrate about their mean positions
They slide freely over each other with no pattern
They are free electrons removed from atoms
mcqs.why: In solids attractive forces are strong and molecules sit in a fixed pattern, only vibrating about mean positions, so a solid has definite shape and volume.

mcqs.q: What is density and what is its SI unit?
options: Extension per unit length, no unit
mcqs.why: Density is mass per unit volume, rho = m / V. Its SI unit is kg/m^3, for example iron has density 7900 kg/m^3 compared with air at 1.3 kg/m^3.

mcqs.q: How is atmospheric pressure measured with a mercury barometer?
options: By weighing the air in a bowl
The atmosphere presses on mercury in a bowl and supports a column about 760 mm high, whose height measures the pressure
By heating mercury until it boils
By counting isobars on a weather map
mcqs.why: In Torricelli barometer the inverted mercury tube column falls to about 760 mm; atmospheric pressure on the bowl mercury supports the column, so its height h measures the pressure.

mcqs.q: Pascal principle states that external pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is
options: Transmitted unchanged to every point within the fluid
mcqs.why: Pascal law says an external pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted unchanged to every point, which is why a hydraulic lift can magnify force by the area ratio.

mcqs.q: Pressure at depth h in a liquid of density rho is given by
options: P = F / A only, independent of depth
mcqs.why: The force on area A is the weight of the liquid column rho A h g; dividing by A gives P = F / A = rho g h, depending only on depth, density and g.

mcqs.q: What is buoyant force or upthrust?
options: The downward force of gravity on a body in fluid
The net upward force on an immersed body because fluid pressure is greater on its lower surface than on its upper surface
The force needed to stretch a wire
The pressure transmitted by a hydraulic fluid
mcqs.why: Pressure increases with depth, so pressure on the lower surface exceeds that on the upper surface; the difference produces a net upward upthrust, felt when pushing cork under water.

mcqs.q: Archimedes principle states that the buoyant force on a submerged object equals
options: The weight of the object itself
Half the weight of the object
The weight of the fluid displaced by the object
The volume of the object in newtons
mcqs.why: Archimedes principle: Fb = weight of displaced fluid = m(fluid) x g, which also equals the apparent loss of weight of the immersed body.

mcqs.q: What is elasticity?
options: The property of returning to original shape and size after the deforming force is removed
The property of flowing like a liquid
The property of staying permanently deformed
The property of breaking at the elastic limit
mcqs.why: Elastic materials such as a rubber band or bow recover after deformation is removed; beyond the elastic limit a material breaks or remains permanently deformed.

mcqs.q: Hooke law for a spring is written for the restoring force as
options: F(res) = -k x, where k is the force constant in N/m
mcqs.why: Within the elastic limit extension x is proportional to applied force; the restoring force is F(res) = -k x, the negative sign showing it acts against the displacement.

mcqs.q: Young modulus Y of a stretched wire is defined as
options: Y = stress / strain = F l / (A x)
Y = F x / (A l) only in liquids
mcqs.why: Stress = F / A and strain = x / l, so Y = stress / strain = (F / A) / (x / l) = F l / (A x); it depends only on the material and is about 20 x 10^10 Pa for steel.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems and Assignments
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Diamond: density = 0.072 kg / 0.00002 m^3 = 3600 kg/m^3.
  • A 900 N concrete block on a 3 m x 3 m base exerts pressure 900 / 9 = 100 Pa.
  • Pressure at 100 m depth in water: 1000 x 9.8 x 100 = 9.8 x 10^5 Pa.
  • A Moon rock weighing 90.9 N with apparent weight 60.6 N in water has density 3000 kg/m^3.
  • Elastic wire: Young modulus = (300 / 0.02) / (0.10 / 2) = 3.0 x 10^5 N/m^2.
  • A cubic metre of steel has mass 7900 kg, far more than a cubic metre of wood, because mass for equal volumes is proportional to density.
  • A 40 kg girl on a heel tip of 0.0001 m^2 exerts pressure 3.92 x 10^6 Pa.
  • Glass block 37.5 N: least pressure 1250 Pa on its largest face and greatest pressure 7500 Pa on its smallest face; water barometer height at atmospheric pressure is about 10.3 m.

Solved Exercises

Assignment 7.1 — Density of Diamond

Q: A diamond has a volume of 0.00002 m^3, its mass is measured as 0.072 kg. Calculate its density.

Ans: Given: mass m = 0.072 kg
Volume V = 0.00002 m^3 = 2.0 x 10^-5 m^3
Formula: density rho = m / V
Substitution: rho = 0.072 kg / 0.00002 m^3
Working: rho = 3600
Answer: 3600 kg/m^3

Assignment 7.2 — Concrete Block

Q: A block of concrete weighs 900 N and its base is a square of side 3 m. What pressure does the block exert on the ground?

Ans: Given: force F = weight = 900 N
Side of square base = 3 m
Formula: area A = side x side
Substitution: A = 3 m x 3 m = 9 m^2
Formula: pressure P = F / A
Substitution: P = 900 N / 9 m^2
Working: P = 100
Answer: 100 Pa (100 N/m^2)

Assignment 7.3 — Pressure at 100 m Depth of Water

Q: What is the pressure at a depth of 100 m below the surface of water?

Ans: Given: depth h = 100 m
Density of water rho = 1000 kg/m^3
g = 9.8 m/s^2
Formula: pressure in a liquid P = rho x g x h
Substitution: P = 1000 kg/m^3 x 9.8 m/s^2 x 100 m
Working: P = 980000
Answer: 9.8 x 10^5 Pa (about 10^6 Pa with g = 10 m/s^2)

Assignment 7.4 — Density of Rock

Q: A geologist finds that a Moon rock whose weight is 90.9 N has an apparent weight of 60.6 N when submerged in water. What is the density of the rock?

Ans: Given: weight in air W = 90.9 N
Apparent weight in water = 60.6 N
Density of water = 1000 kg/m^3
Step 1: buoyant force Fb = W - apparent weight
Substitution: Fb = 90.9 N - 60.6 N = 30.3 N
Formula: density of object rho = (W / Fb) x density of water
Substitution: rho = (90.9 / 30.3) x 1000 kg/m^3
Working: 90.9 / 30.3 = 3.0, so rho = 3.0 x 1000
Answer: 3000 kg/m^3 (3.0 x 10^3 kg/m^3)

Q: Note on Assignment 7.4

Ans: The book's printed key gives 3 kg/m^3; the correct answer is 3000 kg/m^3 (3.0 x 10^3 kg/m^3) because the key has dropped the factor 10^3: the ratio W/Fb is 3.0 and this must still be multiplied by the density of water, 1000 kg/m^3.

Assignment 7.5 — Wire Stretched

Q: An elastic wire of length 2 m and cross sectional area 0.02 m^2 is stretched 0.10 m by a 300 N weight. Calculate the Young modulus of the material.

Ans: Given: original length l = 2 m
Cross-sectional area A = 0.02 m^2
Extension x = 0.10 m
Force F = 300 N
Formula: stress = F / A
Substitution: stress = 300 N / 0.02 m^2 = 1.5 x 10^4 N/m^2
Formula: strain = x / l
Substitution: strain = 0.10 m / 2 m = 0.05
Formula: Young's modulus Y = stress / strain
Substitution: Y = 1.5 x 10^4 / 0.05
Working: Y = 300000
Answer: 3.0 x 10^5 N/m^2

Quiz — Same Volume Objects

Q: Which is a heavier, a cubic metre of steel or a cubic metre of wood? Why? (The book prints the box heading as 'SMAE VOLUME OBJECTS', i.e. Same Volume Objects.)

Ans: Given: both blocks have the same volume V = 1 m^3; density of steel (iron, Table 7.1) = 7900 kg/m^3; the density of wood is only a few hundred kg/m^3, far less than that of steel.
Formula: mass = density x volume, m = rho x V
Substitution (steel): m = 7900 kg/m^3 x 1 m^3 = 7900 kg
Substitution (wood): m = (a few hundred kg/m^3) x 1 m^3 = only a few hundred kg
Working: For equal volumes, the mass is directly proportional to the density; steel's density is more than ten times the density of wood, so the same volume of steel carries more than ten times as much mass.
Answer: A cubic metre of steel is much heavier, because steel has a much greater density than wood — equal volumes contain mass in proportion to their densities.

Extension Exercise 7.1

Q: What will be pressure if she is wearing heeled shoe with an area of tip 0.0001 m^2, and stand with all her weight on that tip? (She is the 40-kg girl of Example 7.2.)

Ans: Given: mass m = 40 kg, so weight F = m x g = 40 kg x 9.8 m/s^2 = 392 N
Area of heel tip A = 0.0001 m^2
Formula: pressure P = F / A
Substitution: P = 392 N / 0.0001 m^2
Working: P = 3920000
Answer: 3.92 x 10^6 Pa (3920 kPa)

Q: Note on Extension Exercise 7.1

Ans: The book's printed key gives 400 kPa; the correct answer is 3920 kPa (3.92 x 10^6 Pa) because 392 N acting on 0.0001 m^2 gives 392 / 0.0001 = 3.92 x 10^6 Pa. The key is about ten times too small.

Exercise — Numerical Problems

Q: 1. A rectangular glass block of dimensions 30 cm by 5 cm by 10 cm weighs 37.5 N. Calculate the least and the greatest pressure it can exert when resting on a horizontal table?

Ans: Given: weight F = 37.5 N
Dimensions = 30 cm x 5 cm x 10 cm
Step 1: greatest face area = 30 cm x 10 cm = 300 cm^2 = 0.03 m^2
Step 2: smallest face area = 5 cm x 10 cm = 50 cm^2 = 0.005 m^2
Formula: pressure P = F / A
Least pressure (block resting on its greatest face):
Substitution: P(min) = 37.5 N / 0.03 m^2 = 1250 Pa
Greatest pressure (block resting on its smallest face):
Substitution: P(max) = 37.5 N / 0.005 m^2 = 7500 Pa
Answer: least pressure 1250 Pa, greatest pressure 7500 Pa

Q: 2. What is the height of a water barometer at atmospheric pressure?

Ans: Given: atmospheric pressure P = 1.013 x 10^5 Pa
Density of water rho = 1000 kg/m^3
g = 9.8 m/s^2
Formula: P = rho x g x h, so h = P / (rho x g)
Substitution: h = 1.013 x 10^5 / (1000 x 9.8)
Working: h = 101300 / 9800 = 10.34
Answer: about 10.3 m (this is why a water barometer needs an impractically tall tube, compared with 0.76 m for mercury)

Q: 3. The small piston of a hydraulic lift has an area of 0.20 m^2. A car weighing 1.20 x 10^4 N sits on a rack mounted on the large piston. The large piston has an area of 0.90 m^2. How large a force must be applied to the small piston to support the car?

Ans: Given: area of small piston A1 = 0.20 m^2
Area of large piston A2 = 0.90 m^2
Force on large piston F2 = weight of car = 1.20 x 10^4 N
Formula: by Pascal's principle F1 / A1 = F2 / A2, so F1 = F2 x A1 / A2
Substitution: F1 = 1.20 x 10^4 N x 0.20 / 0.90
Working: F1 = 2400 / 0.90 = 2667
Answer: 2.7 x 10^3 N

Q: 4. The deepest point in the ocean is 11 km below sea level, deeper than Mt. Everest is tall. What is the pressure in atmospheres at this depth?

Ans: Given: depth h = 11 km = 11000 m
Density of seawater rho = 1025 kg/m^3
g = 9.8 m/s^2
1 atm = 1.013 x 10^5 Pa
Formula: P = rho x g x h
Substitution: P = 1025 x 9.8 x 11000
Working: 1025 x 9.8 = 10045; 10045 x 11000 = 1.105 x 10^8 Pa
