mcqs.q: How do woolen sweaters keep us warmer in winter?
options: Wool produces heat of its own in cold weather
Wool and the air trapped in its pores are poor conductors, forming an insulating layer that greatly reduces loss of body heat
Wool is white and reflects the body heat back
Wool lets warm air convect freely away from the body
mcqs.why: Wool is a bad conductor and its fine pores hold trapped air, also a very poor conductor, so the sweater acts as an insulating layer and greatly reduces the loss of body heat to the cold outside air.

mcqs.q: How can birds fly for hours without flapping their wings?
options: They ride thermals, rising convection currents of warm air that carry them upward
They are lifted by radiation coming from the warm ground
They glide on conduction currents inside the air
Warm air sinks under their wings and pushes them up
mcqs.why: Air heated by the warm ground expands, becomes less dense and rises in streams called thermals; a bird circling inside a rising thermal is carried upward by the moving air itself and can ride from one thermal to the next without flapping.

mcqs.q: In a good thermos flask, how is heat loss by radiation reduced?
options: By evacuating the space between the double walls
By fitting a stopper made of a poor conductor
By making both walls of thick glass
By silvering the inner surfaces like mirrors, so radiant heat is reflected back instead of being absorbed
mcqs.why: The silvered mirror-like inner surfaces reflect radiant heat back instead of absorbing and transmitting it; the vacuum between the walls separately stops convection, and the poor-conductor walls and stopper reduce conduction.

mcqs.q: A piece of wood in the Sun absorbs more heat than a piece of shiny metal, yet the metal feels hotter when picked up. Why?
options: The metal must be at a much higher temperature than the wood
Metal is an excellent conductor, so its heat flows rapidly into the hand, while wood is a poor conductor and passes heat only slowly
Wood reflects back all the heat that it absorbs
The hand feels the total amount of heat absorbed by a body
mcqs.why: The hand feels the rate at which heat flows into it, not the amount absorbed: wood absorbs more radiation but conducts poorly so heat passes slowly into the hand, while metal conducts excellently and its heat flows rapidly into the hand, so it feels hotter.

mcqs.q: What determines whether a pot handle remains cool or becomes unpleasantly hot during cooking?
options: The colour of the handle material
The thermal conductivity of the handle material: wood, plastic or bakelite stay cool, while metal handles become hot
Only the length of the handle
The amount of food inside the pot
mcqs.why: Handles of bad conductors such as wood, plastic or bakelite conduct very little heat from the hot pot and remain cool enough to hold, while metal handles, being good conductors, quickly carry heat along their whole length and become unpleasantly hot.

mcqs.q: When sunlight warms the land beside a cool body of water, why does a breeze blow from the water toward the land?
options: Water has a lower specific heat, so the water warms faster than the land
Land warms faster than water, the air over the land rises, and cooler denser air over the water moves in toward the land to take its place
Radiation from the water pushes the air toward the land
Air over the land becomes denser and sinks onto the water
mcqs.why: This sea breeze is convection: land has a lower specific heat than water and warms faster in sunlight, the air over it expands, becomes less dense and rises, and the cooler denser air over the water moves in toward the land; at night the reverse land breeze blows.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Conduction is the flow of heat through matter from hotter to colder parts without movement of the matter as a whole; atoms pass energy by collisions, and in metals free electrons carry energy much faster, so metals are the best conductors.
  • Rate of flow of heat through a slab: Q/t = k x A x (Th - Tc) / L, where k is the thermal conductivity of the material.
  • Thermal conductivity is the heat flowing through 1 m^2 in 1 s when a temperature difference of 1 K is maintained across a thickness of 1 m; its SI unit is W/m K.
  • Thermal conductivity values: silver 420, copper 390, water 0.6, wool 0.04 and styrofoam 0.010 W/m K, which is why metals feel cold and styrofoam is used for ice boxes.
  • Convection is transfer of heat by bulk motion of a fluid and occurs only in fluids, never in solids; heated fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises, setting up convection currents.
  • Radiation transfers heat by electromagnetic waves, mostly infrared, with or without a material medium; every object radiates continuously unless it is at 0 K, and dull black surfaces are the best absorbers and best emitters.
  • Greenhouse gases are water vapour, carbon dioxide CO2, methane CH4 and ozone O3; about 26 percent of solar radiation is reflected to space, about 19 percent is absorbed by the atmosphere and clouds, and more than 50 percent is absorbed at the Earth surface.
  • The natural greenhouse effect keeps the Earth surface about 33 deg C warmer than it would otherwise be; the global average temperature rose by 0.85 deg C between 1880 and 2012.

Solved Exercises

Exercise — Comprehensive Questions

Q: 1. Explain conduction of heat and its mechanism. Describe any three of its practical applications.

Ans: Conduction is the flow of thermal energy (heat) through matter from places of higher temperature to places of lower temperature, without any movement of the matter as a whole; heat is transferred from particle to particle. Mechanism: in a solid the atoms are closely packed. Atoms in the hotter part vibrate more violently, with greater kinetic energy, and collide with their neighbours, passing part of their energy to them; these in turn pass energy to their own neighbours, and so on along the body. In metals there is an additional, faster mechanism: metals contain a large number of free electrons, which gain kinetic energy in the hot part, move rapidly into the colder part and transfer energy by collisions with other electrons and atoms. That is why metals are the best conductors, non-metals are poor conductors, liquids conduct poorly and gases are the poorest conductors of all. Practical applications (any three): (i) cooking pots and pans are made of metal, a good conductor, so heat passes readily to the food and spreads evenly; (ii) wire gauze is placed under a glass beaker so that it conducts heat away from the centre of the flame and spreads it, protecting the glass from cracking; (iii) in soldering, heat is transferred by conduction from the hot soldering iron through the solder to the circuit board; (iv) ice boxes are double-walled with cork filling, a poor conductor, which prevents outside heat entering and keeps the ice from melting.

Q: 2. Explain thermal conductivity of a substance and its mathematical description.

Ans: The thermal conductivity of a substance is a measure of its ability to conduct heat energy. For a rod or slab of length (thickness) L and cross-sectional area A, with its hot face at temperature Th and cold face at Tc, the rate of flow of heat Q/t is directly proportional to the area A and to the temperature difference (Th - Tc), and inversely proportional to the length L: Q/t = k x A x (Th - Tc) / L, where k is the thermal conductivity of the material. Rearranged, k = Q x L / (A x t x (Th - Tc)). From this, thermal conductivity is defined as the quantity of heat that flows through one square metre of area of the substance in one second when a temperature difference of one kelvin is maintained across a thickness of one metre. Its SI unit is W/m K (J m^-1 K^-1 s^-1). Values range from 420 for silver and 390 for copper down to 0.6 for water, 0.04 for wool and 0.010 for styrofoam, which is why metals feel cold to touch and styrofoam is used for ice boxes.

Q: 3. Explain convection of heat and its mechanism. Explain any three of its practical applications.

Ans: Convection is the transfer of heat from one place to another by the bulk motion of a fluid (a liquid or a gas); it occurs only in fluids, never in solids, whose particles are fixed in place. Mechanism: when the lower part of a fluid is heated, that portion expands, becomes less dense and rises; the colder, denser fluid around it flows in to take its place, is heated in its turn, and also rises. In this way continuous circulatory currents, called convection currents, are set up, and every part of the fluid is heated in turn, as can be seen when potassium permanganate crystals colour the rising streaks in heated water. Practical applications (any three): (i) heating water in a kettle, where convection currents carry heat through the whole water; (ii) sea and land breezes, caused by the unequal heating of land and sea; (iii) the refrigerator, in which air cooled at the top freezer sinks and circulates cold air around the food; (iv) ventilation, in which warm stale air rises and escapes through ventilators near the ceiling while fresh cold air enters through doors and windows; (v) birds and gliders riding on rising thermal currents.

Q: 4. Explain radiation of heat and its mechanism. Describe any three of its practical applications.

Ans: Radiation is the transfer of heat from a hotter place to a colder place with or without a material medium in between; unlike conduction and convection it does not require any medium, which is how the Sun's heat reaches us through millions of kilometres of empty space. Mechanism: heat is transferred by electromagnetic waves. As an object warms up, its molecules vibrate harder, accelerating electric charges, and these emit electromagnetic radiation, mostly in the invisible infrared part of the spectrum at ordinary temperatures. Every object radiates continuously unless it is at absolute zero (0 K). The rate of transfer by radiation depends on the colour and texture of the surface (dull black surfaces are the best absorbers and the best emitters; a good absorber is a good radiator), on the surface temperature and on the surface area. Practical applications (any three): (i) the cooling fins at the back of a refrigerator are painted black so that they radiate and lose heat quickly; (ii) white clothes are worn in hot climates because white is a good reflector and poor absorber, while dark clothes are worn in cold climates; (iii) satellites such as the Hubble Space Telescope are wrapped in highly reflective metal foil to minimise temperature changes by radiation; (iv) the silvering of a thermos flask reflects radiant heat and keeps the contents hot or cold.

Q: 5. Discuss the greenhouse effect. Explain its importance and global warming concern.

Ans: The greenhouse effect is the process by which radiation from a planet's atmosphere warms the planet's surface to a temperature above what it would be without the atmosphere. Mechanism: the Earth receives energy from the Sun as ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared radiation; about 26% is reflected back to space by the atmosphere and clouds, about 19% is absorbed by the atmosphere and clouds, and more than 50% is absorbed at the Earth's surface. The surface, being much colder than the Sun, re-radiates this energy at much longer (infrared) wavelengths. Most of this thermal radiation is absorbed by greenhouse gases in the atmosphere (water vapour, carbon dioxide CO2, methane CH4 and ozone O3), and the atmosphere radiates energy both upwards and downwards; the downward part is absorbed by the surface, so the equilibrium temperature is higher than it would be with no atmosphere. Importance: the natural greenhouse effect keeps the Earth's surface about 33 deg C warmer than it would otherwise be; without it the average temperature would be well below the freezing point of water and life as we know it could not survive. Global warming concern: human activities, above all the burning of fossil fuels in factories and motor vehicles, have increased the amount of greenhouse gases, especially carbon dioxide, in the atmosphere (about half of the CO2 released is not absorbed by vegetation and the oceans). This strengthens the greenhouse effect: between 1880 and 2012 the global average temperature rose by 0.85 deg C. To reduce global warming we must decrease the emission of greenhouse gases and plant more vegetation to absorb the carbon dioxide produced.

mcqs.q: What is conduction of heat?
options: Transfer of heat by the bulk motion of a fluid
Transfer of heat by electromagnetic waves without any medium
Flow of heat through matter from places of higher temperature to places of lower temperature, without any movement of the matter as a whole
Transfer of heat only through the free electrons of a metal
mcqs.why: In conduction heat passes from particle to particle through matter while the matter itself does not move as a whole; bulk motion of a fluid is convection and transfer by waves without a medium is radiation.

mcqs.q: Why are metals the best conductors of heat?
options: Their atoms are loosely packed and far apart
They contain a large number of free electrons that gain kinetic energy in the hot part and transfer it rapidly to the colder part by collisions
They absorb more radiation than any other material
Their atoms do not vibrate at all when heated
mcqs.why: Besides atom-to-atom collisions, metals have many free electrons that move rapidly from the hot part to the cold part and transfer energy by collisions, an extra fast mechanism that non-metals, liquids and gases do not have.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the rate of flow of heat through a rod or slab?
options: Q/t = k x L x (Th - Tc) / A
Q/t = A x (Th - Tc) / (k x L)
Q/t = k x A x L x (Th - Tc)
Q/t = k x A x (Th - Tc) / L
mcqs.why: The rate of flow is directly proportional to the area A and the temperature difference (Th - Tc) and inversely proportional to the thickness L, so Q/t = k x A x (Th - Tc) / L, with k the thermal conductivity.

mcqs.q: Thermal conductivity is the heat flowing through 1 m^2 of a substance in 1 s when a temperature difference of 1 K is maintained across a thickness of 1 m. What is its SI unit?
mcqs.why: From k = Q x L / (A x t x (Th - Tc)), thermal conductivity has the SI unit W/m K, written also as J m^-1 K^-1 s^-1; it measures the ability of a substance to conduct heat energy.

mcqs.q: Which set of thermal conductivity values matches those given in Unit 9?
mcqs.why: Unit 9 gives the values in W/m K as silver 420 and copper 390 for metals, down to water 0.6, wool 0.04 and styrofoam 0.010, which is why metals feel cold to touch and styrofoam is used for ice boxes.

mcqs.q: In which materials can heat be transferred by convection?
options: Only in fluids, that is liquids and gases, and never in solids
mcqs.why: Convection is transfer of heat by the bulk motion of a fluid; it occurs only in liquids and gases because in solids the particles are fixed in place and cannot flow from one place to another.

mcqs.q: What sets up convection currents when the lower part of a fluid is heated?
options: The heated fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises, while colder denser fluid flows in to take its place and is heated in its turn
The heated fluid contracts, becomes denser and sinks to the bottom
Free electrons carry the heat from the bottom to the top
Electromagnetic waves push the fluid upward in streaks
mcqs.why: Heating makes that portion of fluid expand and become less dense so it rises, and the colder denser fluid around it flows in to take its place; these continuous circulatory convection currents heat every part of the fluid in turn.

mcqs.q: How does radiation bring the Sun heat to the Earth?
options: By conduction through the matter filling space
By convection currents flowing through space
By electromagnetic waves, mostly in the invisible infrared part of the spectrum, needing no material medium
By free electrons streaming from the Sun to the Earth
mcqs.why: Radiation transfers heat by electromagnetic waves emitted when vibrating molecules accelerate electric charges; it needs no medium, so the Sun heat crosses millions of kilometres of empty space, mostly as infrared at ordinary temperatures.

mcqs.q: Which statement about radiating surfaces is correct?
options: Highly polished surfaces are the best absorbers and the best emitters
A good absorber of radiation is always a poor radiator
White surfaces are the best emitters of radiation
Dull black surfaces are the best absorbers and the best emitters, and a good absorber is a good radiator
mcqs.why: The rate of radiation depends on the colour and texture of the surface: dull black surfaces absorb and emit best, a good absorber is a good radiator, and that is why refrigerator cooling fins are painted black to lose heat quickly.

mcqs.q: By how much does the natural greenhouse effect warm the Earth surface, and by how much did the global average temperature rise from 1880 to 2012?
options: About 33 deg C warmer, with a rise of 0.85 deg C
About 3.3 deg C warmer, with a rise of 8.5 deg C
About 33 deg C warmer, with a rise of 8.5 deg C
About 0.85 deg C warmer, with a rise of 33 deg C
mcqs.why: Without its atmosphere the Earth would be well below freezing; the natural greenhouse effect keeps the surface about 33 deg C warmer, while increased greenhouse gases from burning fossil fuels raised the global average temperature by 0.85 deg C between 1880 and 2012.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems and Assignments
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • All Unit 9 numericals use the conduction formula Q/t = k x A x (Th - Tc) / L, with thickness in metres and temperature difference in kelvin.
  • Assignment 9.1: concrete wall, A = 6.9 m^2, L = 0.20 m, Th - Tc = 15 K, k = 1.3 J/m s K gives a rate of 672.75 J/s and heat in one hour Q = 2.42 x 10^6 J.
  • Numerical 1: heat lost per second through wool clothing (A = 1.6 m^2, L = 2.0 x 10^-3 m, Th - Tc = 25 K, k = 0.04 W/m K) is 800 W, that is 8.0 x 10^2 W.
  • Numerical 2: rate of heat loss through a brick wall (A = 16 m^2, L = 0.3 m, Th - Tc = 20 K, k = 0.84 W/m K) is 896 W.
  • Numerical 3: heat conducted through window glass (A = 2.0 m^2, L = 4.0 mm = 4.0 x 10^-3 m, Th - Tc = 15 K, k = 0.8 W/m K) is 6000 W, flowing into the room because the outside at 35 deg C is hotter than the inside at 20 deg C.
  • Unit conversions used in Unit 9: 1 hour = 3600 s and 4.0 mm = 4.0 x 10^-3 m.

Solved Exercises

Assignment 9.1 — Concrete Wall 0.20 m Thick

Q: Find the amount of heat transferred in one hour through a concrete wall of area 6.9 m^2, and 0.20 m thick. One side of the wall is held at 20 deg C and the other side is at 5 deg C. The thermal conductivity of concrete is 1.3 J K^-1 m^-1 s^-1.

Ans: Given: area A = 6.9 m^2
Thickness L = 0.20 m
Hot side Th = 20 deg C, cold side Tc = 5 deg C, so Th - Tc = 15 K
Thermal conductivity k = 1.3 J/m s K
Time t = 1 hour = 3600 s
Formula: rate of flow of heat Q/t = k x A x (Th - Tc) / L
Substitution: Q/t = 1.3 x 6.9 x 15 / 0.20
Working: 1.3 x 6.9 = 8.97; 8.97 x 15 = 134.55; 134.55 / 0.20 = 672.75 J/s
Step: heat in one hour Q = 672.75 J/s x 3600 s = 2421900 J
Answer: 2.42 x 10^6 J

Q: Note on Assignment 9.1

Ans: The book's printed key gives 2.6 x 10^6 J; with the data printed in the question the rate is 1.3 x 6.9 x 15 / 0.20 = 672.75 J/s, which in 3600 s transfers 2.42 x 10^6 J, as solved above.

Exercise — Numerical Problems

Q: 1. A person's body is covered with 1.6 m^2 of wool clothing. The thickness of the wool is 2.0 x 10^-3 m. The temperature at the outside surface of the wool is 11 deg C, and the skin temperature is 36 deg C. How much heat per second does the person lose due to conduction? Thermal conductivity of wool is k = 0.04 W m^-1 K^-1.

Ans: Given: area A = 1.6 m^2
Thickness L = 2.0 x 10^-3 m
Skin temperature Th = 36 deg C, outside temperature Tc = 11 deg C, so Th - Tc = 25 K
Thermal conductivity of wool k = 0.04 W/m K
Formula: rate of flow of heat Q/t = k x A x (Th - Tc) / L
Substitution: Q/t = 0.04 x 1.6 x 25 / (2.0 x 10^-3)
Working: 0.04 x 1.6 = 0.064; 0.064 x 25 = 1.6; 1.6 / 0.002 = 800
Answer: 8.0 x 10^2 W (800 J/s)

Q: 2. The external wall of a brick house has an area of 16 m^2 and thickness 0.3 m. The temperatures inside and outside the house are respectively 20 deg C and 0 deg C. Calculate the rate of heat loss through the wall. Thermal conductivity of brick is k = 0.84 W m^-1 K^-1. [533 W]

Ans: Given: area A = 16 m^2
Thickness L = 0.3 m
Inside temperature Th = 20 deg C, outside temperature Tc = 0 deg C, so Th - Tc = 20 K
Thermal conductivity of brick k = 0.84 W/m K
Formula: rate of flow of heat Q/t = k x A x (Th - Tc) / L
Substitution: Q/t = 0.84 x 16 x 20 / 0.3
Working: 0.84 x 16 = 13.44; 13.44 x 20 = 268.8; 268.8 / 0.3 = 896
Answer: 896 W (8.96 x 10^2 W)

Q: Note on Numerical Problem 2

Ans: The book prints [533 W] with this question and repeats 533 W in its printed key; with the data printed in the question the rate is 0.84 x 16 x 20 / 0.3 = 896 W, as solved above, so the book's value does not follow from its own data.

Q: 3. Window glass has thermal conductivity of 0.8 W m^-1 K^-1. Calculate the rate at which heat is conducted through a window of area 2.0 m^2 and thickness 4.0 mm. The temperature inside an air-conditioned room is 20 deg C. The outdoors temperature is 35 deg C.

Ans: Given: area A = 2.0 m^2
Thickness L = 4.0 mm = 4.0 x 10^-3 m
Outside temperature Th = 35 deg C, inside temperature Tc = 20 deg C, so Th - Tc = 15 K (heat flows inward)
Thermal conductivity of glass k = 0.8 W/m K
Formula: rate of flow of heat Q/t = k x A x (Th - Tc) / L
Substitution: Q/t = 0.8 x 2.0 x 15 / (4.0 x 10^-3)
Working: 0.8 x 2.0 = 1.6; 1.6 x 15 = 24; 24 / 0.004 = 6000
Answer: 6.0 x 10^3 W (6000 J/s, flowing into the room)

mcqs.q: Assignment 9.1: What is the amount of heat transferred in one hour through a concrete wall of area 6.9 m^2 and thickness 0.20 m, with one side at 20 deg C, the other at 5 deg C and k = 1.3 J/m s K?
mcqs.why: Formula Q/t = k x A x (Th - Tc) / L. Substitution: Q/t = 1.3 x 6.9 x 15 / 0.20. Steps: 1.3 x 6.9 = 8.97; 8.97 x 15 = 134.55; 134.55 / 0.20 = 672.75 J/s. Heat in one hour: Q = 672.75 J/s x 3600 s = 2421900 J = 2.42 x 10^6 J. Note: the book printed key of 2.6 x 10^6 J is wrong; it does not follow from the data printed in the question.

mcqs.q: Assignment 9.1: What is the rate of flow of heat through the concrete wall (A = 6.9 m^2, L = 0.20 m, Th - Tc = 15 K, k = 1.3 J/m s K)?
mcqs.why: Formula Q/t = k x A x (Th - Tc) / L. Substitution: Q/t = 1.3 x 6.9 x 15 / 0.20. Steps: 1.3 x 6.9 = 8.97; 8.97 x 15 = 134.55; 134.55 / 0.20 = 672.75 J/s. Check: in 3600 s this rate transfers 672.75 x 3600 = 2421900 J = 2.42 x 10^6 J.

mcqs.q: Assignment 9.1: The wall has one side at 20 deg C and the other side at 5 deg C. What temperature difference (Th - Tc) is used in the formula?
mcqs.why: Temperature difference: Th - Tc = 20 deg C - 5 deg C = 15 K. Full working with this value: formula Q/t = k x A x (Th - Tc) / L = 1.3 x 6.9 x 15 / 0.20; steps 1.3 x 6.9 = 8.97, 8.97 x 15 = 134.55, 134.55 / 0.20 = 672.75 J/s, and Q in one hour = 672.75 x 3600 = 2421900 J = 2.42 x 10^6 J.

mcqs.q: Numerical 1: How much heat per second is lost by conduction through wool clothing of area 1.6 m^2 and thickness 2.0 x 10^-3 m, with skin at 36 deg C, outside surface at 11 deg C and k = 0.04 W/m K?
mcqs.why: Temperature difference Th - Tc = 36 - 11 = 25 K. Formula Q/t = k x A x (Th - Tc) / L. Substitution: Q/t = 0.04 x 1.6 x 25 / (2.0 x 10^-3). Steps: 0.04 x 1.6 = 0.064; 0.064 x 25 = 1.6; 1.6 / 0.002 = 800. Final result: 800 W, that is 8.0 x 10^2 W (800 J/s).

mcqs.q: Numerical 1: In the substitution Q/t = 0.04 x 1.6 x 25 / (2.0 x 10^-3) for the wool clothing, what is the value of the numerator 0.04 x 1.6 x 25?
mcqs.why: Numerator steps: 0.04 x 1.6 = 0.064, then 0.064 x 25 = 1.6. Full working: formula Q/t = k x A x (Th - Tc) / L with Th - Tc = 36 - 11 = 25 K; substitution Q/t = 0.04 x 1.6 x 25 / (2.0 x 10^-3) = 1.6 / 0.002 = 800. Final result: 800 W.

mcqs.q: Numerical 2: What is the rate of heat loss through a brick wall of area 16 m^2 and thickness 0.3 m, with inside temperature 20 deg C, outside temperature 0 deg C and k = 0.84 W/m K?
mcqs.why: Temperature difference Th - Tc = 20 - 0 = 20 K. Formula Q/t = k x A x (Th - Tc) / L. Substitution: Q/t = 0.84 x 16 x 20 / 0.3. Steps: 0.84 x 16 = 13.44; 13.44 x 20 = 268.8; 268.8 / 0.3 = 896. Final result: 896 W. Note: the book prints 533 W with this question, but that value is wrong and does not follow from the data printed in the question.

mcqs.q: Numerical 2: Which substitution correctly sets up the rate of heat loss through the brick wall (k = 0.84 W/m K, A = 16 m^2, Th - Tc = 20 K, L = 0.3 m)?
mcqs.why: Formula Q/t = k x A x (Th - Tc) / L, so k, A and (Th - Tc) are multiplied and divided by L: Q/t = 0.84 x 16 x 20 / 0.3. Steps: 0.84 x 16 = 13.44; 13.44 x 20 = 268.8; 268.8 / 0.3 = 896. Final result: 896 W.

mcqs.q: Numerical 3: At what rate is heat conducted through a window of area 2.0 m^2 and thickness 4.0 mm, with inside temperature 20 deg C, outdoors temperature 35 deg C and k = 0.8 W/m K for glass?
options: 600 W, flowing out of the room
6000 W, flowing out of the room
mcqs.why: Thickness L = 4.0 mm = 4.0 x 10^-3 m; temperature difference Th - Tc = 35 - 20 = 15 K. Formula Q/t = k x A x (Th - Tc) / L. Substitution: Q/t = 0.8 x 2.0 x 15 / (4.0 x 10^-3). Steps: 0.8 x 2.0 = 1.6; 1.6 x 15 = 24; 24 / 0.004 = 6000. Final result: 6000 W = 6.0 x 10^3 W, flowing into the room because the outdoors is hotter.

mcqs.q: Numerical 3: The window glass thickness is given as 4.0 mm. What is this thickness in metres, as needed in the formula?
mcqs.why: Conversion: 1 mm = 10^-3 m, so 4.0 mm = 4.0 x 10^-3 m = 0.004 m. Full working: temperature difference = 35 - 20 = 15 K; formula Q/t = k x A x (Th - Tc) / L; substitution Q/t = 0.8 x 2.0 x 15 / (4.0 x 10^-3); steps 0.8 x 2.0 = 1.6, 1.6 x 15 = 24, 24 / 0.004 = 6000. Final result: 6000 W into the room.

mcqs.q: Numerical 1: In the formula Q/t = k x A x (Th - Tc) / L for the wool clothing problem, what is the value of the thermal conductivity k?
mcqs.why: The givens are A = 1.6 m^2, L = 2.0 x 10^-3 m, Th - Tc = 36 - 11 = 25 K and k = 0.04 W/m K for wool. Full working: formula Q/t = k x A x (Th - Tc) / L; substitution Q/t = 0.04 x 1.6 x 25 / (2.0 x 10^-3); steps 0.04 x 1.6 = 0.064, 0.064 x 25 = 1.6, 1.6 / 0.002 = 800. Final result: 800 W.
